text: Which correctly describes a feature of Pacinian corpuscles compared to Meissner corpuscles?
explanation: In Pacinian corpuscles, the afferent fiber passes axially through the center, while in Meissner corpuscles the nerve fiber has a coiled (tortuous) course between lamellar cells.
keyConcept: Corpuscle structural differences
options: Pacinian detect light touch, Meissner detect vibration
Pacinian are mainly in non‑hairy skin, Meissner in hairy skin
Pacinian are in epidermis, Meissner in dermis
Pacinian detect temperature, Meissner detect pain
Pacinian have fibers that pass axially through the corpuscle, Meissner fibers are coiled
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: histology

text: Gamma motor neurons are found in which lamina of the spinal cord?
explanation: Gamma motor neurons are located in Rexed lamina IX of the anterior horn, innervating intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles.
keyConcept: Gamma motor neuron location
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding sensory receptors:
explanation: According to Müller's law of specific nerve energies, each receptor is specific to its adequate stimulus. Receptors have LOW threshold for their specific stimulus. Receptor potential is directly proportional to stimulus intensity, not inversely.
keyConcept: Law of specific nerve energies: each receptor responds only to its adequate stimulus at low threshold.
options: Receptors are non-specific to stimuli according to Muller’s law
Stimulation of certain receptors can produces different modalities of sensations
Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold
Receptor potential is inversely related to the intensity of stimulus according to Weber Fechner law
The same receptor may be stimulated by different stimuli to produce different sensations
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Oblique facial cleft is due to:
explanation: An oblique facial cleft results from failure of fusion between the lateral nasal fold and the maxillary swelling. This cleft runs from the upper lip toward the medial angle of the eye, following the nasolacrimal groove. Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between maxillary and medial nasal prominences.
keyConcept: Oblique facial cleft = failure of fusion between LATERAL NASAL FOLD and MAXILLARY SWELLING; follows nasolacrimal groove.
options: Failure of fusion of lingual swellings.
Failure of fusion of nasal septum and palate.
Failure of fusion of medial and lateral nasal folds.
Failure of fusion of lateral nasal fold and maxillary swelling.
Failure of fusion of medial nasal fold and maxillary swelling.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The hyoid bone is derived from:
explanation: The hyoid bone body is derived from migrating neural crest cells of the 2nd and 3rd pharyngeal arches. The lesser horn and upper body come from the 2nd arch; the greater horn and lower body come from the 3rd arch. This embryological origin explains the dual nerve supply (CN VII for 2nd arch structures, CN IX for 3rd arch structures).
keyConcept: Hyoid bone body derived from neural crest cells of 2nd and 3rd arches; lesser horn from 2nd, greater horn from 3rd.
options: Migrating neural crest cells of 1st & 2nd arches.
Migrating neural crest cells of 2nd & 3rd arches.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The roots of the brachial plexus pass between:
explanation: The roots of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) pass between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius muscles. This anatomical relationship is clinically important for thoracic outlet syndrome.
keyConcept: Brachial plexus roots emerge between anterior and middle scalene muscles before forming trunks.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Impairment of oxidative decarboxylation leads to inability to utilize glucose due to deficiency of which vitamin?
explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for oxidative decarboxylation reactions catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
keyConcept: Thiamine and glucose utilization
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which vitamin deficiency is neurologically affected by folic acid status – folic acid can mask hematological signs but not prevent neurological damage?
explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord; folic acid can mask the anemia but does not prevent neurological progression.
keyConcept: B12 neurological damage
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Clark’s nucleus (dorsal nucleus) is located in which lamina?
explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is located in Rexed lamina VII at T1-L2 levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus lamina
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which one of the following sensations has most of its fibers NOT synapsing in the spinal cord?
explanation: Fine touch and conscious proprioception from the upper limb (position sense) do not synapse in the spinal cord; their first order neurons pass directly to the dorsal column nuclei in the medulla.
keyConcept: Dorsal column sensations bypass spinal synapse
options: Sensation of pain of left lower limb.
Sensation of crude touch of right upper limb.
Sensation of position of left upper limb.
Sensation of temperature of left big toe.
Sensation of pain of left shoulder.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which statement about Clarke’s nucleus is correct?
explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is present at all thoracic levels (T1-L2) and is the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus distribution
options: Clarke’s nucleus is present at all levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all cervical levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all thoracic levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all lumbar levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all sacral levels
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: histology

text: Which stimulates pain receptors?
explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) respond to noxious stimuli including intense mechanical distortion, heat (>45C), and chemical irritants (bradykinin, substance P, prostaglandins).
keyConcept: Nociceptors are polymodal free nerve endings responding to mechanical, thermal, and chemical noxious stimuli.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Which accurately describes the pattern of dissociative sensory loss in syringomyelia?
explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss with loss of pain and temperature but preserved touch and proprioception due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central canal.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia selectively damages crossing spinothalamic fibers, causing cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function.
options: Loss of pain and touch with preservation of temperature
Loss of touch and temperature with preservation of pain
Loss of pain with preservation of touch and temperature
Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch
Loss of temperature with preservation of touch and pain
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: As regards lamina of spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
explanation: Lamina IV corresponds to the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus), not the reticular nucleus. The reticular nucleus corresponds to lamina V. Lamina II = substantia gelatinosa, lamina III = nucleus proprius, lamina VII includes Clarke's nucleus.
keyConcept: Lamina IV = nucleus proprius; lamina V = reticular nucleus
options: Lamina II - corresponds to substantia gelatinosa.
Lamina III - corresponds to main sensory nucleus.
Lamina IV - corresponds to reticular nucleus.
Lamina VIII - receives termination of extrapyramidal tracts.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: A 5-day-old child has been treated in the intensive care unit since birth. A sample of cerebral spinal fluid is required. Where would be the safest place to perform a lumbar puncture?
explanation: In a 5-day-old infant, the spinal cord ends at L3 (newborn level). Lumbar puncture below L3 (between L4 and L5) is safe because the spinal cord has already ended, avoiding risk of cord injury. In adults, the safe lumbar puncture level is L3-L4 or L4-L5. Needles below L3 in newborns avoid the terminated cord.
keyConcept: In newborns, spinal cord ends at L3; safest lumbar puncture = below L3 (e.g., L4-L5) to avoid cord injury.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Which lamina of the spinal cord corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa?
explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) corresponds to Rexed lamina II of the posterior horn, specializing in pain and temperature modulation.
keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa lamina
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text:
Which of the following statements concerning the general functional role of the cerebellum is correct?
A. The cerebellum directly stimulates motor neurons required to make a movement
B. The cerebellum is unable to make corrective adjustments to the movement once it is performed
C. The cerebellum does not receive feedback from muscles that execute the actual movement
D. The cerebellum is not involved in the planning of a movement, only its execution
E. The cerebellum plays an active role in the coordination of the muscles required to make a movement
explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity during movement through its internal models and predictive control, receiving proprioceptive feedback and making real-time adjustments, but does not directly stimulate motor neurons.
keyConcept: Cerebellum coordinates muscles during movement, doesn't directly stimulate motor neurons.
options: The cerebellum directly stimulates motor neurons required to make a movement
The cerebellum is unable to make corrective adjustments to the movement once it is performed
The cerebellum does not receive feedback from muscles that execute the actual movement
The cerebellum is not involved in the planning of a movement, only its execution
The cerebellum plays an active role in the coordination of the muscles required to make a movement
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: physiology

text: Regarding the cerebellum, which is NOT true:
explanation: The cerebellum has INDIRECT stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons via the red nucleus and thalamus, not direct. Option D is incorrect. Options A, B, C, E are all true: cerebellum helps plan and time movements, receives input from motor cortex, receives spindle/GTO input via spinocerebellar tracts, and predicts successive movements.
keyConcept: Cerebellar influence on motor neurons is indirect, acting through the red nucleus and thalamus to modulate cortical output.
options: Cerebellum helps in planning and timing of voluntary movements.
The cerebellum is stimulated by the motor cortex.
The receptor activity of the spindles and Golgi tendons organs reaches the cerebellum through the spinocerebellar tract.
The cerebellum has direct stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons.
The cerebellum predicts and plans for the successive movements
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text:
In lower motor neuron lesion, loss of superficial reflexes could be explained by the fact that:
A. These reflexes need intact corticospinal tract
B. These reflexes were suppressed by corticospinal tract
C. There is damage to the center of these reflexes
D. There is damage to the afferent of these reflexes
E. There is supraspinal inhibition of these reflexes
explanation: Superficial reflexes (abdominal, cremasteric) are polysynaptic reflexes whose centers are in the spinal cord; LMN damage eliminates the efferent limb of these reflexes.
keyConcept: Superficial reflex loss in LMN lesion: damage to reflex center.
options: These reflexes need intact corticospinal tract
These reflexes were suppressed by corticospinal tract
There is damage to the center of these reflexes
There is damage to the afferent of these reflexes
There is supraspinal inhibition of these reflexes
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture, the:
explanation: The median aperture (foramen of Magendie) drains CSF into the cisterna magna.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle communicates with subarachnoid space via lateral apertures of Luschka and median aperture of Magendie.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Martinoti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
explanation: Martinotti cells have axons directed UPWARDS (toward the cortical surface). Their dendrites extend laterally, cell bodies are multipolar (not rounded), and they use various neurotransmitters. They are inhibitory interneurons in the cortex.
keyConcept: Martinotti cells: cortical interneurons with ascending axons; deliver inhibitory signals to superficial layers.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: histology

text: At which anatomical level does the oculomotor nerve emerge?
explanation: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the midbrain on the anterior surface between the cerebral peduncles, just posterior to the posterior clinoid process.
keyConcept: CN III emerges from the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles on the anterior surface.
options: At the level of the superior midbrain colliculus
At the level of the inferior olivary nucleus
At the level of the pons
At the level of the medullary pyramids
At the level of the cerebellar peduncles
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT.
explanation: The superior colliculus has 4 layers (stratum zonale, stratum cinereum, stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci), not 5. The stratum basilare (basal layer) is not a recognized layer of the superior colliculus. It is part of the visual reflex pathway.
keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers (superficial to deep): zonale → cinereum → opticum → lemnisci. Not stratum basilare.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The biopsy of a ring-enhancing tumor in the left parietal lobe of a 60-year-old patient reveals an astrocytic tumor that displays marked cellular atypia, mitotic activity, areas of pseudopalisading necrosis & multifocal microvascular hyperplasia. The diagnosis is:
explanation: Ring-enhancing tumor with pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia is diagnostic of glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV). These features distinguish it from lower-grade astrocytomas.
keyConcept: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia = glioblastoma multiforme (grade IV)
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: histology

text: The facial colliculus is formed by:
explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve (motor root) that curve around it internally. These fibers form the facial nerve genu in the brainstem.
keyConcept: Facial colliculus formed by CN VI nucleus and CN VII fibers
options: Abducent nucleus and facial nerve fibers.
Facial motor nucleus and abducent nerve fibers.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Tympanic membrane is derived from:
explanation: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is derived from THREE germ layers: the outer ectoderm (skin of external ear), the middle fibrous layer (mesoderm), and the inner endoderm (tympanic cavity lining). It develops at the junction of the first pharyngeal cleft (ectoderm) and first pharyngeal pouch (endoderm).
keyConcept: Tympanic membrane derived from ECTODERM (outer), ENDODERM (inner), and MESODERM (middle fibrous layer).
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The thalamic nucleus for pain and temperature sensations of head is:
explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus is the specific relay center for pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the head (face, scalp, meninges, and oral cavity). It receives input from the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve via the trigeminal lemniscus.
keyConcept: VPM nucleus relays pain and temperature sensations specifically from the HEAD via trigeminal lemniscus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The thalamic nucleus that relays pain and temperature sensations from the head is the:
explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus receives somatosensory input specifically from the head and face. It receives the trigeminal lemniscus (carrying pain, temperature, and touch from the face) and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex. VPL handles the body; VPM handles the face.
keyConcept: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays pain, temperature, and touch sensations specifically from the HEAD and face.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following nuclei represents the somatic efferent column?
explanation: This matching tests nuclei: facial nucleus - facial muscles; nucleus ambiguus - pharyngeal muscles; dorsal motor nucleus of X - visceral organs. All are branchiomotor or visceral motor nuclei.
keyConcept: Facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Semantic memory refers to:
explanation: Semantic memory stores general facts, concepts, and knowledge independent of personal experience (declarative/explicit memory).
keyConcept: Semantic memory
options: Memory of facts and general knowledge
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The thalamic nucleus in which spinal & medial lemnisci terminate is:
explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus is the thalamic relay for somatosensory information from the body. Both the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch and proprioception from the body) and the spinal lemniscus (carrying pain and temperature from the body) terminate in the VPL nucleus.
keyConcept: VPL nucleus is where spinal lemniscus (pain/temp from body) and medial lemniscus (touch/proprioception from body) terminate.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The cranial part of the accessory nerve arises from
explanation: The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, carrying fibers that eventually join the vagus nerve to innervate laryngeal muscles.
keyConcept: Accessory nerve nucleus ambiguus origin
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The nucleus that receives taste fibers is:
explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and vertebral artery branches, not the anterior spinal artery.
keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries supply dorsal column nuclei
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which one of the following is NOT true regarding the cerebellum:
explanation: Cerebellar ataxia is sensory ataxia - it worsens with eye closure (positive Romberg). Option B is INCORRECT as stated. Actually, cerebellar ataxia is NOT sensory (sensory ataxia is dorsal column dysfunction). The correct answer is B because cerebellar ataxia is motor ataxia, characterized by clumsiness that is visible with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which hides behind visual compensation. Wait - re-reading: cerebellar ataxia is a motor (not sensory) ataxia that DOES NOT require visual compensation to demonstrate.
keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is a motor coordination deficit visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which requires eye closure to manifest.
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls movements of the ipsilateral muscles.
Cerebellar ataxia is a sensory ataxia.
Cerebellar lesions cause pendular knee jerks.
The intention tremor associated with cerebellar disease is worsened by movement.
The neocerebellar syndrome gait is zig-zag like.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: As regards the dorsal root fibers of spinal nerves, choose the CORRECT statement:
explanation: The dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar (not multipolar). The central processes (axons) of dorsal root ganglion cells enter the spinal cord and may ascend or descend to form long tracts. The peripheral processes (dendrites) connect to receptors.
keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar; central processes form ascending tracts
options: Cells of dorsal root ganglion are multipolar.
Central processes (dendrites) of dorsal root fibers are connected to receptors.
Dorsal root fibers give ascending fibers which form long tracts.
Dorsal root fibers give long descending fibers.
After entering spinal cord, dorsal root fibers give long fibers which form intersegmental tracts.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following foramina gives passage to emissary veins of the cavernous sinuses?
explanation: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery causes extradural hemorrhage. This arterial bleeding creates a biconvex/lens-shaped collection that can cause rapid deterioration due to arterial pressure.
keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery causes extradural hematoma
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced:
explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1–L2 in adults) to avoid cord injury. The needle is typically introduced at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.
keyConcept: Lumbar puncture performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5 to avoid conus medullaris
options: Below or above tip of 4th L spine.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Brown-Sequard syndrome is characterized by:
explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of vibration sense on the same side below lesion. Option A is correct. Hemisection causes ipsilateral dorsal column loss (vibration, proprioception) and corticospinal loss (motor) below; contralateral spinothalamic loss (pain, temperature). Options B, C, D are incorrect (motor loss is ipsilateral, reflex loss at lesion level is LMN, pain loss is contralateral).
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard hemisection produces ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
options: Loss of vibration sense on the same side below level of the lesion
Loss of voluntary movements on the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of reflex movements on the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of pain sensation on the same side below the level of the lesion
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: A reflex arc includes:
explanation: A reflex arc requires at minimum a sensory receptor, a sensory neuron, at least one synapse in the CNS, and an efferent motor neuron. This means at least two sets of sequential neurons (afferent and efferent).
keyConcept: Reflex arc components: receptor → afferent neuron → CNS integration → efferent neuron → effector.
options: At least two sets of sequential neurons
At least two sequential sets of central synapses
At least two types of sensory receptors
At least two types of efferent neurons
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Dentists avoid extraction in infection because of all the following Except:
explanation: Infection's acidic environment (low pH) DECREASES the unionized (active) fraction of local anesthetics, reducing their efficacy.
keyConcept: Infection's acidic environment reduces local anesthetic efficacy by decreasing the unionized (nerve-penetrating) form.
options: Infection decreases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.
Infection reduces crossing of local anesthetics inside nerve cell.
Infection increases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: Regarding Broca’s area, select the correct answer:
explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (not middle) and is a motor speech center (not sensory). It is present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) and is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not anterior cerebral artery.
keyConcept: Broca's area: motor speech center in inferior frontal gyrus of dominant hemisphere, supplied by MCA.
options: It is a sensory speech center
It is located in middle frontal gyrus
It is present in the dominant hemisphere
It is supplied by anterior cerebral artery
None of the above is correct
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced
explanation: In adults, lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (below L2 where spinal cord terminates); the needle passes through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, and arachnoid.
keyConcept: Lumbar puncture anatomical levels
options: Below or above tip of 4th lumbar spine
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: What is the role of Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
explanation: APP (Amyloid Precursor Protein) is sequentially cleaved by enzymes (secretases) to generate Aß peptide. Alpha-secretase cleaves APP first, then beta-secretase (BACE), then gamma-secretase releases Aß. Option A is CORRECT. B) APP generates Aß, not Tau; C) Not alpha-synuclein; D) Not prion protein. The amyloid cascade hypothesis: APP processing → Aß accumulation → plaques → inflammation → tau pathology → neuronal death. The answer is A - APP is cleaved to generate Aß, the main component of amyloid plaques in AD.
keyConcept: APP sequential cleavage by secretases generates Aß peptide, the amyloid plaque component in Alzheimer's disease.
options: APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to generate Aß.
APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to generate Tau protein.
APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to generate Alpha-synuclein.
APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to generate Prion protein.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: pathology

text: Greater wing of sphenoid shows all the following EXCEPT:
explanation: The greater wing of the sphenoid bone contains the superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum. However, foramen lacerum is NOT part of the greater wing—it is located at the junction of the petrous temporal and sphenoid body. Foramen lacerum transmits the internal carotid artery (its pteryoid segment) and is closed inferiorly by fibrocartilage.
keyConcept: Greater wing of sphenoid has: superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum. Foramen lacerum is at petrous-sphenoid junction, not part of greater wing.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Lesion of facial nerve at stylomastoid foramen leads to:
explanation: A lesion at stylomastoid foramen causes lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting all muscles on that side, including the forehead (loss of frontalis and orbicularis oculi).
keyConcept: Stylomastoid lesion: LMN facial paralysis (entire ipsilateral face).
options: Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Motor loss on the contralateral half of the face.
Motor loss on the ipsilateral half of face.
Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral half of soft palate.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The maxillary nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, passing from the middle cranial fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
keyConcept: Maxillary nerve exits via foramen rotundum.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Sleep, all are true EXCEPT:
explanation: Increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus PROMOTES wakefulness and arousal, not sleep. These nuclei are part of the ascending activating system.
keyConcept: Raphe magnus and locus coeruleus = wakefulness/REM-on neurons; NOT sleep centers.
options: It helps brain rest and brain plasticity.
It may be due to synaptic fatigue of RAS neurons.
It may be due to active inhibition of RAS by sleep centers.
It may be due to increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus brain stem nuclei.
It may be due to accumulation of sleep inducing lipids or peptide in the CSF.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Choose the correct order of CSF circulation:
explanation: CSF flows from lateral ventricles through interventricular foramina to third ventricle, then through cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle, and finally into subarachnoid space.
keyConcept: CSF flow: lateral -> third -> fourth -> subarachnoid space.
options: Third ventricle, lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, third ventricle, central canal.
Lateral ventricles, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Fourth ventricle, third ventricle, lateral ventricles, central canal.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: What are neurodegenerative diseases?
explanation: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by FUNCTION, not necessarily physical location. Example: Parkinson's affects dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra that form a functional circuit. Option A correctly states 'related by function, rather than physical location' - this is the definition. Option B says 'physical location' only - not accurate. Option C says 'function and physical location' - not precise. Option D says 'all neurons' - incorrect (neurodegenerative diseases are selective). The answer is A. Examples: Alzheimer's (cholinergic neurons), Parkinson's (dopaminergic neurons), Huntington's (GABAergic neurons) - all functionally related.
keyConcept: Neurodegenerative diseases selectively destroy neurons that share functional characteristics, not necessarily physical proximity.
options: Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by function, rather than physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by function and physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of all neurons.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: pathology

text: The nucleus is:
explanation: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the CNS. A ganglion is the equivalent in the PNS. Nerve fibers form tracts or nerves, not nuclei.
keyConcept: Nucleus = cluster of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS
options: A group of cell bodies within peripheral nervous system.
A group of cell bodies within central nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within peripheral nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within central nervous system.
A collection of nerve fibers in brain stem.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is purely sensory?
explanation: The dorsal root of the spinal nerve is purely sensory, containing afferent fibers from the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor/efferent. The mixed spinal nerve trunk and its rami contain both sensory and motor fibers.
keyConcept: Dorsal root = purely sensory
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Posterior column is ........ while lateral, anterior is............
explanation: The posterior column carries only ascending (sensory) fibers, while both lateral and anterior columns contain mixed ascending and descending fibers.
keyConcept: Spinal column fiber types
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The main benefit of adding carbidopa to levodopa in Sinemet is that carbidopa:
explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, preventing peripheral levodopa conversion and increasing CNS availability.
keyConcept: Carbidopa mechanism
options: Inhibits peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which characteristic is true of *Listeria monocytogenes*?
explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
keyConcept: Listeria cold tolerance
options: It is strictly a human pathogen.
It can grow at refrigerator temperature (4°C).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: In the urea cycle, which two compounds are end products (released from the cycle)?
explanation: The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.
keyConcept: Urea cycle products
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following releases free ammonia in the body?
explanation: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.
keyConcept: Ammonia production
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which statement about ester local anesthetics is false?
explanation: Ester local anesthetics are MORE liable to cause allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite, not less.
keyConcept: Ester local anesthetic allergy
options: They are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases.
Procaine is a member of this group.
They are shorter acting than amides.
They are less liable to induce allergy.
They are less liable to systemic toxicity than amides.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Lateral medullary syndrome includes the following Except:
explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome includes vestibular symptoms (vertigo, nystagmus) due to involvement of the vestibular nuclei. This is a key feature that distinguishes Wallenberg syndrome from medial medullary syndrome.
keyConcept: Lateral medullary includes vestibular symptoms
options: Ipsilateral paralysis of palate, pharynx & larynx.
Contralateral pain & temperature loss from face.
Ipsilateral loss of taste of posterior 1/3 of tongue.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: clinical

text:
Semantic memory is characterized by which of the following?
A. It is the memory of personal events
B. A type of implicit memory
C. It is the memory of facts
D. It is non-declarative memory
E. It is a procedural memory
explanation: Semantic memory is explicit/declarative memory for facts and knowledge about the world (general facts), distinct from episodic memory (personal events) and procedural memory (skills).
keyConcept: Semantic memory: memory of facts (general knowledge).
options: It is the memory of personal events
It is the memory of facts
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: What is phenylketonuria?
explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
keyConcept: PKU phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency
options: A condition caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin reductase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin biosynthesis
A condition caused by a deficiency of homocystinuria
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: What is maple syrup urine disease?
explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and their ketoacids.
keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain dehydrogenase deficiency
options: A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in phenylalanine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tyrosine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tryptophan catabolism
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: What is the treatment for maple syrup urine disease?
explanation: MSUD treatment requires lifelong restriction of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in diet, with careful monitoring of amino acid levels to prevent neurological damage.
keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain amino acid restriction
options: A diet low in branched-chain amino acids
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: In the urea cycle, which aminoacids should be transported between the mitochondria and the cytosol in either direction?
explanation: Ornithine must be transported from mitochondria to cytosol (where it combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline), and citrulline must travel back to mitochondria for the next step. This mitochondrial-cytosolic transport is essential for urea cycle function.
keyConcept: Mitochondrial-cytosolic transport of ornithine and citrulline
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The enzyme dopamine beta-oxidase (hydroxylase) which catalyzes conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine requires:
explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor for the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. The enzyme also contains copper. This is why ascorbate deficiency can impair catecholamine synthesis.
keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as cofactor
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The defective enzyme in histidinemia is:
explanation: Histidinemia is caused by a deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), which normally converts histidine to urocanic acid. This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder presenting with intellectual disability and speech defects.
keyConcept: Histidase deficiency causes histidinemia (histidine ammonia-lyase)
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The nitrogen atoms of urea are derived from which sources?
explanation: Urea contains two nitrogen atoms: one from ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase reaction).
keyConcept: Urea nitrogen sources
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which vitamin is required for one‑carbon transfer reactions involved in nucleotide synthesis?
explanation: Folic acid (as N5, N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate) provides one-carbon units for thymidylate synthase and purine synthesis reactions in nucleotide biosynthesis.
keyConcept: Folate in nucleotide synthesis
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Lateral column lies between:
explanation: The lateral column lies between the anterior and posterior columns, containing ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.
keyConcept: Lateral column location
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following can be found in a patient diagnosed with syringomyelia?
explanation: Syringomyelia damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution over upper limbs and chest.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia presentation
options: loss of pain and temperature in the upper limbs and chest.
loss of touch in the upper limbs and chest
loss of pain and temperature in the abdomen and lower limbs
loss of touch in the abdomen and lower limbs
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Loss of proprioception on the same side of a lesion with loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side is characteristic of which condition?
explanation: This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome where ipsilateral proprioception (dorsal column) is lost with contralateral pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic) due to hemisection of the spinal cord.
keyConcept: Ipsilateral proprioception + contralateral pain loss indicates hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome).
options: Complete spinal cord transection at C4
Complete spinal cord transection at T5
Complete spinal cord transection at T8
Complete spinal cord transection at T12
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which statement is true regarding deep pressure sensation?
explanation: Deep pressure sensation is transmitted by A-beta fibers via dorsal column pathways and by A-delta fibers via spinothalamic tracts. It has a high threshold compared to light touch.
keyConcept: Deep pressure uses A-beta fibers in dorsal columns and A-delta fibers in spinothalamic tracts.
options: It is mediated by slowly adapting receptors
It is transmitted only by free nerve endings
It adapts rapidly to sustained stimulus
It is carried exclusively by Aδ fibers
It is not associated with vibration
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Anterior external arcuate fibres connect:
explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Posterior external arcuate fibres connect:
explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Posterior external arcuate fibers
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Accessory cuneate nucleus give rise to:
explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: histology

text: After falling down from a staircase, a young woman is found to have loss of voluntary movement on the right side of the body and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side below the mid thoracic region. The probable site of lesion is:
explanation: Transection of the right half of spinal cord in upper thoracic region. Option A is correct. Right hemiplegia (right voluntary movement loss) and left pain/temperature loss indicate right Brown-Sequard syndrome. The motor fibers decussate at the cervicomedullary junction, so hemisection causes ipsilateral motor loss below the lesion.
keyConcept: Ipsilateral motor paralysis with contralateral pain/temperature loss indicates hemisection on the side of motor deficits.
options: Transection of the right half of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of the left side of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of sensory and motor pathways on the right side of the pons
Transection of the left half of the spinal cord in the lumbar region
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: physiology

text: Which correctly describes the difference between tramadol and morphine?
explanation: Tramadol is a mixed mechanism analgesic with both mu-opioid agonist activity and inhibition of serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake, unlike pure morphine.
keyConcept: Tramadol vs morphine
options: Tramadol is a mixed opioid–nonopioid analgesic that increases serotonin and norepinephrine, while morphine is a pure opioid agonist
Tramadol is a pure opioid agonist, morphine is mixed
Both act only on μ receptors
Morphine increases serotonin and norepinephrine, tramadol does not
Tramadol has no effect on opioid receptors
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: How is L-Dopa converted to dopamine?
explanation: L-Dopa is converted to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA decarboxylase), also called DOPA decarboxylase. This enzyme requires pyridoxine (B6) as cofactor. The reaction occurs in the brain (after L-dopa crosses BBB) and in peripheral tissues.选项A正确. The answer is A. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral conversion, allowing more L-dopa to reach the brain.
keyConcept: DOPA decarboxylase converts levodopa to dopamine - carbidopa inhibits this peripheral conversion.
options: L-Dopa is decarboxylated by the central dopa decarboxylase enzyme to dopamine (DA) in the dopaminergic neurons
L-Dopa is converted to dopamine by MAO-B
L-Dopa is converted to dopamine by COMT
L-Dopa is converted to dopamine by aldehyde dehydrogenase
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: A lesion of mandibular nerve immediately after its exit from foramen oval may lead to:
explanation: Lesion of mandibular nerve immediately after foramen ovale causes: sensory loss in face/teeth/tongue, motor loss in muscles of mastication, and paralysis of tensor tympani/stapedius.选项E正确. The answer is E. All functions of V3 would be lost.
keyConcept: Foramen ovale V3 lesion: loss of facial sensation, mastication muscles, tensor tympani - complete V3 deficit.
options: Loss of taste sensation from anterior part of tongue.
Loss of general sensations from posterior part of tongue.
Loss of sensation of lower lip.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding servocomparator function of the cerebellum:
explanation: Cerebellum compares intended plan with actual movement (servocomparator function). Option B is correct. The cerebellum receives copies of motor commands (efference copy) and actual movement feedback, comparing them to correct ongoing movements. Options A, C, D are wrong: cerebellum sends indirect (via thalamus) not direct messages; receives unconscious (not conscious) proprioception; receives plan from cortex not basal ganglia.
keyConcept: The cerebellum acts as a servocomparator, matching intended movement with actual execution through continuous feedback.
options: Cerebellum sends direct corrective messages to muscles.
Cerebellum compares the intended plan of movement with the actual movement.
Cerebellum receives feedback information from muscles through conscious proprioceptive receptors.
Cerebellum receives a copy of plan of movement from basal ganglia.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Which vitamins are directly required for the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine?
explanation: Homocysteine remethylation to methionine requires methyltetrahydrofolate (from folic acid) as methyl donor and methionine synthase (which needs B12).
keyConcept: Homocysteine remethylation
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: biochem

text: A 33-year-old male presents with seizures, MRI shows an ill-defined area of infiltrative tumor expanding the frontal lobe. Biopsy of this lesion shows glial tissue with slightly increased cellularity and mild nuclear pleomorphism. No mitotic activity, no necrosis & no vascular proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Grade II astrocytomas show increased cellularity, mild nuclear pleomorphism, but no mitotic activity, necrosis, or vascular proliferation. They are diffuse astrocytomas in young adults, slower growing than anaplastic or GBM.
keyConcept: Grade II astrocytoma: slightly increased cellularity, mild pleomorphism, no necrosis/mitosis
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: Functions of the limbic system do NOT include:
explanation: Olfactory perception and discrimination is primarily a function of the olfactory bulb and temporal lobe, not the limbic system. The limbic system controls feeding, maternal/sexual behaviors, emotions, water balance, and motivations.
keyConcept: Limbic functions: emotions, motivation, feeding, sexual behavior, memory. Olfaction: olfactory bulb/piriform cortex.
options: Control of feeding, maternal & sexual behaviors.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: physiology

text: A 26-year-old man presents with spinal cord injury. Neurological examination reveals motor weakness of his left lower limb and loss of pinprick sensation on the right side of his body from the C8 dermatome downward. Which of the following might be an associated finding in this patient?
explanation: This is Brown-Sequard syndrome: left motor weakness (ipsilateral corticospinal tract lesion) and right pinprick loss (contralateral spinothalamic tract lesion, which crosses at the spinal cord level). The Babinski sign: dorsiflexion (upgoing) of the great toe on plantar stimulation indicates UMN lesion on the LEFT side. Plantar flexion would be a normal (flexor) response or indicate LMN lesion.
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral motor + contralateral pain/temperature loss. Left motor loss + right pinprick loss = LEFT cord hemisection. Left Babinski sign (dorsiflexion).
options: Plantar flexion of right great toe on plantar stimulation
Plantar flexion of left great toe on plantar stimulation
Dorsiflexion of right great toe on plantar stimulation
Dorsiflexion of left great toe on plantar stimulation
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: anatomy

text: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for headache and ataxia over the last 2 months. A CT scan reveals a midline partially cystic cerebellar mass, microscopic examination shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with fibrillar processes and Rosenthal fibers. The diagnosis is:
explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I) shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers and fibrillar processes. It is benign, cystic, midline cerebellar tumor in children with good prognosis.
keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: Rosenthal fibers, bipolar astrocytes, cystic cerebellar tumor
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: histology

text: What is dementia?
explanation: Dementia is defined as the development of memory impairment and other cognitive deficits severe enough to DECREASE the affected person's capacity to function at the previous level, despite a NORMAL level of consciousness. Key points: 1) Memory AND other cognitive deficits; 2) Functional impairment (decreased capacity); 3) NORMAL consciousness (distinguishes from delirium). Option A matches this definition exactly. Option B adds 'altered level of consciousness' - that's delirium, not dementia. Option C says 'increase capacity' - wrong. Option D adds 'hallucinations' and 'altered consciousness' - not the core definition. The answer is A. Delirium differs from dementia by altered consciousness and acute onset.
keyConcept: Dementia is cognitive decline with functional impairment but NORMAL consciousness - distinguishing it from delirium.
options: The development of memory impairment and other cognitive deficits severe enough to decrease the affected person's capacity to function at the previous level despite a normal level of consciousness.
The development of memory impairment and other cognitive deficits severe enough to decrease the affected person's capacity to function at the previous level with an altered level of consciousness.
The development of memory impairment and other cognitive deficits severe enough to increase the affected person's capacity to function at the previous level despite a normal level of consciousness.

The development of memory impairment and other cognitive deficits severe enough to decrease the affected person's capacity to function at the previous level with an altered level of consciousness and hallucinations.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: pathology

text: What is the crucial event in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
explanation: The crucial event in AD pathogenesis is accumulation of Beta Amyloid Peptide (Aß) in the brain. Aß is derived from APP (amyloid precursor protein) via proteolytic cleavage by beta-secretase and gamma-secretase. Aß 1-42 is particularly prone to aggregation and forms the amyloid plaques. Option A is CORRECT. B) Tau protein accumulation is also important (forms neurofibrillary tangles) but Aß accumulation is considered the initiating/crucial event. C) Alpha-synuclein is seen in Parkinson's disease (Lewy bodies). D) Prion protein is in prion diseases. The answer is A - Aß accumulation is the key initiating event in AD pathogenesis.
keyConcept: Beta-amyloid accumulation is the crucial initiating event in Alzheimer's disease, leading to plaque formation and neuronal dysfunction.
options: The accumulation of Beta Amyloid Peptide (Aß) in the brain over time.
The accumulation of Tau protein in the brain over time.
The accumulation of Alpha-synuclein in the brain over time.
The accumulation of Prion protein in the brain over time.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: pathology

text: The scalp is:
explanation: The scalp is: 5 layers (SCALP), highly vascular, innervated by multiple nerves, and the danger lies in the loose areolar layer connecting to intracranial sinuses.选项C正确. The answer is C. Infection can spread to meninges via this layer.
keyConcept: Scalp has 5 layers - loose areolar tissue is the 'dangerous' layer connecting to intracranial venous sinuses.
options: Supplied by the great auricular nerve in front of the auricle.
Supplied by the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries branches of the facial artery.
Supplied posteriorly by the greater occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
Supplied behind the auricle by the lesser occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
Drained by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, which unite to form the superior ophthalmic vein.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The aqueduct of Sylvius connects which of the following ventricular structures?
explanation: The aqueduct of Sylvius connects the third ventricle (above) to the fourth ventricle (below) in the midbrain. It passes through the cerebral peduncle.
keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles, passing through the midbrain.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: A 10-year-old girl develops ataxia & hydrocephalus. CT scan shows a midline partially cystic cerebellar mass. Microscopic examination shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with fibrillar processes and Rosenthal fibers. The diagnosis is:
explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I) in children shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers and fibrillary processes. These are benign, often cystic cerebellar tumors with good prognosis.
keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: Rosenthal fibers, bipolar astrocytes, cystic cerebellar tumor in children
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: histology

text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: The superior colliculus has layers: stratum zonale (superficial), stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci, and stratum basale (deep). The dorsal tegmental tract is a fiber tract, not part of the colliculus structure.
keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers: zonale, opticum, lemnisci, basale (NOT dorsal tegmental tract)
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: histology

text: Describe the gross pathology of Ependymomas.
explanation: Ependymomas appear as: well-demarcated, grayish-red masses that may be solid or cystic. They may have areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. Intracranial ependymomas often fill the ventricle; spinal ependymomas are intramedullary. The answer is A. The well-circumscribed nature allows for surgical resection.
keyConcept: Ependymomas are well-demarcated masses - intracranial tumors fill ventricles, spinal tumors are intramedullary.
options: Ependymomas are well-circumscribed tumors that are soft and spongy
Ependymomas are highly vascular with necrosis
Ependymomas are mucinous with myxoid stroma
Ependymomas are often cystic with a mural nodule
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: pathology

text: Anterior column lies between:
explanation: The anterior column lies between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neurons for voluntary movement.
keyConcept: Anterior column location
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: The thalamic nucleus that shares in formation of limbic system is:
explanation: The dorsomedial (mediodorsal) nucleus of the thalamus is reciprocally connected with the prefrontal cortex and is a key component of the limbic system. It is involved in cognitive functions, emotion, and memory. It receives input from the hypothalamus and limbic structures, and projects to the prefrontal cortex.
keyConcept: Dorsomedial nucleus is limbic-related; connects with prefrontal cortex for cognition and emotion.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The cisterna magna of subarachnoid space is a name given to the:
explanation: The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern located between the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.
keyConcept: Cisterna magna location
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Choose the correct statement about the sensory homunculus:
explanation: The sensory homunculus represents the body upside-down (inverted) in the postcentral gyrus, with larger representations for areas with higher receptor density like lips and fingertips.
keyConcept: Sensory homunculus: body represented upside-down in postcentral gyrus.
options: It is the body representation within the motor cortex.
Somatosensory cortex corresponds point by point with regions in ipsilateral side of the body.
The body is represented upside down.
The body representation depends on the size of the target part.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Emissary veins of cavernous sinus pass through all the following foramina Except:
explanation: Emissary veins from the cavernous sinus pass through the foramen lacerum, foramen ovale, and emissary sphenoidal foramen (foramen of Vesalius) to connect with the pterygoid venous plexus. The mastoid foramen, however, transmits an emissary vein connecting the sigmoid sinus to the posterior auricular veins, not the cavernous sinus. Therefore, mastoid foramen is not a route for cavernous sinus emissary veins.
keyConcept: Mastoid foramen connects sigmoid sinus to extracranial veins, not cavernous sinus emissary veins.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Posterior column lies between:
explanation: The posterior (dorsal) column lies between the posterior median septum and the posterior horn, carrying proprioception and fine touch sensation.
keyConcept: Posterior column location
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Dorsal spinocerebellar enters cerebellum through ............. while ventral spinocerebellar through.............
explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle while the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Cerebellar peduncle entries
options: Superior cerebellar peduncle, inferior cerebellar peduncle
inferior cerebellar peduncle, superior cerebellar peduncle
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Arterial supply of the speech areas is from:
explanation: The speech areas (Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus and Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus) are supplied by the middle cerebral artery. The MCA also supplies the motor cortex for the face and hand. Broca's area is typically dominant in the left hemisphere for language function.
keyConcept: Middle cerebral artery supplies speech areas (Broca's and Wernicke's areas).
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The two bones that develop from the 1st pharyngeal arch are:
explanation: The two bones that develop from the 1st pharyngeal arch are the malleus and incus. Meckel's cartilage (1st arch cartilage) forms the malleus and incus; the mandible develops from membranous ossification around Meckel's cartilage. The stapes, styloid process, and hyoid are 2nd arch derivatives.
keyConcept: Malleus and incus are the two ear ossicles derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Middle meningeal artery supplies dura of:
explanation: The middle meningeal artery supplies the dura mater of the cranial vault (convexities), not the cranial base. The base of the skull dura is supplied by branches from the vertebral, ascending pharyngeal, and other arteries.
keyConcept: Middle meningeal supplies vault dura, not base
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which statement is true regarding the layers of the cerebral cortex?
explanation: The outer band of Baillarger (optic radiation fibers) is found in the inner granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex, while the inner band is in layer V.
keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers
options: The outer band of Baillarger is present in the inner granular layer
The inner band of Baillarger is present in the molecular layer
The molecular layer contains large pyramidal cells
The inner granular layer lacks stellate cells
The multiform layer is the most superficial layer

subject: histology

text: Concerning speech, all are true EXCEPT:
explanation: Anomic aphasia is due to lesion in the angular gyrus (not auditory cortex), which connects visual, auditory, and tactile information. The patient can comprehend but cannot name objects. Broca's aphasia is characterized by sparse, effortful speech, not excessive speech.
keyConcept: Anomic aphasia: angular gyrus lesion; can't name objects despite comprehension.
options: Sensory aphasia occurs due to defect in visual association area, auditory association area or Wernicke’s area.
Expressive aphasia occurs due to lesion in Broca’s area or Exner’s area.
Anomic aphasia is due to lesion in and around auditory cortex.
In anomic aphasia, the patient cannot give name for seen pictures and words.
Aphasia occurs only in case of lesion in the categorical hemisphere.
