text: A patient with a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle (midbrain) would present with:
explanation: Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle lesion
options: Loss of fine touch on the left side of the body
Loss of pain sensation on the right side
Skeletal motor loss on the entire left side
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Inner Pyramidal cells are present in layer …. of cerebral cortex:
explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called Betz cells when giant) are found in layer V of the motor cortex, not in layers I-IV. Layer V is the internal pyramidal layer. The options I-IV are incorrect - inner pyramidal refers to layer V.
keyConcept: Layer V (internal pyramidal): Betz cells, corticospinal neurons. Layer IV: thalamocortical input.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: histology

text: Which part of the brain controls motor function of the right leg?
explanation: The leg area of the primary motor cortex is located on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, controlling the contralateral lower limb.
keyConcept: Motor control of the leg is represented medially in the paracentral lobule of the primary motor cortex.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is an absolute requirement for the brain at all times?
explanation: The brain absolutely requires glucose and oxygen at all times; it cannot use fatty acids as an energy source and depends almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for ATP production.
keyConcept: Brain absolute glucose requirement
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: biochem

text: Luschka connects which two structures?
explanation: The foramina of Luschka (lateral apertures) connect the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space at the cerebellopontine angle, allowing CSF to exit the ventricular system.
keyConcept: Luschka apertures are lateral openings of fourth ventricle to subarachnoid space.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding dysarthria, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
explanation: Dysarthria due to Wernicke's area lesion would cause receptive aphasia, not dysarthria. Wernicke's area controls language comprehension. Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder affecting articulation due to UMN/LMN lesions to speech muscles, not a cortical language area lesion.
keyConcept: Dysarthria = motor speech disorder (articulation); Wernicke's area = receptive aphasia (comprehension).
options: It is a speech abnormality due to defect in articulation.
It occurs in UMNL & LMNL affecting speech muscles.
Is of slow monotonous type in Parkinsonism.
Is of spastic type due to lesion in Wernicke’s area.
Is of ataxic staccato type in neocerebellar syndrome
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: physiology

text:
To management of rabies, which of the following must use 

A) Active immunization 
B) Passive immunization
explanation: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) includes both active and passive immunization. A) Active immunization - rabies vaccine (inactivated virus) stimulates antibody production; B) Passive immunization - rabies immune globulin (RIG) provides immediate antibodies. Both are needed because vaccines take 2 weeks to generate antibodies while RIG provides immediate protection. The answer is C - both A and B. Standard PEP: wound cleaning, RIG (infiltrated around wound), and 4-dose vaccine series.
keyConcept: Rabies PEP requires both vaccine (active) and immune globulin (passive) immunity for complete protection.
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text: Anterior column is present between:
explanation: The anterior column is located between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neuron pools.
keyConcept: Anterior column boundaries
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which cranial nerve nucleus contains both general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA) fibers?
explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla contains both GVA (visceral sensation including baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input) and SVA (taste) fibers, making it unique in having both modalities.
keyConcept: Solitary nucleus processes both visceral afferent and special visceral afferent (taste) information.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A female patient has reduced pain and temperature sense in upper limbs and chest but her sense of tactile discrimination is perfectly normal in these areas. State which tract/tracts is/are involved and name the disease.
explanation: Syringomyelia damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved tactile discrimination.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia mechanism
options: Lateral spinothalamic and gracile – Tabes dorsalis.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of form and texture) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway for fine touch and proprioception to reach the sensory cortex.
keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioception for object recognition.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Arterial supply of anterior ends of caudate & lentiform nuclei is derived from:
explanation: Anterior cerebral artery central branches supply anterior portions of caudate nucleus and lentiform nucleus, forming lenticulostriate arteries that also supply internal capsule.
keyConcept: Anterior cerebral central branches
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Sensory impulses from spindles of a stretched muscle could antagonistic muscles by:
explanation: Sensory impulses from muscle spindles activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that inhibit alpha motor neurons of antagonistic muscles. This is the basis of reciprocal inhibition during voluntary movement.
keyConcept: Reciprocal inhibition: spindle afferents activate inhibitory interneurons that suppress antagonist motor neurons.
options: Directly inhibiting γ-motor neurons of the antagonistic muscles
Directly inhibiting the α -motor neurons of the antagonistic musce
Inhibiting the transmitter release from the central terminals of afferents from the spindles of the antagonistic muscles
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: physiology

text: The special visceral efferent column of nuclei:
explanation: This matching tests nucleus functions: hypoglossal - tongue movement; nucleus ambiguus - swallowing/phonation; dorsal motor X - parasympathetic to viscera; vestibular - balance; cochlear - hearing.
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus involved in swallowing and speech
options: Supplies muscles derived from pharyngeal arches.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The nerve to the pterygoid canal is formed by the union of which nerves?
explanation: The nerve to the pterygoid canal (Vidian's nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
keyConcept: Vidian's nerve joins parasympathetic (greater petrosal) and sympathetic (deep petrosal) fibers to the pterygoid canal.
options: Auriculotemporal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve and lesser petrosal nerve
Deep petrosal nerve and chorda tympani
Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
Auricular branch of vagus and glossopharyngeal nerve
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei has a motor function?
explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) thalamic nucleus is the primary motor relay nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellum (via dentatothalamic tract) and basal ganglia (via medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the motor cortex. It helps coordinate voluntary movement planning and execution.
keyConcept: Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the motor relay nucleus of the thalamus; receives cerebellar and basal ganglia input.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei is related to the limbic system?
explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus is a key component of the limbic system Papez circuit, which includes the hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, and cingulate gyrus. It receives input from the hippocampus via the fornix and mammillothalamic tract, and projects to the cingulate gyrus, playing a central role in emotion and memory.
keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus is part of Papez circuit (limbic system); connected to hippocampus and cingulate gyrus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Arterial supply of upper 1/2 of internal capsule is derived from:
explanation: Upper half of internal capsule is supplied by central branches of anterior cerebral artery; lower half receives branches from anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries.
keyConcept: Internal capsule upper half supply
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to be due to streptococcal Agalactiae in a 55‑year‑old patient?
explanation: For a 55‑year‑old patient with suspected GBS meningitis, empiric coverage includes vancomycin (for DRSP), ceftriaxone, and ampicillin (to cover GBS and Listeria monocytogenes in patients >50 years).
keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage in elderly requires ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes and GBS in addition to standard vancomycin and ceftriaxone.
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: pharma

text: Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to streptococcal agalactia in 55 year old patient?
explanation: For meningitis suspected of Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep) in a 55-year-old, vancomycin (for resistant pneumococcus) plus ceftriaxone is empiric coverage. Ampicillin is added for Listeria in elderly, but the primary coverage is vancomycin + ceftriaxone.
keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage in elderly: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone (for resistant Strep)
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: pharma

text: Which type of fibers are carried by the Edinger-Westphal nucleus?
explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus contains preganglionic parasympathetic (visceral efferent) fibers that travel with the oculomotor nerve (III) to the ciliary ganglion, innervating the ciliary and pupillary sphincter muscles.
keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic fibers to intraocular muscles via CN III.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Sympathetic Nuclei is present in:
explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn from thoracic to upper 2 lumbar segments (T1-L2).
keyConcept: Sympathetic outflow
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following nuclei has motor function?
explanation: The anteromedial nucleus (in the anterior horn) has motor function, containing motor neuron pools for axial and proximal limb muscles.
keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Concerning synapses:
explanation: Chemical synapses are widely distributed in the CNS, not rare. Electric synapses are characterized by rapid transmission without delay, are bidirectional (not unidirectional), and do not use gap junctions in the typical chemical synaptic cleft.
keyConcept: Chemical synapses: neurotransmitter-based, drug-sensitive, unidirectional, wide distribution in CNS.
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs & chemicals
In chemical synapses, gap junction conduct impulses between presynaptic & postsynaptic structure
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which of the following is a normal flow of nitrogen in human metabolism?
explanation: Valine (amino acid) transaminated to alanine, alanine transaminated to glutamate, glutamate deaminated to release ammonia, and ammonia enters the urea cycle. This describes normal nitrogen flow from amino acid catabolism to urea excretion.
keyConcept: Valine to alanine to glutamate to urea represents normal nitrogen flow
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which enzymatic change explains the slow rate of glycolysis in neurons?
explanation: Neurons have reduced PFK-2/FBPase3 activity, resulting in low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, which inhibits glycolysis and makes neurons dependent on oxidative metabolism.
keyConcept: Neuronal glycolytic regulation
options: High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which inhibits formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of hexokinase with decreased intracellular glucose
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate (variant)
High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which stimulates formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which disease and metabolite pair is correctly matched?
explanation: Phenylketonuria is correctly matched with phenylpyruvate; the disease causes phenylalanine accumulation and its transamination products (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate) are excreted.
keyConcept: PKU metabolite
options: Maple syrup urine disease and isolysine
Maple syrup urine disease and lysine
Maple syrup urine disease and glycine
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which reaction uses methyltetrahydrofolate as a cofactor?
explanation: Methyltetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
keyConcept: Methyltetrahydrofolate function
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Loss of sensation from the left upper limb indicates a lesion in which of the following areas?
explanation: The left upper limb sensory representation is in the right postcentral gyrus (postcentral gyrus), located in the parietal lobe, specifically the upper part near the central sulcus.
keyConcept: Upper limb somatosensory cortex is located in the postcentral gyrus, above the lateral sulcus.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: A patient who has a right hemisection of spinal cord at the level of T6 will suffer from all the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Right hemisection at T6 causes ipsilateral paralysis and proprioception loss in the right lower limb, contralateral pain/temperature loss in the left lower limb. Fine touch from upper limb uses dorsal columns which are unaffected.
keyConcept: Hemisection spares ipsilateral upper limb fine touch
options: Paralysis of muscles of 6th right intercostal space.
Loss of proprioception of right lower limb.
Loss of fine touch in right upper limb.
Loss of pain & temperature in left lower limb.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: The following occur in Brown Sequard Syndrome Except
explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, the LMN lesion at the level of lesion is ipsilateral (not contralateral); the lesion involves corticospinal tract (ipsi UMN signs) and dorsal columns (ipsi proprioception).
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard LMN lesion side
options: Ipsilateral UMN lesion below level of lesion
Contralateral loss of exteroceptive sensations below level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of proprioceptive sensations below level of lesion
Contralateral L.M.N. lesion at same level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature at same level of lesion
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Lesion of the anterior spinal artery most likely produces which finding?
explanation: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causes bilateral loss of motor function (corticospinal tracts) and pain/temperature sensation (spinothalamic tracts), with dorsal column function (proprioception, vibration) preserved.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts; dorsal columns are supplied by posterior arteries.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is a common microscopic feature between muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ?
explanation: Both muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs are encapsulated receptors with connective tissue capsules surrounding their sensory endings, distinguishing them from free nerve endings.
keyConcept: Both muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ are encapsulated receptors.
options: They are both present in series with extrafusal fibres.
They both respond only to active contraction.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which fibers are afferent to cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle?
explanation: Afferents through the inferior cerebellar peduncle include: dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column), cuneocerebellar fibers from accessory cuneate nucleus, and vestibulocerebellar fibers.
keyConcept: Inferior cerebellar peduncle carries proprioceptive and vestibular afferents to cerebellum.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: As regards the nuclei of the posterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT matching:
explanation: The intermediomedial nucleus is associated with the lateral horn and visceral afferent fibers, not the posterior horn. The posteromarginal nucleus is at the tip of the posterior horn. Nucleus proprius lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
keyConcept: Intermediomedial nucleus belongs to the lateral horn, not the posterior horn
options: Posteromarginal nucleus - tip of posterior horn.
Nucleus proprius - lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
Posterior commissural nuclei - form intersegmental tracts.
Intermediomedial nucleus - serves in transmission of visceral afferent impulses.
Reticular nucleus - lies medial to nucleus proprius.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: As regards the prevertebral fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles (longus colli, longus capitis) and scalene muscles (anterior, medius, posterior). It is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, extends laterally to form the axillary sheath, and lies in front of (anterior to) the prevertebral muscles. The prevertebral fascia does NOT lie in front of the trachea; that is the preTRACHEAL fascia.
keyConcept: Prevertebral fascia covers prevertebral muscles, NOT trachea (that's pretracheal fascia).
options: It is related anteriorly to pharynx.
It is attached superiorly to base of skull.
It lies infront of Scalenus medius.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
explanation: Grey matter is central in spinal cord with neuron cell bodies; white matter is peripheral with myelinated fibers; the CNS lacks connective tissue framework.
keyConcept: Grey white matter distribution
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text:
Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
I. It is rich in connective tissue cells.
II. It is soft jelly like.
III. It has grey matter and white matter.
explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft and jelly-like (due to high water content), and has grey and white matter.
keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: histology

text: Which statement regarding muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ is correct?
explanation: Muscle spindles detect length changes and initiate stretch reflexes; Golgi tendon organs detect tension changes and provide protective inhibition. Both contribute to proprioception.
keyConcept: Muscle spindles respond to length; Golgi tendon organs respond to tension for reflexive motor control.
options: Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tension
Golgi tendon organ initiates the stretch reflex
Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tone
Golgi tendon organ has damping function
Muscle spindle is located in the tendon
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: physiology

text: Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine but not fluoxetine because
explanation: Imipramine has anticholinergic effect (treats enuresis); fluoxetine does not. Option C is correct. Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine's anticholinergic effect (reduces bladder contractions). Fluoxetine has no anticholinergic activity. Both can cause insomnia (A is wrong), and imipramine is not necessarily safer than fluoxetine.
keyConcept: Imipramine's anticholinergic effect reduces detrusor muscle activity, treating enuresis; fluoxetine lacks this mechanism.
options: Imipramine induces insomnia while fluoxetine induces sedation.
Imipramine possess anticholinergic effect but fluoxetine does not.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: General visceral efferent column includes the following nuclei Except:
explanation: The nucleus ambiguus supplies muscles of the larynx. However, all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of X).
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles via X
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The muscles attached to pterygomandibular raphe are supplied by the following nerves:
explanation: The pterygomandibular raphe is attached to the pterygoid hamulus and the posterior end of the mylohyoid line. Anteriorly, it gives attachment to the buccinator muscle (supplied by the facial nerve, CN VII). Posteriorly, it gives attachment to the superior pharyngeal constrictor (receiving supply from the pharyngeal plexus formed by glossopharyngeal, vagus, and sympathetic nerves). Therefore, the muscles attached to the raphe are supplied by facial and glossopharyngeal nerves.
keyConcept: Buccinator = CN VII; superior constrictor = pharyngeal plexus (CN IX + X).
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: All the following are nuclei of facial nerve EXCEPT:
explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord: anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column?
explanation: The tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V3), not by nucleus ambiguus. All other pharyngeal arch muscles are supplied by nucleus ambiguus.
keyConcept: Tensor muscles supplied by CN V, not nucleus ambiguus
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve has the following functional component:
explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the only nucleus in the CNS that contains pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies. It carries proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication and other structures, making it a General Somatic Afferent (GSA) nucleus.
keyConcept: Medial longitudinal bundle coordinates vestibular-eye reflexes
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which one of the following decussations is associated with red nucleus?
explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the motor nucleus supplying muscles of the larynx (and pharynx/soft palate). It is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI for these muscles.
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles
options: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding digastric triangle, all are true Except:
explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and superiorly by the lower border of the mandible. It contains the submandibular gland and submandibular lymph nodes. The hyoid bone is NOT the superior boundary; the mandible is.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle is bounded superiorly by mandible, NOT hyoid bone.
options: It is bounded anteriorly by anterior belly of digastric.
It is bounded posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric & stylohyoid.
It is bounded superiorly by hyoid bone.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding digastric triangle. All are true Except:
explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded by the inferior border of the mandible superiorly (not the hyoid bone), the anterior belly of digastric anteriorly, and the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid posteriorly.
keyConcept: Digastric triangle bounded superiorly by mandible, not hyoid bone - FALSE statement
options: It is bounded anteriorly by anterior belly of digastric.
It is bounded posteriorly by posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid.
It is bounded superiorly by hyoid bone.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: The common motor nucleus of IX, X and XI cranial nerves is:
explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It gives rise to special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) fibers that supply pharyngeal arch muscles (stylopharyngeus via IX, pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles via X, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius via XI).
keyConcept: SVE column - pharyngeal arch muscles
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: As regards accessory nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The spinal accessory nerve has a cranial part arising from the nucleus ambiguus (joining the vagus and exiting via jugular foramen) and a spinal part arising from the anterior horn cells of C1-C5, entering the skull through the foramen magnum, and exiting via the jugular foramen. The spinal part does NOT unite with the cranial part at the foramen ovale; rather, the cranial part exits with the glossopharyngeal and vagus through the jugular foramen, and the spinal part also exits through the jugular foramen but courses independently to supply the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
keyConcept: Spinal accessory does NOT unite with cranial part at foramen ovale; both exit via jugular foramen.
options: Its cranial part arises from nucleus ambiguus.
Its spinal part unites with its cranial part at foramen ovale.
It exits from skull with vagus & glossopharyngeal nerves.
Its cranial part is distributed through pharyngeal & recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Its spinal part enters cranial cavity through foramen magnum.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: A patient that had trauma to the spinal accessory nerve is expected to suffer from:
explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Damage causes inability to shrug the shoulder (trapezius) and difficulty rotating the head (sternocleidomastoid).
keyConcept: CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius for neck rotation and shoulder abduction.
options: Paralysis of muscles of the lower part of the face
Deviation of the tongue towards the damaged side
Deviation of the tongue towards the healthy side
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: The hypothalamus performs all of the following functions EXCEPT:
explanation: The hypothalamus controls autonomic functions, pituitary regulation, temperature, and appetite - but NOT voluntary movements. Voluntary movements are controlled by the motor cortex and basal ganglia. Hypothalamus handles autonomic and homeostatic functions.
keyConcept: Hypothalamus: autonomic, endocrine, temperature, appetite. Motor cortex: voluntary movement.
options: Regulation of anterior and posterior pituitary hormonal secretion.
Control of appetite and food intake.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Parkinson's disease:
explanation: Parkinson's disease is caused by lesion in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Option A is correct. The substantia nigra produces dopamine; its degeneration leads to dopamine deficiency in the striatum, causing Parkinsonian symptoms. Option B is wrong (thalamic lesions cause sensory symptoms, not Parkinsonism). Option C is wrong (Parkinsonism has resting tremors, not kinetic). Option D is wrong (clasp-knife rigidity is UMN, not Parkinsonian). Option E is wrong (pendular jerks are cerebellar).
keyConcept: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
options: Is caused by a lesion in the substantia nigra.
Is caused by lesion in the posteroventral nucleus of the thalamus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Riluzole is prescribed in Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to:
explanation: Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor that modestly extends survival and delays ventilator dependence in ALS by reducing excitotoxic neuronal death.
keyConcept: Riluzole reduces glutamate‑mediated excitotoxicity to modestly prolong survival and delay ventilation in ALS.
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: pharma

text: Which of the following nuclei, located in the midbrain, contains general visceral efferent (GVE) fibers?
explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (accessory oculomotor nucleus) is located in the midbrain and contains preganglionic parasympathetic neurons that supply the ciliary and sphincter pupillae muscles.
keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to intraocular muscles.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: A 44-year-old female patient has a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. She would present with a loss of:
explanation: The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. After decussation, the fibers descend in the lateral column of the spinal cord. A right cerebral peduncle lesion affects fibers that have NOT yet decussated, therefore causing CONTRALATERAL (left-sided) motor weakness. The corticospinal fibers to the lower limb are most medial in the peduncle.
keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle contains corticospinal fibers BEFORE their decussation in the medulla; right peduncle lesion = LEFT-sided weakness.
options: fine touch and pain sensation from the entire left side of the body
fine touch and pain sensation from the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to both sides of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire left side of the body
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects:
explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is a narrow channel passing through the midbrain that connects the third ventricle (anteriorly, at the level of the midbrain) with the fourth ventricle (posteriorly, at the pontomedullary junction). It is surrounded by the periaqueductal gray matter.
keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects the third and fourth ventricles, surrounded by periaqueductal gray matter.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The pain analgesic system includes which structure?
explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter in the midbrain is a key component of the descending pain inhibitory system, connecting to nucleus raphe magnus and inhibiting dorsal horn pain transmission.
keyConcept: Periaqueductal gray is the central controller of descending pain inhibition to dorsal horn.
options: Local cord neurons which secrete serotonin
Local cord neurons which secrete endorphin
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: physiology

text: Concerning headache:
explanation: Headache is a form of referred pain where intracranial and extracranial structures refer pain to the head through shared sensory innervation from trigeminal and cervical nerves.
keyConcept: Headache is referred pain from intracranial/extracranial structures.
options: It is an example of referred pain.
It is only caused by intracranial causes.
It is only caused by extracranial causes.
Nausea and vomiting are not symptoms occurring during migraine attack.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: pharma

text: The sphincter of the lips is the:
explanation: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle of the lips. The buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
keyConcept: Orbicularis oris = sphincter of the lips
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Cuneate tract arise from:
explanation: The cuneate fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the upper body (cervical and upper thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract origin
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The mechanism of synaptic transmission includes:
explanation: Ca++ ions enter the presynaptic terminal (not released from it) to trigger vesicle fusion. Presynaptic knobs release both excitatory and inhibitory transmitters. Transmitters cause either EPSPs or IPSPs. Excitatory transmitters cause depolarization (not hyperpolarization).
keyConcept: Synaptic transmission: Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis; transmitter binds specific receptors causing EPSP or IPSP.
options: Ca++ ions are released from the presynaptic knob
Presynaptic knobs release only an excitatory transmitter
Chemical transmission causes development of only excitatory postsynaptic state
Excitatory transmitters hyperpolarize the postsynaptic membrane
The released transmitter combines with specific receptors on postsynaptic membrane
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Ornithine is an aminoacid formed from
explanation: Ornithine is produced from arginine by arginase and can be transaminated to glutamate via ornithine aminotransferase. Conversely, glutamate can be converted to ornithine through acetylation (N-acetylglutamate) and subsequent reactions in the urea cycle.
keyConcept: Ornithine-glutamate interconversion in nitrogen metabolism
options: arginine and can be transformed to glutamate in two steps.
glutamate and can be transformed to arginine in the urea cycle.
arginine and transformed to aceto-acetate on fasting.

text: Glutamate can be the source of both nitrogen atoms of urea through which reactions?
explanation: Glutamate provides nitrogen via both glutamate dehydrogenase (oxidative deamination) and glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase (transamination).
keyConcept: Glycine cleavage system in mitochondria for glycine catabolism
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following statements concerning the nucleus dorsalis of Clark is TRUE?
explanation: The nucleus dorsalis of Clark projects to the cerebellum via the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, carrying proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and tendon organs. It is in the dorsal horn, present only at certain levels (C8-L3).
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus projects to cerebellum via dorsal spinocerebellar tract
options: It is found in the ventral horn.
It is present at all spinal levels.
It is homologous in function to the main sensory nucleus.

text: Which feature characterizes the nerve ending in a Meissner’s corpuscle?
explanation: The nerve fiber in Meissner's corpuscle has a characteristic tortuous (coiled) course between the lamellar cells, unlike the straight axial course in Pacinian corpuscles.
keyConcept: Meissner corpuscle structure
options: Myelinated afferent fiber enters the base of the corpuscle

subject: histology

text: Which of the following tracts is present in all segments of spinal cord?
explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract is present in all spinal cord segments, carrying proprioceptive information from lower limbs to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract present in all spinal cord segments
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.

subject: histology

text: Medial longitudinal bundle continue in spinal cord through:
explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus continues in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal and sulcomarginal tracts, coordinating head-eye movements.
keyConcept: MLF continuation

text: The muscle that causes firm closure of eyelids is:
explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi is responsible for firm (forced) closure of the eyelids. The palpebral part closes the eye gently.
keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi = forced eye closure; palpebral part = gentle closure

text: As regards buccinator muscle, all the following is true EXCEPT:
explanation: The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) via its buccal branches. It is NOT innervated by the mandibular nerve.
keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the mandibular nerve
options: It is the muscle of the cheecks.
It arises from maxilla and mandible.
It is inserted in upper and lower lips.
It prevents accumulation of food in oral vestibule.
It is innervated by mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve.

text: All the following form boundaries of interpeduncular fossa EXCEPT:
explanation: The optic nerve is not a boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The boundaries are: cerebral peduncles (posterolateral), upper border of pons (inferior), optic chiasma (superior), and optic tract (posterolateral).
keyConcept: Optic nerve not boundary of interpeduncular fossa

subject: anatomy

text: The cartilages of the larynx develop embryologically from which of the following pharyngeal arches?
explanation: The laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) develop from pharyngeal arch 4 (and 6), with the exception of the epiglottis which develops from the ventral pharyngeal wall.
keyConcept: Laryngeal cartilages originate from pharyngeal arches 4 and 6, except epiglottis from ventral pharyngeal wall.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Rootlets of glossopharyngeal nerve lie:
explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons and medulla.

subject: anatomy

text: The first-order neuron carrying pain and temperature from the face lies in the:
explanation: Cell bodies are in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion.
keyConcept: Pain and temperature first-order neuron: pseudounipolar cell body in trigeminal ganglion.
options: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

subject: anatomy

text: Rootlets of hypoglossal nerve lie:
explanation: The hypoglossal nerve rootlets emerge from the anterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the pyramid and olive. This is the anterior surface of the medulla.
keyConcept: CN XII between pyramid and olive
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons & pyramid.

text: When the sole is stroked firmly by a key:
explanation: In UMNL, the other toes show fanning. Option D is correct. Positive Babinski (upgoing plantar response) in UMNL involves big toe extension and often toe fanning due to corticospinal release. Option A is wrong (plantar flexion = normal). Option B is wrong (Babinski is UMNL, not area 6 lesion). Option C is wrong (dorsiflexion in LMNL is not typical; LMNL causes absent plantar response).
keyConcept: The Babinski sign (toe extension/fanning) indicates upper motor neuron lesion with corticospinal tract dysfunction.
options: The big toe planter-flexes in a patient having an UMNL.
The big toe dorsi-flexes in a patient with damaged area 6.
The big toe dorsi-flexes in a patient having LMNL.
The other toes show fanning in UMNL.

text: A patient complains of unsteadiness during that is profound during darkness. Examination shows a marked diminution of position sense, vibration sense, and stereognosis of all extremities. He is unable to stand without wavering for more than a few seconds when his eyes are closed. There are no other abnormal findings. The lesion most likely involves the:
explanation: Bilateral dorsal column lesion causes loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and stereognosis in all extremities, with a positive Romberg sign (falls when eyes closed because proprioception is lost). The patient uses visual input to compensate, hence the profound unsteadiness in darkness. Spinocerebellar tract lesions cause ataxia but not sensory loss; lateral column lesions affect corticospinal tracts.
keyConcept: Bilateral dorsal column lesion = loss of proprioception/vibration/stereognosis, positive Romberg; profound unsteadiness in darkness because vision cannot compensate.
options: Lateral columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally
Dorsal columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Concerning the basal ganglia function:
explanation: Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements. Option D is correct. The caudate circuit (caudate-putamen-GP-SNr-thalamus-caudate) is involved in movement scaling and timing. Option A is wrong (putamen executes learned patterns). Option B is wrong (caudate circuit is cognitive, putamen is motor). Option C is wrong (caudate circuit terminates in premotor, not motor area 4).
keyConcept: Caudate nucleus circuits process movement scaling and timing through cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops.
options: Caudate circuit helps execution of learned pattern of movement.
Putamen circuit is important for cognitive control of voluntary movements.
Caudate circuit terminates in motor area 4.
Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements.

subject: physiology

text: What is the main function of the hypothalamus?
explanation: The hypothalamus maintains internal homeostasis through autonomic control, regulates endocrine function via pituitary connection, controls food intake, temperature, thirst, and circadian rhythms.
keyConcept: Hypothalamus integrative functions
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Which of the following structures connects the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space?
explanation: The foramen of Magendie is the median aperture connecting the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space (cisterna magna), allowing CSF flow from the ventricle to the basal cisterns.
keyConcept: Median aperture (Magendie) connects fourth ventricle to subarachnoid space at the cisterna magna.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Dura matter characterized by being:
explanation: Dura mater is a fibrous, avascular layer (contains few blood vessels). It forms the outermost meninx. Arachnoid has trabeculae; pia is vascular; arachnoid barrier layer is cellular. Dura's toughness comes from collagen fibers.
keyConcept: Dura mater: tough outer meninx, fibrous, relatively avascular; attached to periosteum of skull/vertebrae.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: The plane of movement of the scalp is between:
explanation: The plane of movement of the scalp is between the aponeurosis and pericranium (the loose areolar tissue layer). This allows scalp movement.选项B正确. The answer is B. Infection can spread in this 'dangerous layer' to intracranial structures.
keyConcept: Scalp movement occurs between aponeurosis and pericranium - the loose areolar 'dangerous' layer.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: The central canal is lined by:
explanation: The central canal is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells) that is partially ciliated, similar to the ventricular lining.
keyConcept: Central canal epithelium
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Special visceral efferent nuclei include:
explanation: Special visceral efferent nuclei include: trigeminal motor nucleus (V), facial motor nucleus (VII), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII).选项D正确. The answer is D. These innervate pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.
keyConcept: Special visceral efferent nuclei: CN V, VII, IX, X, XI motor nuclei - innervate pharyngeal arch muscles.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The rate limiting step in the biosynthesis of catecholamines is:
explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA, which is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by catecholamines.
keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine biosynthesis
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Destruction of the ventral horn results in one of the following:
explanation: Destruction of the ventral horn (lower motor neuron) causes flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy, loss of reflexes, and fasciculations. Crude touch (dorsal column), fine touch (dorsal column), and pain sensation (spinothalamic) are not affected.
keyConcept: Ventral horn destruction causes flaccid paralysis (LMN lesion)
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: histology

text: The following statement is Wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of Benzodiazepines
explanation: Clinical duration of long-acting BZDs is longer than actual half-life - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Long-acting BZDs form active metabolites that prolong their effect beyond the parent compound's half-life. Options A, B, D are correct: IM absorption is slower (except lorazepam), lorazepam uses glucuronidation not oxidation, lorazepam has no active metabolites.
keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines have prolonged effects due to active metabolites, making actual duration longer than parent half-life.
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BDZs is shorter than the actual half life as they form active metabolites
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: pharma

text: The following statement is wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of benzodiazepines:
explanation: Long-acting BZDs (diazepam) form active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam) that have long half-lives. This means their clinical duration of action is LONGER than the actual half-life because active metabolites accumulate and contribute to effects. Option C states 'Clinical duration of action of long acting BZDs is shorter than the actual half-life' which is INCORRECT - it's actually LONGER due to active metabolites. This is why long-acting BZDs can accumulate with repeated dosing and why they have prolonged effects even after the parent drug is cleared.
keyConcept: Long-acting BZDs have CLONGER clinical duration than half-life due to active metabolite accumulation.
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except Lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except Lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BZDs is shorter than the actual half-life as they form active metabolites
chapter: The Sensory System

text: Abuse potential of buspirone is low because
explanation: Buspirone has delayed onset of action - this explains low abuse potential. Option C is correct. Unlike benzodiazepines which act immediately, buspirone takes 2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect. This delayed onset, combined with lack of sedation and no GABA activity, results in low abuse potential.
keyConcept: Buspirone's delayed onset of action contributes to its minimal abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines.
options: It has a weak anxiolytic effect
It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters.
It has a delayed onset of action.
Its marked sedating effect is troublesome.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: Abuse potential of Buspirone is low because:
explanation: Buspirone's low abuse potential is due to its delayed onset of action (takes 2-4 weeks for full anxiolytic effect). This delayed onset means users don't experience immediate psychoactive effects that typically lead to abuse. Additionally, buspirone doesn't cause sedation, dependence, or withdrawal. Option A is wrong - buspirone does have significant anxiolytic effects when given time to work. Option B is wrong - it does affect brain neurotransmitters (partial agonist at 5-HT1A). Option D is wrong - buspirone does NOT have marked sedating effects (unlike BZDs). The correct answer is C because the delayed therapeutic effect prevents the immediate gratification that fosters addiction.
keyConcept: Buspirone's delayed onset of action (2-4 weeks) contributes to its low abuse potential.
options: It has a weak anxiolytic effect
It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters
It has a delayed onset of action
It’s marked sedating effect is troublesome

subject: pharma

text: Special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) column includes:
explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the only pontine cranial nerve attached at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle, supplying the second pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) muscles.
keyConcept: CN V attached at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

text: Nuclei of the vagus nerve include the following except:
explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus. The vagus has: nucleus ambiguus (branchial GSE), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE), and solitary nucleus (SVA, GVA).
keyConcept: Vagus nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic), solitary nucleus (sensory).
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The floor of digastric triangle ; formed by:
explanation: The digastric triangle is bounded anteriorly by the anterior belly of digastric, posteriorly by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and superiorly by the inferior border of the mandible. Its floor is formed by the mylohyoid muscle anteriorly and by the hyoglossus and geniohyoid muscles more posteriorly and medially, separating the submandibular region from the oral cavity floor.
keyConcept: Floor of digastric triangle = mylohyoid and hyoglossus (and geniohyoid).
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: Concerning cerebellum:
explanation: Neocerebellum helps planning of movements. Option D is correct. The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) receives input from motor and premotor cortex and helps in movement planning and timing. Option A is wrong (each hemisphere controls ipsilateral muscles). Option B is wrong (spinocerebellar tracts provide unconscious proprioception). Option C is wrong (paleocerebellum调节肌张力). Option E is wrong (cerebellar ataxia has hypotonia, not spasticity).
keyConcept: The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is crucial for movement planning and coordination with the motor cortex.
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the contralateral muscles.
Spinocerebellar tracts give rise to conscious recognition of joint position sense.
Paleocerbellar is facilitatory to muscle tone.
Cerebellar ataxia is associated with spasticity.

text: Which parts of the hypothalamus control autonomic responses?
explanation: The hypothalamus controls autonomic responses primarily through the posterior and lateral hypothalamus (sympathetic) and anterior/ventromedial regions (parasympathetic), via descending pathways to brainstem autonomic centers.
keyConcept: Hypothalamic autonomic regulation
options: Regulation of food intake and appetite
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the
explanation: Denticulate ligaments are pial extensions that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater laterally; the coccygeal ligament (filum terminale externum) attaches the cord terminus to the coccyx.
keyConcept: Denticulate ligaments spinal cord anchoring
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the:
explanation: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the denticulate ligaments (21 pairs), which are extensions of the pia mater located between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots.
keyConcept: Denticulate ligaments anchor the spinal cord to the dura
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: 10 years old boy has a severe headache & vomiting that began yesterday. He is now confused.
explanation: A 10-year-old with severe headache, vomiting, confusion suggests bacterial meningitis (likely N. meningitidis given age and presentation). Close contacts need chemoprophylaxis. Rifampicin is the standard prophylaxis for N. meningitidis contacts. A) 'No prophylaxis necessary' - FALSE; B) 'Vaccine' - vaccines exist but don't protect immediately (not for serogroup B); C) 'Rifampicin' - TRUE for prophylaxis; D) 'Sulfonamide' - not used for meningococcal prophylaxis (sulfonamides were used historically but resistance is now common). The answer is C - contacts should receive rifampicin prophylaxis. Ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone are also options.
keyConcept: N. meningitidis contacts receive rifampicin prophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent disease.
options: They should be given Rifampicin as prophylaxis.
They should be given sulfonamide as prophylaxis.
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text: Which of the following share in the cerebellar islands:
explanation: Cerebellar islands (islands of granular cells) contain rosettes of mossy fiber terminals surrounded by dendrites of granule cells. Mossy fibers synapse with granule cell dendrites in these glomeruli.
keyConcept: Cerebellar glomeruli: mossy fiber rosettes + granule cell dendrites; input from spinal cord/brainstem.

subject: histology

text: As regards the occipital bellies of occipito-frontalis, choose the CORRECT statement:
explanation: The two occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis are separated by the median tendinous intersection and take origin from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line.
keyConcept: Occipital bellies originate from the highest nuchal line
options: They are separated by an extension of epicranial aponeurosis.
They take origin from epicranial aponeurosis.
They are inserted into lateral 2/3 of highest nuchal line.
They are supplied by temporal branch of facial nerve.

text: A lesion in the right gracile tract leads to loss of:
explanation: A lesion in the right gracile tract affects proprioception and fine touch from the right lower limb. Vibration sense testing of the right tibia would be diminished because this tract carries vibration sense.
keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion affects ipsilateral lower limb vibration
options: Sense of position of left big toe.
Sense of movement of right elbow joint.
Feeling of a pencil put in the right hand.
Site of touch on the right iliac fossa.

subject: anatomy

text: Injury to the right paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
explanation: The right paracentral lobule controls the left leg. Since motor pathways cross (decussate), injury to the right paracentral lobule causes paralysis of the contralateral (left) lower limb.
keyConcept: Right paracentral lobule controls left leg
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT
explanation: The main inferior olivary nucleus is present in the OPEN (not closed) medulla, located ventrolaterally. The closed medulla contains: motor decussation (lower), sensory decussation (higher), gracile and cuneate nuclei and tracts.
keyConcept: Closed medulla: decussations, gracile/cuneate nuclei. Open medulla: inferior olivary nucleus.
options: in the lower part there are motor decussation
at a higher level there are sensory decussation
contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.

subject: anatomy

text: Central canal in CNS is lined by:
explanation: The central canal of the CNS is lined by simple cuboidal epithelial cells (ependymal cells), which also line the ventricles.
keyConcept: Central canal lining
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Gracile tract arise from:
explanation: The gracile fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower body (sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
keyConcept: Gracile tract origin
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: One of the following is true about cuneate tract:
explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia in the upper half of the body (cervical and upper thoracic) and carries upper limb proprioception.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract origin
options: It arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on same side.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on opposite side.
It is present in lateral column of white matter in spinal cord.

subject: anatomy

text: First neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication is:
explanation: The posterior columns (gracile and cuneate nuclei) are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and vertebral arteries, NOT by the anterior spinal artery. The anterior spinal supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord.
keyConcept: Posterior columns not supplied by anterior spinal artery
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas show activation of the MAPK pathway and BRAF alterations (especially BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion). NF1 inactivation is seen in optic pathway gliomas. IDH1/IDH2 mutations are seen in adult diffuse astrocytomas, not pilocytic.
keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: BRAF activation, MAPK pathway (NOT IDH1/IDH2 mutations)
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are present in lamina «.. of spinal cord gray matter:
explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, corresponding to lamina VII of Rexed. Parasympathetic neurons are in sacral segments (S2-S4), not thoracic lamina II.
keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in lateral horn (lamina VII, T1-L2/3)
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
explanation: All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit - this is NOT true. Option E is INCORRECT. Multiple alpha motor neurons innervate a single muscle; each alpha neuron with its fibers constitutes ONE motor unit, not all alpha cells. Option A is wrong (alpha are larger, not more numerous). Option B is true (supply extrafusal). Option C is true (lateral horn for fine movements). Option D is wrong (flexor alphas are rostral to extensor).
keyConcept: Motor units are individual alpha motor neurons plus all muscle fibers they innervate; many motor units compose a single muscle.
options: They are larger and more numerous than gamma neurons.
They supply extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.
Alpha in the lateral part of anterior horn are concerned with fine movements
Alpha of flexors are dorsally present to alpha of extensors
All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit.

text: Sudden increase in skin temperature above 50 °C leads to:
explanation: Heat above 50C stimulates thermal nociceptors (via TRPV1 channels) causing burning pain. Temperatures above 45C begin to activate pain receptors, with noxious heat stimulating C and A-delta fibers.
keyConcept: TRPV1 receptors on nociceptors respond to temperatures above 43-45C, triggering burning pain sensation.
options: Transient impulses due to damage of cold receptors above 40 °C
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Methionine is synthesized in human body from:
explanation: Methionine is synthesized from homocysteine and serine via methionine synthase (requires B12) and other enzymes. The pathway involves converting homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
keyConcept: Methionine synthesis: homocysteine + serine → methionine (requires B12, folate). Cysteine is made from serine + homocysteine separately.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following passes in the urine of a patient with phenylketonuria?
explanation: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, so phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvic acid, phenyllactic acid, phenylacetylglutamine) accumulate and appear in urine.
keyConcept: PKU causes urinary excretion of phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, and phenylacetylglutamine
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: In phenylketonuria, deficiency of which substance occurs?
explanation: In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency leads to inability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, resulting in tyrosine deficiency and catecholamine synthesis impairment.
keyConcept: PKU biochemical defect
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The binding of a neurotransmitter to its receptor at an inhibitory synapse can lead to the ______ of ______ channels.
explanation: At inhibitory synapses, neurotransmitter binding opens potassium channels, allowing K+ efflux that hyperpolarizes the neuron and reduces neuronal excitability.
keyConcept: Inhibitory synapse: opening of potassium channels.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: pharma

text: 30-year-old male suffers a traumatic injury to his spine. He cannot move his legs and has lost all sensation below the level of the injury. Most likely diagnosis:
explanation: Bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain/temperature suggest anterior cord syndrome from anterior spinal artery occlusion. Posterior column function (proprioception) is preserved because they are supplied by posterior spinal arteries.
keyConcept: Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal columns while affecting lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts.
options: Complete spinal cord transection at C4
Complete spinal cord transection at T5
Complete spinal cord transection at T8
Hemisection of spinal cord at T12

subject: anatomy

text: Right hemisection of the spinal cord most likely produces which finding?
explanation: Right spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome) causes ipsilateral motor paralysis and proprioception loss below the lesion, with contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1-2 segments below.
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral UMN paralysis and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss.
options: Loss of all types of sensation of the left side at the level of the lesion
Loss of proprioception of the left side below the level of the lesion
Loss of pain and temperature sensations of the left side below the level of the lesion
Left lower motor neuron lesion at the level of the lesion
Left upper motor neuron lesion at the level of the lesion
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors (Pacinian corpuscles at joints), providing limb position sense.
keyConcept: Proprioception receptors
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Loss of sensation from both the left face and left body indicates a lesion in which of the following areas?
explanation: Loss from both left face and left body indicates a lesion at the left principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal (for face) combined with left medial lemniscus (for body), which is the lateral pontine tegmentum.
keyConcept: ipsilateral face and body sensory loss indicates a lesion affecting both trigeminal and spinothalamic pathways.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: A woman wore a dress on the beach. Later, wearing a jacket over the same area caused pain. This is an example of:
explanation: Wearing a jacket over tanned skin causes referred pain from sunburned skin, demonstrating referred pain where visceral or deep somatic injury is perceived as cutaneous pain.
keyConcept: Referred pain from deep tissue injury can be perceived as cutaneous pain due to convergence of somatic and visceral afferents on dorsal horn neurons.
options: Increase receptor sensitivity by tissue products
Activity-dependent increase in excitability of dorsal horn neurons
Increased threshold of peripheral nociceptors due to inflammatory mediators
Decreased inhibitory interneuron function in the spinal cord
Impaired saltatory conduction in primary afferent neurons
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: The upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain:
explanation: Due to the cephalad ascent of the spinal cord relative to the vertebral column during development, the upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain the upper 10 thoracic spinal cord segments. There is approximately a 1–2 segment discrepancy.
keyConcept: Upper 9 thoracic vertebrae house the upper 10 thoracic cord segments
options: Upper 6 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 8 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Upper 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
Lower 10 thoracic segments of spinal cord.
All thoracic segments of spinal cord.

text: Hemisection of the spinal cord most likely produces which finding?
explanation: Spinal cord hemisection produces the classic Brown-Sequard pattern: ipsilateral upper motor neuron paralysis, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few segments below.

Loss of proprioception of the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of dorsal column sensations of the same side below the level of the lesion
Lower motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Upper motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion

text: Grey matter is .......... While white matter is ...........
explanation: Grey matter (cell bodies) is centrally located in the spinal cord while white matter (myelinated fibers) is peripherally located, the reverse of the brain.

text: Inner pyramidal cells are present in layer .... of cerebral cortex:
explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called giant pyramidal cells or Betz cells in motor cortex) are found in layer V of the cerebral cortex. They give rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers.

C. Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand

text: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a WHO grade I tumor (benign) with good prognosis. Option D states 'bad prognosis' which is INCORRECT - pilocytic astrocytoma has excellent prognosis with complete surgical resection (5-year survival >90%). This is the EXCEPT question, so D is the answer. In contrast, diffuse astrocytoma (grade II) and anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III) have progressively worse prognoses.

explanation: The external auditory meatus (EAM) develops from the deepening of the first pharyngeal cleft, which is an ectodermal invagination between the first and second branchial arches. text: The retromandibular vein divides within the parotid gland into anterior and posterior divisions. Each division then unites with which veins respectively?
explanation: The retromandibular vein divides into anterior and posterior branches within the parotid gland. The anterior branch joins the facial vein, and the posterior branch joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

text: Regarding the medulla oblongata, the medial zone containing the pyramid is supplied by:

text: In the CNS Injury, which of the following cells are abundant:
explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.

text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.

text: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:

The statement that it is related to the posterior border of sternomastoid is INCORRECT—the cyst lies along the ANTERIOR border of sternocleidomastoid, not posterior.

explanation: Left lower limb motor weakness with Babinski sign and increased deep tendon reflexes (UMN signs) indicates a lesion of the LEFT lateral corticospinal tract. text: Thalamic nucleus that relays basal ganglia output:
explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is the thalamic relay for basal ganglia output. explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus is part of the limbic system's Papez circuit.
