text: Conscious sedation may be induced by
explanation: Fentanyl with Midazolam induces conscious sedation. Option A is correct. This combination (opioid + benzodiazepine) provides analgesia and amnesia for conscious sedation in minor procedures. Droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia (B). Domperidone is antiemetic (C).
keyConcept: Conscious sedation combines fentanyl (analgesia) with midazolam (anxiolysis/amnesia) for procedural sedation.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: pharma

text: Conscious sedation may be induced by:
explanation: Conscious sedation is achieved by combining a benzodiazepine (for anxiolysis, amnesia, sedation) with an opioid (for analgesia). Fentanyl (opioid) + Midazolam (benzodiazepine) is the classic combination. Fentanyl provides analgesia while midazolam provides anxiolysis and sedation. Option B (Midazolam/Droperidol) - droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia, not conscious sedation. Option C (Fentanyl/Domperidone) - domperidone is an antiemetic, not a sedative. Option D is incorrect. The combination allows reduced doses of each drug while achieving adequate sedation and analgesia for procedures like dental work.
keyConcept: Conscious sedation uses fentanyl (analgesic) + midazolam (benzodiazepine) for safe procedural sedation.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: pharma

text: Muscle spindles:
explanation: Muscle spindles are found in virtually all skeletal muscles, not just large ones. They consist of a few intrafusal muscle fibers (nuclear bag and chain types) surrounded by a capsule, NOT extrafusal fibers.
keyConcept: Muscle spindles: present in all muscles; contain intrafusal fibers (not extrafusal); detect stretch.
options: Are found in all skeletal muscles
Are found only in large skeletal muscles
Consist of small numbers of extrafusal muscle fibers
Consist of a large number of extrafusal muscle fibers
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: physiology

text: The nasolacrimal groove lies between the:
explanation: The nasolacrimal groove is a furrow between the maxillary swelling and the lateral nasal swelling. It gives rise to the nasolacrimal duct, which drains tears from the eye to the nasal cavity. Failure of canalization of this duct leads to congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
keyConcept: Nasolacrimal groove lies between MAXILLARY SWELLING and LATERAL NASAL SWELLING; gives nasolacrimal duct.
options: Frontal prominence and medial nasal swelling.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding tentorium cerebelli
explanation: The tentorium cerebelli roofs over the posterior cranial fossa (not middle); its free border is attached to the anterior clinoid process (not post clinoid), and oculomotor/trochlear nerves pierce dura at this junction.
keyConcept: Tentorium cerebelli attachments and relations
options: It roofs over middle cranial fossa
Its free border is attached to anterior clinoid process
Its attached border is attached to post clinoid process
It includes transverse venous sinus in its attached border
Oculomotor and trochlear nerves pierce dura at the point of crossing of its free & attached borders
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Thrombosis of posterior inferior cerebellar artery affects:
explanation: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, nystagmus), cerebellar ataxia, facial pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
keyConcept: PICA thrombosis causes lateral medullary syndrome
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The corticospinal fibers are broken into bundles in:
explanation: In the pons, the corticospinal fibers are broken into bundles by the transverse pontocerebellar fibers, creating the scattered appearance of the basis pontis.
keyConcept: Corticospinal fibers scattered in basis pontis
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Special visceral afferent nuclei include:
explanation: This is an INCORRECT question about medial longitudinal bundle connections. The MLF does connect the vestibular nuclei with cranial nerve nuclei III, IV, and VI to coordinate eye movements.
keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which tract is responsible for spino‑visual reflexes (turning the head and eyes toward a cutaneous stimulus)?
explanation: The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.
keyConcept: Spinotectal reflex
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Cells of Cajal are present in
explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: histology

text: Which response occurs when the right foot is suddenly struck?
explanation: A sudden foot strike (ankle jerk) causes dorsiflexion stretch of the gastrocnemius, activating muscle spindles that monosynaptically trigger calf muscle contraction (ankle jerk reflex).
keyConcept: Ankle jerk is a stretch reflex where gastrocnemius stretch elicits contraction via Ia afferents to alpha motor neurons.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text: The posterior part of the floor of carotid triangle is formed by:
explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded posteriorly by the sternocleidomastoid, superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and inferiorly by the superior belly of omohyoid. Its floor is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering the pharyngeal constrictors; specifically, the posterior part of the floor consists of the middle and inferior constrictors of the pharynx.
keyConcept: Posterior floor of carotid triangle = middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: 24-year-old man was brought to the ER following a driving accident. Neurological testing revealed paraplegia and loss of all sensory modalities in bilateral lower limbs. Sensation for the upper limbs and the trunk was intact. Which of the following might be the nature and location of the lesion in this patient?
explanation: The presentation of bilateral lower limb paralysis with intact upper limbs and trunk suggests central cord syndrome. Option C is correct because complete transection at T8 would paralyze everything below T8 (including trunk). Option E (central cord syndrome) is typically at C5-C6 levels and affects upper limbs more than lower due to the somatotopic arrangement of the corticospinal tract. The patient has paraplegia with intact upper limbs, which is most consistent with a T8 cord lesion where the corticospinal fibers for lower limbs are most affected.
keyConcept: Central cord syndrome preferentially affects upper extremities due to the somatotopic organization of corticospinal fibers in the spinal cord.
options: Complete section of spinal cord at C8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at C8 level
Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at T8 level
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Lesion in frontal lobe speech center produces:
explanation: Lesion in Broca's area (frontal lobe speech center) produces expressive aphasia - difficulty producing speech despite understanding. The patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate. Sensory aphasia (Wernicke's) affects comprehension; motor aphasia affects speech production.
keyConcept: Broca's area lesion: expressive (motor) aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: physiology

text: Choose from the following pair of antibiotics not crossing BBB even if inflamed:
explanation: Amphotericin B (for fungal CNS infections) and aminoglycosides have minimal BBB penetration even when the meninges are inflamed; chloramphenicol and rifampicin cross well.
keyConcept: Amphotericin B and aminoglycosides are notable for poor CNS penetration even with meningeal inflammation.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: pharma

text: Principles of antimicrobial therapy for meningitis:
explanation: Once the causative organism is identified in meningitis, antibiotic treatment duration typically ranges from 7 days (N. meningitidis) to 21 days (S. pneumoniae), depending on the pathogen and clinical response.
keyConcept: Duration of meningitis treatment is pathogen‑dependent, generally 7–21 days after organism identification.
options: Antibiotics should be lipophilic‑ionized in physiological pH
Steroids should be administered after starting empiric antibiotics
Lumbar puncture should be done before choosing empiric antibiotics
Once organism is identified, treatment should be continued for 7 to 21 days
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: pharma

text: Which of the following is true about the intracranial hemorrhage?
explanation: Subdural hemorrhage crosses suture lines because it's venous bleeding with low pressure that accumulates slowly, unlike arterial extradural bleeding which is confined by suture attachments.
keyConcept: Subdural bleeding crosses suture lines (venous).
options: Extradural bleeding means bleeding between dura and arachnoid maters.
Extradural bleeding is commonly venous in origin.
Subdural bleeding is commonly arterial in origin.
Subdural bleeding crosses the suture line.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Type of junction between endothelium or ependymal:
explanation: Tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between endothelial cells and ependymal cells create the selective permeability barrier in the CNS.
keyConcept: Tight junction function
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion:
explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion?
explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: The medial medullary syndrome includes:
explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal), contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal), and contralateral loss of proprioception/fine touch (medial lemniscus). Pain and temperature are preserved.
keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome includes tongue paralysis
options: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of XII.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: clinical

text: Concerning synapses, which of the following is true?
explanation: Chemical synapses are the most common type in the CNS and are susceptible to modulation by neurotransmitters, drugs, and toxins. Electrical synapses allow direct ionic coupling and are bidirectional.
keyConcept: Chemical synapses are the predominant CNS synapse type and are targetable by drugs unlike electrical synapses.
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS.
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission.
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse.
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs and chemicals.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which of the following is the source of urea carbon?
explanation: The carbon of urea comes from CO2 (as bicarbonate) via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondria.
keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting enzyme requiring NAG for activation
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: What is a contusion in traumatic head injury? And what is its types?
explanation: Contusion is direct parenchymal brain injury with three types: coup injury at the point of impact, contrecoup injury opposite the impact, and intermediate coup. This includes direct neuronal and glial damage, hemorrhage, and edema. Option D 'All of the above' is correct. Contusions occur from deceleration-acceleration forces causing brain to impact skull. The answer is D. Contusions may evolve into contrecoup injuries due to brain movement within the skull.
keyConcept: Contusions are direct brain injuries including coup (impact), contrecoup (rebound), and intermediate injuries.
options: Direct parenchymal injury to the brain
Coup injury at the point of impact
Contrecoup injury opposite the point of impact
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: pathology

text: How do general anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity?
explanation: General anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA-A receptor activation - barbiturates, benzodiazepines, propofol, isoflurane) or inhibiting excitatory neurotransmission (NMDA receptor blockade - ketamine, nitrous oxide).选项C正确. The answer is C. Some agents do both. The net effect is decreased neuronal excitability and consciousness.
keyConcept: General anesthetics enhance GABA (inhibitory) or block NMDA (excitatory) to inhibit neuronal activity.
options: They facilitate inhibitory effects of GABA at GABA receptors
Inhibit excitatory effects of glutamate at NMDA receptors
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: pharma

text: Sense of movement and sense of position are lost after lesion of:
explanation: Sense of movement (kinesthesia) and position sense are carried by the dorsal column tracts (gracile and cuneate). Loss of these sensations indicates damage to the posterior columns.
keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate tracts carry position/movement sense
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Gracile and cuneate nuclei are supplied by medullary branches of:
explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei (dorsal column nuclei) are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, not the anterior spinal artery.
keyConcept: Posterior spinal/PICA supply dorsal column nuclei
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: 43 year old woman is evaluated in the hospital and is found to have multiple neurologic abnormalities from the level T 12 down. She has loss of vibration and proprioception on the left but these senses are present on the right side. She has absent pain and temperature sensation in the right side from T12 down. Motor power was lost in the left leg but normal motor strength in her right leg. What is the most likely cause of her neurologic symptoms?
explanation: Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord. Option C is correct. Left hemisection explains: left vibration/proprioception loss (dorsal columns), right pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), left leg paralysis (corticospinal). Complete transection would affect both sides. Right hemisection would cause opposite findings.
keyConcept: Ipsilateral dorsal column and motor loss with contralateral spinothalamic loss indicates spinal cord hemisection on the side of motor/dorsal column deficits.
options: Complete spinal cord transection at upper thoracic segments.
Complete spinal cord transection at lower thoracic segments.
Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord
Hemisection on the right part of spinal cord
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 2 days is used in case of:
explanation: Rifampicin 2-day prophylaxis is used for meningococcal contacts. None of the listed organisms (H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae) have this specific prophylaxis regimen.
keyConcept: Rifampicin 2‑day prophylaxis is for meningococcal contacts, but none of the listed organisms match this indication.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: One of the following pairs of drugs used in treatment of migraine could be used intra nasally:
explanation: Both sumatriptan (triptan) and dihydroergotamine can be given intranasally for migraine treatment. Sumatriptan nasal spray and dihydroergotamine nasal spray are both available formulations. Other intranasal options for migraine include NSAIDs. Option D shows triptan and dihydroergotamine which both have nasal formulations. The answer is D - both sumatriptan and dihydroergotamine can be given intranasally. Ergotamine is also available as nasal spray but less commonly used now.
keyConcept: Sumatriptan and dihydroergotamine both have intranasal formulations for acute migraine treatment.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: What is the mechanism of action of antidepressants?
explanation: Antidepressants work mainly by increasing synaptic monoamine levels (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine). SSRIs inhibit serotonin reuptake; SNRIs inhibit both; TCAs inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin; MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase.选项C正确. The answer is C. The monoamine hypothesis suggests depression involves decreased serotonin/norepinephrine.
keyConcept: Antidepressants increase synaptic monoamines (serotonin, norepinephrine) via reuptake inhibition or enzyme blockade.
options: Increase brain biogenic amines (norepinephrine and serotonin)
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: pharma

text: Which one of the following scalp nerves is derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves?
explanation: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It supplies the skin of the occipital region of the scalp. The auriculotemporal, great auricular, lesser occipital, and posterior auricular nerves are ventral ramus derivatives.
keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve = dorsal ramus of C2
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Lesion of which cerebral area in left hemisphere causes motor aphasia?
explanation: Motor aphasia (Broca's aphasia) results from lesion of Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which is responsible for speech production. In the dominant hemisphere, this is typically the left side.
keyConcept: Broca's area in inferior frontal gyrus causes motor aphasia
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Nerve of pterygoid canal is formed by union of ……… nerves.
explanation: The nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidians nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal: greater petrosal + deep petrosal nerves.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The corticonuclear tract has unilateral connections with:
explanation: The corticonuclear tract has bilateral connections with most cranial nerve nuclei, except the lower facial nucleus (which is only contralateral) and the trochlear/trigeminal motor nuclei.
keyConcept: Lower 7 facial nucleus has unilateral corticonuclear input
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The facial nerve leaves the cranial cavity by passing through:
explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the cranial cavity through the stylomastoid foramen located between the styloid and mastoid processes.
keyConcept: Facial nerve exits via stylomastoid foramen.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: What are the therapeutic uses of anticholinergic drugs?
explanation: Anticholinergic drugs therapeutic uses in PD: control of tremor and rigidity (not bradykinesia), drooling, excessive salivation, and oily skin. They work by blocking muscarinic receptors in the striatum, reducing cholinergic activity that becomes relatively increased in PD.选项C正确. The answer is C. Anticholinergics are less effective for bradykinesia and are now second-line due to side effects.
keyConcept: Anticholinergics treat PD tremor and rigidity by blocking excess cholinergic activity in the striatum.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: pharma

text: Occlusion of this artery in dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia:
explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the posterior temporal lobe including Wernicke's area (sensory speech area). Occlusion of the PCA in the dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia), characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension. Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus.
keyConcept: Posterior cerebral artery supplies Wernicke's area; PCA occlusion in dominant hemisphere causes sensory aphasia.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Broca’s area:
explanation: Broca's area is the motor speech center present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). It is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and coordinates speech production, not sensory aspects.
keyConcept: Broca's area present in dominant hemisphere only
options: It is located in middle frontal gyrus.
It is present in the dominant hemisphere.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by.
explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (which faces the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is attached to periosteum. This creates the dural sinus spaces between the two layers.
keyConcept: Dura mater: outer surface = periosteum; inner surface = simple squamous mesothelium facing arachnoid.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by:
explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (the epidural boundary facing the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is also lined by mesothelium.
keyConcept: Dura mater inner surface lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium)
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: The cause of death in rabies is:
explanation: Death in rabies is due to respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy affecting respiratory muscles), not heart failure or direct respiratory center failure. The virus destroys motor neurons in the brainstem.
keyConcept: Rabies death from respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy)
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: pathology

text: A patient with a tumour in the left frontal eye field (area 8) will have difficulty:
explanation: The left frontal eye field (area 8) controls conjugate gaze to the right by sending signals that move both eyes rightward; a lesion here causes difficulty gazing to the contralateral (right) side.
keyConcept: Left frontal eye field controls gaze to the right (contralateral).
chapter: Neurodegenerative, Myelin Diseases, Trauma, Vascular, Tumors, and Dementia
subject: anatomy

text: The commonest site of spina bifida is:
explanation: Spina bifida is most common in the lumbosacral region because the lumbar and sacral vertebrae are the last to close their vertebral arches (sacral arches close last, around puberty). The most common type is spina bifida occulta at L5-S1. The thoraco-lumbar region is also a common site, but lumbosacral is the most common overall.
keyConcept: Commonest site of spina bifida = lumbosacral region; vertebrae close from cranial to caudal direction.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: As regards orbicularis oculi muscle, all are true EXCEPT:
explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi has bony attachments both medially (medial palpebral ligament) and laterally (lateral palpebral raphe). Therefore, the statement that it has no medial bony attachment is incorrect.
keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi has bony attachments medially and laterally
options: Its lacrimal part helps drainage of tears.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its orbital part has no bony attachment medially.
Its palpebral part lies in the eyelids.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The ability to recognize an unseen familiar object placed in the hand depends on the integrity of which tract?
explanation: Recognizing a familiar object by touch (stereognosis) requires fine touch and proprioception, carried by the cuneate tract from the upper limb. The gracile tract carries these sensations from the lower body.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Conscious proprioception from right lower limb are carried by:
explanation: Conscious proprioception from the right lower limb is carried by the right gracile tract, which ascends ipsilaterally in the posterior column and decussates in the medulla.
keyConcept: Gracile tract is ipsilateral for lower limb proprioception
options: Tracts of left posterior white column.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A patient has a lesion affecting the right gracile tract. Which of the following sensory deficits is most likely?
explanation: Gracile tract lesion causes loss of vibration and proprioception from the ipsilateral lower limb below the midthigh, as the gracile nucleus receives input from the leg and lower trunk.
keyConcept: Gracile tract carries ipsilateral lower limb proprioceptive information to the medulla.
options: Pain and temperature loss in the right tibia
Vibration loss in the right tibia
Pain and temperature loss in the left tibia
Vibration loss in the left tibia
Complete loss of all sensations in both legs
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: All the following characters of Golgi Cell except:
explanation: Golgi cells have large cell bodies with many long dendrites that extend into all cortical layers (not just the Golgi layer), and their axons synapse with granular cells in the granular layer.
keyConcept: Golgi cell characteristics
options: dendrite extend in all cortex layer
its axon in granular layers that synapse with granular cell
its dendrite in golgi layer only
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The second order neuron in proprioception from lower half of the body is in:
explanation: Second order neurons for lower body proprioception are in the gracile nucleus on the same side, which then decussates as internal arcuate fibers.
keyConcept: Proprioception second neuron lower
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Origin of medial lemniscus is:
explanation: The medial lemniscus originates from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side after their fibers cross (internal arcuate fibers).
keyConcept: Medial lemniscus origin
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of same side.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of opposite side.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The neurologist observes a patient with a high stamping gait. He asks the patient to stand and to close his eyes. The patient immediately starts to sway over. Name the ascending pathways that are involved and name the disease.
explanation: Bilateral gracile tract degeneration in tabes dorsalis causes loss of proprioception leading to sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign (swaying with eyes closed).
keyConcept: Tabes dorsalis pathology
options: Gracile on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Gracile on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A muscle DOESN'T share in boundaries of the suboccipital triangle is:
explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A nerve seen in the floor of the suboccipital triangle is:
explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Rotation of the head to say "No" occurs at ……… joint.
explanation: Saying 'No' involves rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2), where the dens of the axis articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.
keyConcept: Saying no: rotation at atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: One of the following nuclei is not present in all segments of the spinal cord:
explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: The main sensory nucleus of spinal cord is:
explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: The second order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Which structure is found in lamina I of the spinal cord gray matter?
explanation: The posteromarginal nucleus is located in lamina I of the spinal cord and receives pain and temperature afferents from the periphery.
keyConcept: Spinal cord lamina I
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Glutamate is secreted by:
explanation: Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.
keyConcept: Corticostriatal projection
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which of the following is true about the aminoacid neurotransmitters?
explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate is excitatory, glycine/GABA are inhibitory; glycine is in collagen; glutamate produces MSG; all above is correct.
keyConcept: Amino acid NT properties
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen aminoacids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other aminoacids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is
explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action on catecholamines, then further metabolism to VMA. Elevated VMA is a key diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
keyConcept: VMA as the end product of catecholamine catabolism and tumor marker
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: How many carbon and nitrogen atoms are there in a urea molecule?
explanation: Urea has the formula (NH2)2C=O, containing ONE carbon atom and TWO nitrogen atoms.
keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibition of TCA cycle enzymes and glutamate accumulation
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following is true about the amino acid neurotransmitters?
explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are correct: glutamate is excitatory, glycine and GABA are inhibitory; glycine constitutes one-third of collagen; glutamic acid is produced from other amino acids; monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
keyConcept: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate excitatory, glycine/GABA inhibitory
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while Glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen amino acids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other amino acids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: GABA (gamma amino butyric acid) is:
explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A (ionotropic, chloride channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors. It is produced postsynaptically from glutamate by GAD.
keyConcept: GABA is the major postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in CNS
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Vitamin B6 is important for which of the following regarding brain metabolism?
explanation: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) is essential for synthesizing major neurotransmitters: dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, GABA, and histamine, all produced by PLP-dependent decarboxylation reactions.
keyConcept: Vitamin B6 (PLP) required for synthesis of major CNS neurotransmitters
options: Detoxification of ammonia by formation of glutamine.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is:
explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
keyConcept: VMA as end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which reaction is impaired in thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency?
explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; its deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids.
keyConcept: Thiamine-dependent reactions
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The cuneate tract carries which of the following sensations?
explanation: The cuneate tract carries fine (discriminative) touch from the upper limb only. Crude touch from upper limb is carried by the ventral spinothalamic tract. Lower limb fine touch uses the gracile tract.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb only
options: Crude touch from upper & lower limbs.
Fine touch from upper & lower limbs.
Unconscious proprioception from upper and lower limbs.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Spinal lemniscus made by joining:
explanation: The spinal lemniscus is formed by the union of ventral and lateral spinothalamic tracts, carrying pain and temperature sensation through the brainstem.
keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus composition
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from which nucleus?
explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus (nucleus dorsalis) located in the intermediate grey matter at T1-L2 levels, carrying proprioceptive information to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Crude touch is carried on which tract?
explanation: Crude touch and pressure are carried by the ventral (anterior) spinothalamic tract. Pain and temperature are carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, while fine touch uses the dorsal columns.
keyConcept: Ventral spinothalamic carries crude touch
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following might be the location of lesion in this patient? (referring to Question 31)
explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of spinal cord), the lesion affects the ipsilateral corticospinal tract (motor paralysis) and ipsilateral dorsal column (loss of proprioception/vibration) below the lesion, while the contralateral spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) is lost because it crosses within one or two segments. Left motor deficit + right pinprick loss = LEFT cord hemisection. At C8 level, this causes motor weakness in the left lower limb and sensory loss on the right below C8.
keyConcept: Left motor + right pain loss = LEFT Brown-Sequard syndrome. Left C8 cord hemisection causes left lower limb weakness and right C8-dermatome pain loss.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: A patient with a traumatic lesion of the left half of the spinal cord at the level of the eighth cervical segment might present the following sign(s) and symptom(s):
explanation: In left hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome), the corticospinal tract is damaged on the left side, causing ipsilateral UMN signs below the lesion. Option D is correct because the left corticospinal damage produces left-sided positive Babinski sign below C8. Option A is wrong (pain/temp loss is contralateral in spinothalamic tract damage). Option B is wrong (position sense loss is ipsilateral in dorsal column damage). Option C is wrong (hemiplegia would be ipsilateral, not right). Option E is wrong (LMN signs occur at the lesion level, not below).
keyConcept: In spinal cord hemisection, ipsilateral UMN paralysis and Babinski sign occur below the lesion due to corticospinal tract damage.
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensations on the left side below the level of the lesion
Loss of position sense of the right leg
Right-sided lower motor paralysis in the segment of the lesion and muscular atrophy
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Which receptors are located most deeply in the skin (dermis and hypodermis)?
explanation: Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings are the deepest tactile receptors, located in the dermis and hypodermis for vibration and stretch detection.
keyConcept: Deep skin receptors
options: Krause end bulb and free nerve endings
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding the cervical spinal cord, which statement is correct?
explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) is located in lamina II of the spinal cord gray matter and processes pain and temperature sensations.
keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa location
options: Substantia gelatinosa receives mostly motor input
Substantia gelatinosa is located in lamina II
Clarke’s nucleus is located in lamina VI
Clarke’s nucleus is found in all cervical segments
Retropostero‑lateral column of cervical segments supplies the distal part of the lower limb

subject: histology

text: Which structure is found in the cervical segment (internal structures of spinal cord)?
explanation: Clarke's nucleus is found in lamina VII (intermediate gray matter) at cervical levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus location
options: Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII grey matter
Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII white matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII grey matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII white matter
Substantia gelatinosa in lamina VII grey matter
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: histology

text: Which type of sensory receptors in the skin respond quickly at the onset of a stimulus but stop firing if the stimulus is constant?
explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors that respond quickly at the onset and offset of a stimulus but cease firing during sustained stimulation due to their large, encapsulated structure.
keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors detecting vibration and rapid changes.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text:
Which of the following maneuvers will weakens the stretch reflex in skeletal muscle?
A. Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
B. Disruption of the spinocerebellar tract
C. Disruption of the corticospinal tract
D. Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
E. Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
explanation: Sectioning the dorsal root eliminates the afferent limb of the stretch reflex (Ia fibers from muscle spindles), causing immediate weakening or loss of the reflex.
keyConcept: Dorsal root sectioning: weakens stretch reflex by cutting afferent limb.
options: Sectioning the dorsal root of a spinal nerve
Sectioning the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side of the skeletal muscle in question
Creating a lesion in the contralateral globus pallidus
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: physiology

text: Concerning sensory receptors, all the followings are true, Except:
explanation: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily (unlike many other excitable tissues); they maintain responsiveness during sustained stimulation, though they may adapt at different rates.
keyConcept: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily.

subject: pharma

text: In a neurological examination, while performing cotton wool test:
explanation: The cotton wool test assesses fine touch (discriminative touch) using Meissner's corpuscles and hair follicle receptors that are moderate adaptors, particularly sensitive on glabrous skin like fingertips.
keyConcept: Cotton wool test: fine/discriminative touch via mechanoreceptors (Meissner's corpuscles).
options: The sensation tested is fine touch.
The sensation tested is carried on C fibers only.
The receptors are moderately adapting receptors.
The cotton is felt better on the palmar side of the hands.

text: Addition of epinephrine to local anesthetic do not
explanation: Epinephrine does NOT increase potency. Option D is correct. Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, decreasing absorption (A), prolonging duration (B), and decreasing systemic toxicity (C). It does not affect the intrinsic potency of the local anesthetic molecule.
keyConcept: Epinephrine reduces local anesthetic systemic absorption and toxicity but does not alter drug potency.
chapter: The Sensory System
subject: pharma

text: Commissural Nuclei is between:
explanation: Commissural nuclei connect sensory and motor nuclei on opposite sides of the spinal cord, facilitating crossed reflexes and coordinated movement.
keyConcept: Commissural nuclei

subject: anatomy

text: Which cerebellar structures are separated by fissura prima?
explanation: The fissura prima separates the anterior and posterior lobes of the cerebellum. It divides the culmen (anterior lobe) from the declive, folium, and tuber (posterior lobe).
keyConcept: Fissura prima divides the anterior and posterior cerebellar lobes, separating motor from non-motor regions.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: A lesion in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory can result in which of the following neurological deficits?
explanation: PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum. PICA syndrome causes ipsilateral dysphagia, hoarseness, decreased gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus), and cerebellar signs, with contralateral pain/temperature loss.
keyConcept: PICA syndrome presents with ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits and contralateral sensory loss.
options: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: Anterior spinal artery supplies the following structures Except:
explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord including the anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is:
explanation: The largest branch of the vertebral artery is the basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction.
keyConcept: Largest vertebral branch: basilar artery.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: The Charcot's artery is the largest branch of ……… set of central branches of circle of Willis.
explanation: Charcot's artery (also called the artery of cerebral hemorrhage) is the largest anterolateral central branch of the circle of Willis, supplying the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
keyConcept: Charcot's artery: largest anterolateral central branch of circle of Willis.
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: anatomy

text: A male patient 40 years old presented with hemiplegia & deafness. Radiological examination showed a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle. Biopsy from this tumor showed a neurogenic tumor formed of hypercellular and hypocellular areas. The most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Schwannomas (neurilemmomas) at the cerebellopontine angle show hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas. They arise from Schwann cells.
keyConcept: Schwannoma: Antoni A and B areas, hypercellular/hypocellular, cerebellopontine angle
chapter: The Motor System, Spinal Cord Internal Structure and Lesions
subject: histology

text: Which of the following is true about the grey matter?
explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)
options: It is located outside the white matter in spinal cord.
It is formed of nerve cells mainly.
It has satellite cells sheath around its cells.

subject: histology

text: Regarding the muscle spindle, which sentence is NOT true:
explanation: Intrafusal fibers are NOT excited during overstretch - this is NOT true. Option C is INCORRECT. Overstretch actually stimulates the muscle spindle, exciting intrafusal fibers. Options A, B, D, E are correct: primary afferent responds to static length and rate, extrafusal stretch does stretch intrafusal, spindles are parallel to extrafusal, two fiber types exist.
keyConcept: Muscle spindles detect stretch; overstretch excites intrafusal fibers, increasing Ia afferent discharge.
options: The primary afferent fibers responds to the static length of muscle as well as to its rate of change in length.
Stretching the extrafusal fibres causes the intrafusal muscle fibres to be stretched.
They are excited during overstretch of the muscle.
They are parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Consists of two types of intrafusal fibers

text: NSAIDs are best avoided in:
explanation: NSAIDs should be avoided in asthmatics (especially aspirin-induced asthma), patients with aspirin hypersensitivity, and those with GI bleeding history. All three represent absolute or relative contraindications to NSAID use.
keyConcept: NSAID contraindications: asthma, aspirin allergy, and GI bleeding history
options: Patients with a history of gastric bleeding

text: Synaptic delay is:
explanation: Synaptic delay refers to the minimal time (approximately 0.5 msec) required for neurotransmitter release, diffusion across the cleft, and receptor activation at a chemical synapse.
keyConcept: Synaptic delay is approximately 0.5 milliseconds in CNS.
options: The time needed for release of neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles.
The minimal delay time in the central nervous system is about 0.5 millisecond.
Determined by the type of the neurotransmitter.
Determined by the number of postsynaptic receptors.
The time needed for breakdown of neurotransmitter.

text: Concerning referred pain:
explanation: Referred pain is pain perceived in somatic structures distant from the diseased viscus, occurring when visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal segments.
keyConcept: Referred pain: visceral pain perceived in somatic area sharing same dorsal root level.
options: It is felt in the somatic structure innervated by different dorsal root from that innervating the diseased viscus.
It can’t be explained by convergence projection theory.
It can’t be explained by convergence facilitation theory.

subject: pharma

text: The correct statement regarding extrapyramidal effects of antipsychotics:
explanation: Extrapyramidal effects (EPS) occur most commonly with HIGH POTENCY agents (like haloperidol), not low potency. Option A is FALSE. Tardive dyskinesia is NOT relieved by anticholinergics - anticholinergics may actually worsen it. Option B is FALSE. Anticholinergics ARE useful in neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism (drug-induced parkinsonism responds to anticholinergics). Option C is TRUE. The answer is C - anticholinergics are useful in neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism. Typical antipsychotics: low potency (chlorpromazine) have less EPS but more sedation/anticholinergic; high potency (haloperidol) have more EPS but less sedation.
keyConcept: High potency antipsychotics (haloperidol) cause most EPS; anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism but not tardive dyskinesia.
options: Occur most commonly with low potency agents
Tardive dyskinesia is relieved by anticholinergics
Anticholinergics are useful in neuroleptic induced parkinsonism

subject: pharma

text: What is the cause of iatrogenic Parkinson’s disease?
explanation: Iatrogenic Parkinson's disease is caused by drugs that block dopamine receptors: antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, risperidone), antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), and some calcium channel blockers.选项A正确. The answer is A. Drug-induced parkinsonism is reversible upon drug discontinuation but may take weeks to months.
keyConcept: Dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) cause iatrogenic parkinsonism - reversible upon discontinuation.

subject: pharma

text: Mandibular nerve is sensory to:
explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) carries sensation from the lower lip (via the mental nerve), chin, temporal region, and anterior ear. It does not supply the upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or tip of the nose.
keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory supply includes the lower lip and chin

text: As regards the subcutaneous connective tissue layer of scalp, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The subcutaneous connective tissue layer of the scalp is dense and fibrous. Infections here are localized because the tissue is dense. Wounds bleed profusely because fibrous septa prevent vasoconstriction.
keyConcept: Subcutaneous connective tissue of scalp is dense; infection is localized and wounds bleed profusely
options: It contains arteries & nerves of scalp.
It connects skin of scalp with aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis.

subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following fibers is contained in nerve of pterygoid canal:
explanation: The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic from facial nerve) and the deep petrosal nerve (postganglionic sympathetic from internal carotid plexus). It runs through the pterygoid canal to reach the sphenopalatine ganglion and also provides sympathetic fibers to the nose and palate.
keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal contains postganglionic sympathetic fibers (deep petrosal nerve).
options: Taste from anterior part of tongue.
Taste from posterior part of tongue.

text: All the following are branches of the middle cervical sympathetic ganglion Except:
explanation: The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion (at C6 level) gives branches to the thyroid gland, cardiac branches, gray rami communicantes to C5-C6, and connections to superior and inferior cervical ganglia. The pharyngeal branch, however, arises primarily from the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion, not the middle cervical ganglion.
keyConcept: Pharyngeal branch arises from superior cervical sympathetic ganglion, NOT middle cervical ganglion.
options: Gray rami communicates to the fifth and sixth cervical nerves.
Connections with the inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The thymus gland originates mainly from:
explanation: The thymus gland originates from the VENTRAL wing of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. The dorsal wing of the 3rd pouch gives the inferior parathyroids. The thymus and inferior parathyroids develop together and migrate caudally; failure of this migration causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic and parathyroid aplasia).
keyConcept: Thymus originates from VENTRAL wing of 3rd pharyngeal pouch; migrates with inferior parathyroids (from dorsal 3rd pouch).
options: Ventral wing of the third pharyngeal pouch.
Dorsal wing of the third pharyngeal pouch.
Ventral wing of the fourth pharyngeal pouch.
Dorsal wing of the fourth pharyngeal pouch.

subject: anatomy

text: Congenital absence of parathyroid glands is due to aplasia of:
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome results from failure of development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches. Both the dorsal part (parathyroids) and ventral part (thymus) of the 3rd pouch are affected, as well as the 4th pouch. The correct answer is both dorsal 3rd and dorsal 4th pouches (E). The ultimobranchial body is a 5th pouch derivative and is not related to parathyroid development.
keyConcept: Congenital parathyroid absence (DiGeorge syndrome) = aplasia of dorsal 3rd pouch AND dorsal 4th pouch; thymus from ventral 3rd pouch.
options: Dorsal part of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch.
Dorsal part of the 4th pharyngeal pouch.
Ventral part of the 4th pharyngeal pouch.
Ventral part of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Congenital absence of thymus and parathyroid glands would result from absence of all the following, Except:
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome involves defective development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, causing thymic and parathyroid aplasia. The ultimobranchial body (5th pouch derivative giving parafollicular C cells) is NOT involved in DiGeorge syndrome. Therefore, absence of the ultimobranchial body would NOT cause thymus and parathyroid defects—making D the exception.
keyConcept: DiGeorge syndrome affects 3rd and 4th pouches; ultimobranchial body (5th pouch) is NOT involved—its absence causes C cell defects, not thymus/parathyroid defects.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The malleus and incus, which undergo endochrondral ossification, are thought to be derived from the:
explanation: The malleus and incus develop from Meckel's cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch. They undergo endochondral ossification and become the two largest ear ossicles. The stapes develops from Reichert's cartilage of the second arch. The otic placode gives rise to the inner ear structures.
keyConcept: Malleus and incus derived from Meckel's cartilage of 1st arch; undergo endochondral ossification.

subject: anatomy

text: Regarding lips all are true Except:
explanation: Lips: highly vascular, sensory innervation (upper V2, lower V3), motor by facial nerve, and lymph drainage varies by region.选项A正确. The answer is A. Upper lip lymph drains laterally to submandibular, medial to submental.
keyConcept: Lips: V2 (upper), V3 (lower) sensation, facial nerve motor, lateral lymph drainage to submandibular.
options: The main sensory supply to upper lip is facial nerve.
The main sensory supply to lower lip is mental nerve.
Their muscles are formed mainly by orbicularis oris.
Their blood supply is through facial artery.
In facial palsy lips can’t be dilated.

text: Regarding chorda tympani; all are correct statements Except:
explanation: Chorda tympani: carries taste from anterior 2/3 tongue (via lingual nerve), carries parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands, crosses middle ear, joins lingual nerve.选项C正确. The answer is C. It does NOT supply the tongue directly - runs with lingual nerve.
keyConcept: Chorda tympani: taste + parasympathetic to submandibular/sublingual - runs with lingual nerve to tongue.
options: It is a branch of facial nerve.
It joins lingual nerve deep to lateral pterygoid.
It is related to medial side of lower third molar.

subject: anatomy

text: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the DORSAL aspect of the closed medulla, forming the tubercles seen on the posterior surface. These nuclei receive proprioception and fine touch from the lower and upper body respectively.
keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei: dorsal closed medulla; receive proprioception and fine touch.

text: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior a branch of the retromandibular vein to form external jugular vein?
explanation: The posterior auricular vein joins the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) to form the external jugular vein. The facial vein drains into the common facial vein, then internal jugular.
keyConcept: Posterior auricular vein unites with retromandibular vein to form external jugular
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The first order neurons for pain and temperature pathway from face and head are located in:
explanation: First order neurons for pain and temperature from the face have cell bodies in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion, with central processes entering the spinal nucleus.
keyConcept: Facial pain first neuron
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: As regards back of pons, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus, not the facial nucleus. The facial nucleus lies more laterally and is overlain by the facial colliculus formed by fibers wrapping around the abducent nucleus.
keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus, not facial
options: Its apex is continuous with cerebral acqueduct.
Locus ceruleus lies at upper end of sulcus limitans.
Sulcus limitans lies lateral to medial eminence.
Vestibular area lies lateral to superior fovea.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior branch of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein?
explanation: The retromandibular vein unites with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.选项A正确. The answer is A. The external jugular drains the face and scalp.
keyConcept: Retromandibular vein + posterior auricular vein = external jugular vein.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa

text: All are contents of infratemporal fossa Except:
explanation: Infratemporal fossa contents: lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion.选项E正确. The answer is E. The pterygoid muscles and vessels are key contents.
keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa: pterygoid muscles, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion - NOT the orbit.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Basis pontis contain the following except:
explanation: Basis pontis contains corticospinal fibers (descending to spinal cord), corticonuclear fibers (to cranial nerve nuclei), and transverse pontine fibers (to cerebellum). Pontine reticulospinal fibers are in the tegmentum (not basis), along with other tegmental structures.
keyConcept: Basis pontis: corticospinal, corticonuclear, transverse pontine fibers. Tegmentum: reticulospinal, sensory nuclei.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: What is the lateral lemniscus formed of?
explanation: The lateral lemniscus is formed from ALL THREE acoustic stria (dorsal, intermediate, and ventral) plus fibers from the superior olivary nucleus and trapezoid body nuclei. It carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus.
keyConcept: Lateral lemniscus: from all 3 acoustic stria + superior olive + trapezoid nuclei → inferior colliculus.
options: Fibers from the nuclei of the trapezoid body
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa

text: A patient has difficulty voluntarily moving both eyes to the right side. This deficit is most likely due to a lesion in which area?
explanation: Horizontal gaze palsy indicates lesion in the abducens nucleus (CN VI) or PPRF (paramedian pontine reticular formation). The patient cannot voluntarily move eyes to the right, suggesting left PPRF/nucleus lesion.
keyConcept: Horizontal gaze control localizes to the pons (PPRF/CN VI nucleus) for voluntary eye movements.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which structure serves as the communication pathway between the infratemporal fossa and the pterygopalatine fossa?
explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure serves as the communication between the infratemporal fossa and the pterygopalatine fossa, allowing passage of vessels and nerves including the maxillary artery and pterygopalatine nerve branches.
keyConcept: Pterygomaxillary fissure connects infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae for neurovascular transmission.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The first order neurons in proprioception pathway from face and head are in:
explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains first order neurons for proprioception from the face, the only case of sensory neurons in the CNS.
keyConcept: Facial proprioception neurons
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The second order neuron in simple touch pathway from face and head are in:
explanation: Second order neurons for simple touch from the face are in the main (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.
keyConcept: Facial touch second neuron
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve belongs to which column of cranial nerve nuclei?
explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is a special visceral efferent (SVE) nucleus, innervating muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (muscles of mastication).
keyConcept: Motor nucleus of V is special visceral efferent (SVE).
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Cells of Cajal are present in:
explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: histology

text: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting between:
explanation: The central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting the red nucleus to the inferior olivary nucleus. It is involved in the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit that modulates cerebellar function.
keyConcept: Central tegmental tract connects red nucleus to inferior olivary nucleus
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: histology

text: Contralateral representation of face and body is found in:
explanation: The primary somatosensory and motor cortices have contralateral representation (homunculus). The face representation is in the lateral hemisphere near the Sylvian fissure, while body representation is medial near the longitudinal fissure.
keyConcept: Cortical representation is somatotopically organized with contralateral control for both motor and sensory functions.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text: Concerning the basal ganglia function, which is NOT true:
explanation: Basal ganglia mainly regulate/inhibit movement, not increase muscle tone. Option D is correct. The basal ganglia work through indirect pathways to inhibit excessive movement and regulate motor planning. Increased muscle tone is a brainstem/spinal cord function. Options A, B, C, and E all accurately describe basal ganglia functions in movement planning, timing, and suppression of unwanted movements.
keyConcept: The basal ganglia modulate movement patterns and timing while suppressing involuntary movements, rather than directly increasing muscle tone.
options: Caudate nucleus plan the sequence of patterns of movement.
Caudate nucleus modifies the timing of movements.
Putamen helps execution of subconscious learned pattern of movement.
Basal ganglia mainly increases the muscle tone.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text:
Which of the following describes learning?
A. Memory is not essential for it
B. Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
C. Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
D. Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
E. Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli
explanation: Operant (instrumental) conditioning is a type of associative learning where behavior is modified by consequences (reward or punishment), distinguishing it from non-associative learning.
keyConcept: Operant conditioning: associative learning via consequences.
options: Memory is not essential for it
Sensitization means decreased response to repeated stimuli
Operant conditioning is a type of associative learning
Habituation and sensitization are types of conditioning learning
Habituation means increased response to repeated stimuli
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text: The following muscle bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly:
explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded posteriorly by the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Anteriorly it is bounded by the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, superiorly by the posterior belly of digastric, and inferiorly by the superior belly of omohyoid. The sternocleidomastoid forms the posterior muscular boundary.
keyConcept: Sternocleidomastoid bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by ……… nerve.
explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and lower ear region as part of cervical plexus distribution.
keyConcept: Angle of mandible: great auricular nerve (C2-C3).
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: The following are branches of the vagus nerve in the neck Except:
explanation: The vagus nerve gives several branches in the neck: pharyngeal branch, superior laryngeal nerve, recurrent laryngeal nerve (left and right), and cardiac branches. The carotid body and carotid sinus, however, receive their sensory innervation from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the branch of Hering (carotid branch), NOT from the vagus nerve.
keyConcept: Branches to carotid body are from glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), NOT vagus.
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: The falx cerebri
explanation: The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus in its superior border; the diaphragma sellae separates the pituitary from the brain.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri anatomy
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: A patient complains of tremors in the right hand while doing fine movements. When asked to walk along a straight line on the floor, the patient sways over to the right side. When asked to touch his nose with his right index finger, the right hand displays tremor, and the finger tends to overshoot the target. At surgery, he is found to have tumour. Locate the possible site of tumour.
explanation: Intention tremor, overshoot (dysmetria), and swaying to the right during gait indicate a right cerebellar lesion; the tumor is in the right cerebellum.
keyConcept: Cerebellar lesion signs
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar fibers to the cerebral cortex is the:
explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the principal relay nucleus for cerebellar output destined for the cerebral cortex. It receives input from the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract, and projects to the motor and premotor cortices, influencing voluntary movement.
keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar fibers from the dentate nucleus to the motor cortex.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The second-order neuron transmitting pain and temperature sensation from the face is located in which nucleus?
explanation: For pain from the face, the second-order neuron is in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (not the principal sensory nucleus). Fibers then cross and ascend as the trigeminothalamic tract to the thalamus.
keyConcept: Spinal trigeminal nucleus is the second-order neuron for facial pain and temperature sensation.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Trigeminal lemniscus is present in:
explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) is present in the medulla and pons, carrying facial sensory information to the VPM thalamus.
keyConcept: Trigeminal lemniscus location
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Which thalamic nuclei receive input from the paleospinothalamic tract?
explanation: The paleospinothalamic tract (archispinothalamic) carries slow, dull pain and temperature to the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, which project diffusely to association cortex.
keyConcept: Paleospinothalamic tract terminates in intralaminar thalamic nuclei for poorly localized pain.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text:
The declarative memory is described by which one of the following?
A. It can be remembered after thinking of related events
B. Recall of general facts is the episodic type
C. Memory of personal experiences is the semantic type
D. Its center is in hippocampus and cerebellum
E. It cannot be converted to non-declarative memory
explanation: Declarative memory can be recalled by thinking of related events; it includes episodic (personal experiences) and semantic (general facts) components, primarily mediated by hippocampus.
keyConcept: Declarative memory: recalled through related events, hippocampal.
options: It can be remembered after thinking of related events
Recall of general facts is the episodic type
Memory of personal experiences is the semantic type
Its center is in hippocampus and cerebellum
It cannot be converted to non-declarative memory
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: How does the hypothalamus control endocrine functions Through nervous control?
explanation: Hypothalamic neurons directly control the posterior pituitary via axonal projections, releasing oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH) into systemic circulation in response to neural stimuli.
keyConcept: Hypothalamic-posterior pituitary connection
options: Control of posterior pituitary gland leads to secret oxytocin & vasopressin
Control of Adrenal medulla leads to secret catecholamines
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: How does the hypothalamus control endocrine functions Through hormonal control?
explanation: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones travel through the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system to control anterior pituitary hormone secretion, which then regulates peripheral endocrine glands.
keyConcept: Hypothalamic-anterior pituitary portal system
options: Control of Anterior pituitary gland, which controls most body endocrine glands
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Two reactions of the urea cycle take place in the mitochondria. These are
explanation: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in mitochondria: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate, and ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine. The remaining reactions occur in the cytosol.
keyConcept: Mitochondrial steps of urea cycle: CPS I and OTC
options: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamoylase.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: biochem

text: Intrapartum Group B streptococcus prophylaxis requirements:
explanation: All listed are established indications for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: GBS colonization, prior infant with GBS disease, and GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy all mandate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
keyConcept: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is indicated for colonization, prior affected infant, or GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy.
options: History of delivery of infant with GBS
History of GBS bacteriuria at any time during pregnancy
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy

text: Falx cerebri:
explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to the crista galli anteriorly and the tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri is dura between hemispheres
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The genu of the corpus callosum is supplied mainly by the:
explanation: The ACA supplies the genu of the corpus callosum.
keyConcept: Genu of corpus callosum supplied by anterior cerebral artery.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The falx cerebri:
explanation: The falx cerebri: a dura mater fold between cerebral hemispheres, attached to crista galli anteriorly and tentorium posteriorly, contains superior sagittal sinus.选项B正确. The answer is B. It prevents hemisphere displacement.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dura fold between hemispheres, contains superior sagittal sinus - prevents midline shift.
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Arachnoid barrier is the barrier between:
explanation: The arachnoid barrier cell layer separates extracerebral capillaries from the subarachnoid space, contributing to the blood-CSF barrier.
keyConcept: Arachnoid barrier function
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Concerning the pia matter, which of the following statements is true:
explanation: Pia mater is highly vascular (contains blood vessels that penetrate to supply superficial brain tissue). It is the innermost meninx, in direct contact with brain. Arachnoid contains spaces (subarachnoid) for CSF, not pia. Dura contains venous sinuses.
keyConcept: Pia mater: highly vascular, innermost meninx, follows brain contours closely.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: In the same patient (alcoholic, confusion, ataxia), which enzyme is affected?
explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; its deficiency impairs this enzyme causing neurological dysfunction in Wernicke-Korsakoff.
keyConcept: Thiamine-dependent enzymes
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: biochem

text: What is the triple therapy for cases with patients > 50 years or immunocompromised?
explanation: Triple therapy for patients >50 years or immunocompromised: Ampicillin + 3rd gen cephalosporin + Vancomycin. Adds Listeria and resistant pneumococcus coverage.选项A正确. The answer is A. Immunocompromised patients need broader coverage.
keyConcept: Elderly/immunocompromised meningitis: ampicillin + 3rd gen cephalosporin + vancomycin triple therapy.
options: Aminoglycosides, 1st & 2nd Generation of cephalosporines, Amphotericin B
