text: Neuroepithelial cells give rise to:
explanation: Neuroepithelial cells (radial glial cells) in the ventricular zone of the developing neural tube give rise to all the cellular elements of the CNS: neuroblasts (neurons), glioblasts (astrocytes and oligodendrocytes), and ependymal cells (lining the ventricles and central canal). The marginal zone contains axon tracts.
keyConcept: Neuroepithelial cells give rise to neuroblasts (neurons), glioblasts (astrocytes/oligodendrocytes), and ependymal cells.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Alar plates form:
explanation: The alar plates are the dorsal sensory horns of the spinal cord that develop from the alar (sensory) region of the neural tube. They form the dorsal (posterior) horns which receive sensory (afferent) fibers from the dorsal root ganglia. The basal plates form the ventral horns (motor).
keyConcept: Alar plates form the DORSAL HORNS of spinal cord (sensory); basal plates form VENTRAL horns (motor).
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Basal plates form:
explanation: Basal plates are the anterior (ventral) portions of the alar and basal plates in the developing neural tube. The basal plate gives rise to motor neurons that form the VENTRAL (anterior) horns of the spinal cord, which contain lower motor neurons. The alar plates form the dorsal (posterior) horns. Lateral horns appear only at T1-L2 levels (sympathetic neurons).
keyConcept: Basal plates form VENTRAL HORNS of spinal cord (motor neurons); alar plates form dorsal horns (sensory neurons).
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Dorsal tegmental decussation:
explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract, which crosses at the level of the inferior colliculus in the midbrain. It descends to control neck muscles in response to visual stimuli. It is not the rubrospinal tract and does not descend in all spinal segments.
keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level, controls neck muscles.
options: Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
Present in inferior level of midbrain.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Which structure is present at the level of the midbrain?
explanation: The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.
keyConcept: Midbrain structures
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following nerves arises from the union of the vagus and accessory nerves?
explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve is formed by the union of the external laryngeal nerve (from superior laryngeal of vagus) and the recurrent laryngeal nerve, but they join at the larynx, not intracranially.
keyConcept: Internal laryngeal nerve arises at the larynx from the superior laryngeal nerve division of CN X.
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding the fourth ventricle
explanation: The fourth ventricle is the cavity of the hindbrain (rhombencephalon), communicates with third ventricle above and subarachnoid space below via median/lateral apertures, and has a roof and floor.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle features
options: Is the cavity of hind brain
chapter: Miscellaneous and Embryology
subject: anatomy

text: Loss of sensation from lower eye lid indicates injury of:
explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits through the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. Loss of sensation indicates injury to this nerve.
keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid skin
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Orbicularis oris originates from:
explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle originates from the modiolus (a fibromuscular condensation at the angle of the mouth) and inserts into the lips. It acts as the sphincter of the mouth.
keyConcept: Orbicularis oris originates from the modiolus
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The Occipito-frontalis muscle:
explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The frontalis portion inserts into the epicranial aponeurosis.
keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis elevates the eyebrows
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Orbicularis oculi muscle:
explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: In adults the spinal cord usually terminates at the:
explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically ends at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is important clinically to avoid spinal cord injury during lumbar puncture, which is performed below this level.
keyConcept: Adult conus medullaris ends at lower border of L1
options: Upper border of the 12th thoracic vertebra.
Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 4th lumbar vertebra.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: As regards the nuclei of the anterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the CORRECT statement:
explanation: The anteromedial nuclear group extends at all levels of the spinal cord and supplies the axial muscles. Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal fibers; gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal fibers. The medial group supplies axial muscles, while the lateral group supplies limb muscles.
keyConcept: Anteromedial nucleus extends at all cord levels and supplies axial muscles
options: Its alpha neurons supply intrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anteromedial nucleus extends in all levels of spinal cord.
Its medial nuclear group supply muscles of limbs.
Its gamma neurons supply extrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anterolateral nucleus supplies muscles of hands & feet.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Cuneate tract:
explanation: The cuneate tract begins at the C8 spinal segment and carries conscious proprioception and fine touch from the upper limb. It does not start at mid-thoracic region—that level marks the beginning of the gracile tract.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract starts at C8, carries upper limb proprioception
options: Its main 2nd neuron is the accessory cuneate nucleus.
Its 3rd neuron passes in the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Its 3rd neuron terminates in the precentral gyrus.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament is called:
explanation: The membrana tectoria is the upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament that covers the dens and cruciate ligaments of the atlas. It extends from the body of the axis to the basiocciput, covering the odontoid process. The alar ligaments connect the dens to the occipital condyles; the apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
keyConcept: Membrana tectoria = upward extension of posterior longitudinal ligament covering dens and cruciate ligaments; covers C1-C2 joint.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The median atlanto-axial joint:
explanation: The median atlanto-axial joint is a PIVOT (trochoid) joint that allows rotation of the head (turning the head from side to side). This is the key movement tested in the question. The lateral atlanto-axial joints are also pivot joints. The atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid and allows nodding. The apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
keyConcept: Median atlanto-axial joint is PIVOT type; allows head rotation. Atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid; allows nodding.
options: Has the apical ligament connecting dens to atlas.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A patient presents with paralysis of the right foot. Which artery is most likely affected?
explanation: Foot drop indicates common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury, which is supplied by the anterior tibial artery. The anterior tibial artery supplies the deep compartment of the leg including the fibularis muscles.
keyConcept: Common peroneal nerve injury causes foot drop; nerve supplied by anterior tibial artery.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Second order neuron starts in ....... goes via ...........
explanation: Second order neurons in the crude touch pathway start in the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus) of the spinal cord and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
keyConcept: Crude touch second neuron
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: First order neuron of pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
explanation: First order neurons for pain/temperature are small cells in dorsal root ganglia whose fibers enter via the lateral division of the posterior root and synapse in substantia gelatinosa.
keyConcept: Pain first order neuron
options: small cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
small cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root
medium cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
large cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Second order neuron in pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
explanation: Second order neurons for pain/temperature start in the substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) of the posterior horn and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
keyConcept: Pain second order neuron
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is a character of thoracic level of spinal cord?
explanation: Thoracic spinal cord has lateral horns (intermediolateral cell columns) containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons, giving it 4 horns.
keyConcept: Thoracic spinal cord
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A patient with lesion in the right gracile nucleus is expected to have diminished:
explanation: Lesion of the right gracile nucleus impairs fine touch and stereognosis on the right lower limb (ipsilateral) because the gracile tract is already ipsilateral.
keyConcept: Gracile nucleus lesion effects
options: tactile localization at the right arm
fine touch at the left leg
tactile discrimination at the right leg
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Concerning the interpeduncular fossa, one of the following is a boundary of the fossa:
explanation: The optic tract forms the lateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa; the cerebral peduncles form the posterior boundary.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The internal arcuate fibres are axons of which nucleus?
explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of the cuneate and gracile nuclei that cross at the sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fiber origin
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The representational (non‑dominant) hemisphere in most people is described by which feature?
explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere in most people lies in the right hemisphere and is specialized for spatial and holistic processing.
keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere
options: It is responsible for language comprehension.
It always lies in the left hemisphere.
It is concerned with analytical tasks.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Methyl‑THF donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form:
explanation: Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
keyConcept: Methyl-THF function
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The central nervous system is soft because it:
explanation: The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.
keyConcept: CNS softness cause
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: The pterion is a clinically important landmark because it overlies the:
explanation: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, making it a critical landmark as fractures here can cause epidural hemorrhage.
keyConcept: Pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
options: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Tight scalene muscles can compress:
explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Choose the wrong statement about the subclavian vein:
explanation: The subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to the anterior scalene muscle (not posterior), making it vulnerable to compression during clavicle fractures.
keyConcept: Subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to anterior scalene.
options: It is the continuation of the axillary vein.
It is separated from subclavian artery by anterior scalene muscle.
It grooves the 1st rib posterior to scalene tubercle.
It receives the external jugular vein.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Internal carotid blood is lost in injury of the:
explanation: The internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via branches of the ophthalmic artery. Injury to the forehead region would lead to blood loss from the internal carotid system. The chin and cheek are supplied by external carotid branches.
keyConcept: Forehead injury can lead to internal carotid blood loss
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: One of the following arteries does not share in formation of circle of Willis:
explanation: Middle cerebral artery does NOT directly participate in the circle of Willis; it arises from the internal carotid as a branch outside the circle. The circle includes ACA, PCA, ICA, and posterior communicating arteries.
keyConcept: Circle of Willis exclusion
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding vagus nerve; all are true Except:
explanation: The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve, descends within the carotid sheath, has two ganglia (jugular and nodose), and injury causes tachycardia due to loss of parasympathetic tone. However, the vagus is NOT joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve. Only the cranial root of accessory joins the vagus; the spinal root forms the separate spinal accessory nerve supplying SCM and trapezius.
keyConcept: Vagus is joined by cranial root of accessory, NOT spinal root.
options: It is the longest cranial nerve.
It is joined by the spinal root of the accessory nerve.
It descends within the carotid sheath.
Its injury leads to palpitation and tachycardia (increase in heart rate).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: anatomy

text: About spinal nerve all true except:
explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Which of the following statements concerning the lateral horn of the spinal cord is TRUE?
explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels
options: Gives origin to pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers.
It is most prominent at sacral levels.
It is present in all spinal cord levels.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: The following histological picture is not characteristic of Glioblastoma multiforme:
explanation: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma multiforme. GBM shows highly anaplastic cells, necrosis, tumor giant cells, and vascular proliferation. Papillary architecture is seen in papillary ependymomas or papillary meningiomas.
keyConcept: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma - EXCEPTION
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT:
explanation: In the closed medulla, the main inferior olivary nucleus is present, and it contains the gracile and cuneate nuclei on the dorsal aspect. The motor decussation is in the lower part, and sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers) is at a higher level - making 'higher level has sensory decussation' TRUE, not the exception.
keyConcept: Closed medulla: motor decussation lower, sensory decussation at higher level
options: In the lower part, there are motor decussation.
At a higher level, there are sensory decussation.
Contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: histology

text: Mass reflex:
explanation: Mass reflex has pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder. Option B is correct. Mass reflex is a spinal reflex appearing after spinal shock resolution in complete transection; strong stimuli to skin trigger flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge. Options A, C, D are incorrect (upper limb rigidity is wrong, immediate occurrence is wrong, basoganglia involvement is wrong).
keyConcept: Mass reflex (flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge) indicates complete spinal cord transection with recovered spinal reflexes.
options: Has a pattern of rigidity of upper limbs.
Has a pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder.
Occurs immediately after spinal cord transcetion.
Is elicited by in patients with basal ganglia lesions.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Regarding the stretch reflex, which sentence is NOT true:
explanation: Stretch reflex is a polysynaptic reflex - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Stretch reflex is MONOsynaptic (one synapse between Ia afferent and alpha motor neuron). Options A, B, D, E are correct: elicited by passive stretch, depends on spindle parallel to extrafusal, causes muscle contraction, inhibits antagonists.
keyConcept: The stretch reflex is the prototypical monosynaptic reflex with a single excitatory synapse.
options: Can be elicited by passive stretch.
Depends on the muscle spindle which is a mechanoreceptor present parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Stretch of a muscle is followed by its contraction.
Is associated with simultaneous inhibition of the antagonist muscle.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: What is the role of normal limbic system in maternal & sexual behavior?
explanation: Normal limbic system function is essential for maternal behavior (nurturing and bonding) and proper sexual behavior, with the medial preoptic area and limbic circuits coordinating these instinctual behaviors.
keyConcept: Limbic system and reproductive behaviors
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which statement regarding sensory fiber conduction is correct?
explanation: Sensory fiber conduction velocity correlates with fiber diameter: A-delta fibers (5-15 m/s) transmit fast pain; C fibers (0.5-2 m/s) transmit slow pain. Myelination increases conduction velocity.
keyConcept: Conduction velocity in sensory fibers depends on diameter and myelination: A-delta > C fibers.
options: Crude touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Fine touch is carried on C fibers
Fine touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Vibration sense is carried on Aδ fibers
Nociceptive stimuli are carried on Aβ fibers
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which clinical sign is seen in chronic gastritis due to inflammation of the stomach wall?
explanation: Chronic gastritis causing inflammation of the stomach body (where parietal cells are located) leads to loss of intrinsic factor and reduced acid production, resulting in pernicious anemia with neurological manifestations.
keyConcept: Parietal cell destruction in body gastritis causes intrinsic factor deficiency and pernicious anemia.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: physiology

text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin-secreting tumor)?
explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (serotonin-secreting tumor) is diagnosed by measuring 5-Hydroxyindole-acetic acid (5-HIAA) in 24-hour urine - this is the main serotonin metabolite. 5-HIAA is elevated in carcinoid tumors. VMA is for pheochromocytoma. Phenylacetylglutamine is a phenylalanine metabolite.
keyConcept: Carcinoid diagnosis: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite). VMA = catecholamine metabolite (pheochromocytoma).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: All of the following are ketogenic Amino acids except:
explanation: Glycine is a glucogenic amino acid, not ketogenic. Leucine and isoleucine are purely ketogenic. Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Lysine is also purely ketogenic. Glycine is converted to serine (glucogenic) or to porphyrins.
keyConcept: Purely ketogenic: leucine, lysine. Both glucogenic/ketogenic: isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan. Glucogenic: glycine, alanine, serine.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of which of the following?
explanation: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of GLUTAMINE (via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes). The brain uses this pathway to detoxify ammonia. Alanine synthesis occurs in liver (not brain). Glutamate is made from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia but requires different enzymes.
keyConcept: Normal ammonia disposal in brain: glutamine synthetase (astrocytes) converts glutamate + NH3 → glutamine.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Ammonia toxicity to the brain is Probably through which of the Following mechanisms?
explanation: Ammonia toxicity primarily inhibits the citric acid cycle (energy production) by depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate. It does NOT increase GABA (it decreases it). It causes alkalosis (not acidosis). Brain can still use amino acids.
keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibits TCA cycle (depletes alpha-ketoglutarate), depletes glutamate → decreased GABA → neurological symptoms.
options: Inhibition of energy production in brain Cells.
Production of increased amounts of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
Acidifying effect on the intra- and extracellular fluids.
Conversion to urea, increasing the Osmotic pressure.
Inability of the brain cells to utilize any of the amino acids.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Hyperammonemia may be caused by
explanation: Primary hyperammonemia results from genetic defects in any urea cycle enzyme. Secondary hyperammonemia results from liver failure (inability to convert ammonia to urea). Both causes lead to ammonia accumulation.
keyConcept: Hyperammonemia: primary (urea cycle enzyme defect) or secondary (liver failure). Both cause ammonia accumulation.
options: genetic defect of any enzyme of urea cycle (primary hyperammonemia).
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of
explanation: PKU results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency prevents the normal metabolism of phenylalanine, leading to accumulation and conversion to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate).
keyConcept: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones → intellectual disability if untreated.
options: Conversion of phenylalanine to  a phenylketoacid.
Production of phenylalanine from  a phenylketoacid.
Reaction of phenylalanine with an α-ketoacid.
Conversion of phenylalanine to another aminoacid.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Conversion of Phenylalanine to tyrosine is catalyzed by phenylalanine hydroxylase which requires.
explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, along with oxygen and NADPH. BH4 is also required for tyrosine hydroxylase (dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin synthesis).
keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: requires BH4, O2, NADPH. BH4 deficiency causes malignant PKU.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: In brain cells, glucose is phosphorylated by
explanation: Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.
keyConcept: Brain hexokinase glucose phosphorylation
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is
explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages.
keyConcept: iNOS as calcium-independent NOS isozyme in phagocytes
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: In the urea cycle, urea is produced from
explanation: Arginine is cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine in the final step of the urea cycle. Fumarate is produced earlier from argininosuccinate. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase initiates the cycle by fixing ammonia and CO2.
keyConcept: Arginase cleavage of arginine to produce urea and ornithine
options: carbon dioxide and ammonium ions by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Although arginine is formed in the urea cycle, it is considered an essential amino-acid. Why?
explanation: Although the urea cycle synthesizes arginine, the rate of endogenous synthesis is insufficient for the demands of rapid growth in infants and children, making it a conditionally essential amino acid during development. Adults normally synthesize adequate arginine.
keyConcept: Arginine as conditionally essential amino acid in children
options: It must be broken down by arginase enzyme.
Its rate of synthesis is not enough for growing children.
It is formed in the cytosol, therefore it cannot be used.
It is formed in the D-configuration.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Ammonia is introduced in the urea cycle by
explanation: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes the reversible interconversion of serine and glycine in the cytosol and mitochondria. This reaction transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, essential for nucleotide synthesis.
keyConcept: Serine-glycine interconversion via SHMT generating one-carbon units
options: reacting as ammonium ion with carbon dioxide and ATP.
making a part of N-acetyl glutamate.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: ATP is consumed in which of the following reactions?
explanation: ATP is consumed in the CPS I reaction (2 ATP to 1 ADP) and the argininosuccinate synthetase reaction (ATP to AMP + PPi, effectively 2 ATP). Ornithine transcarbamylase does not require ATP; it transfers the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine.
keyConcept: ATP consumption at CPS I and ASS steps of urea cycle
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which reaction of the urea cycle is the primary control reaction of the pathway?
explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, controlled allosterically by N-acetylglutamate (NAG). This ensures the cycle activates only when ammonia and acetyl-CoA are available for detoxification.
keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting, NAG-regulated step of urea cycle
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin secreting tumor)?
explanation: Carcinoid syndrome diagnosis uses elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main serotonin metabolite, not serotonin itself.
keyConcept: 5-HIAA in 24-hour urine is diagnostic for carcinoid syndrome
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following reactions produces carbon dioxide?
explanation: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase produces CO2 as a byproduct of the decarboxylation reaction. Acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis) also produces CO2.
keyConcept: Decarboxylation of 5-HTP to serotonin produces carbon dioxide
options: Conversion of acetyl CoA to malonyl CoA.
Synthesis of serotonin from its precursor.
Action of monoamine oxidase on norepinephrine.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) occurs by a:
explanation: GABA is synthesized by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. This is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
keyConcept: GABA synthesis by PLP-dependent decarboxylation of glutamate
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following may be considered a physiological ammonia-fixing reaction?
explanation: Both glutamine synthetase (in brain and peripheral tissues) and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (in liver mitochondria) fix ammonia. Glutamine synthetase incorporates ammonia into glutamine for safe transport; CPS I initiates the urea cycle.
keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase and CPS I are physiological ammonia-fixing reactions
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Glutamine is important.
explanation: Glutamine serves multiple critical functions: safe ammonia transport (amide nitrogen), ammonia detoxification (brain and muscle), and as nitrogen donor for asparagine, purine, and pyrimidine synthesis.
keyConcept: Glutamine as safe ammonia carrier and nitrogen donor for nucleotides
options: For safe transport of ammonia as the amide nitrogen.
As the major source of ammonia for urinary excretion.
For synthesis of asparagine, purines, and pyrimidines.
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: A genetic defect of an enzyme of urea cycle leads to
explanation: Urea cycle enzyme defects cause hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine (as the body compensatorily shunts ammonia to glutamine synthesis). Blood urea is typically low; ammonia is high.
keyConcept: Urea cycle defect: high blood glutamine, high ammonia, low urea
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of
explanation: Ammonia is normally used for glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase (the primary ammonia detoxification pathway). The glutamine amide nitrogen is then transported to the liver for urea synthesis.
keyConcept: Ammonia is normally fixed into glutamine for safe transport and excretion
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which statement about ketone bodies is correct?
explanation: Ketone bodies are not a major energy source in the well-fed state; the brain preferentially uses glucose. They become important during starvation when glucose is scarce.
keyConcept: Ketone body utilization states
options: Main energy source for the brain
Main energy source for the liver during starvation
Not a major source of energy in well‑fed state
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: During starvation, which of the following occurs?
explanation: During starvation, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) as an alternative fuel when glucose availability decreases.
keyConcept: Starvation brain metabolism
options: Ketone bodies are utilized in liver
Ketone bodies are utilized in brain
Fatty acids are utilized in brain
Amino acids are utilized in brain
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which enzyme is absent in neurons?
explanation: Neurons lack PFK2/FBPase3 (the bifunctional enzyme that produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate), resulting in low glycolytic rate and dependence on oxidative metabolism.
keyConcept: Neuronal metabolic enzymes
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which laboratory finding is used as a marker for carcinoid tumor?
explanation: 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main metabolite of serotonin, is elevated in urine and used as a marker for carcinoid tumors that secrete serotonin.
keyConcept: Carcinoid tumor markers
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: Which substance acts as an antioxidant in astrocytes by forming reduced glutathione?
explanation: NADPH in astrocytes provides reducing equivalents for the glutathione reductase system, converting GSSG to reduced glutathione (GSH) to combat oxidative stress.
keyConcept: Astrocyte antioxidant systems
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: The conversion of which requires vitamin B12 and folic acid?
explanation: Homocysteine to methionine conversion requires both vitamin B12 (as methylcobalamin) and folic acid (as methyltetrahydrofolate) for the methionine synthase reaction.
keyConcept: Homocysteine metabolism vitamins
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: biochem

text: What are the microscopic features of Ependymomas?
explanation: Ependymoma microscopic features include: perivascular pseudorosettes (tumor cells arranged around blood vessels with fibrillary processes) and true ependymal rosettes (tumor cells arranged around central lumen). The cells have uniform, round to oval nuclei. The answer is A. Perivascular pseudorosettes are the most distinctive feature. GFAP is positive.
keyConcept: Ependymomas show perivascular pseudorosettes and true rosettes - diagnostic histological features.
options: Uniform small cells, round to oval nuclei with granular chromatin
Highly cellular with marked nuclear atypia
chapter: Introduction to CNS
subject: pathology

text: What are the key microscopic features of oligodendrogliomas WHO grade II?
explanation: Oligodendroglioma WHO grade II shows: sheets of regular cells with rounded nuclei containing finely granular rounded chromatin ('fried egg' appearance), surrounded by clear halo (perinuclear halo), and characteristic 'chicken-wire' or anastomosing capillary network. Option A is CORRECT. Highly cellular with marked nuclear atypia (B) suggests higher grade (anaplastic). Rosenthal fibers (C) and eosinophilic granular bodies (D) are seen in pilocytic astrocytoma. The answer is A. The 'fried egg' cells and capillary network are classic histological features.
keyConcept: Oligodendrogliomas show 'fried egg' cells with perinuclear halos and 'chicken-wire' capillary network.
options: Sheets of regular cells with rounded nuclei containing finely granular rounded chromatin surrounded by a clear halo of cytoplasm and anastomosing capillaries
Highly cellular with marked nuclear atypia

Adding propranolol (beta-blocker) to lidocaine is CORRECT because propranolol decreases hepatic blood flow, reducing lidocaine metabolism, potentially increasing lidocaine levels and toxicity. All anterior limb of internal capsule.

text: A 2-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty sucking. His mother reports that he has been having trouble breastfeeding for the past few weeks. She also notices that he has difficulty closing his lips completely. Which of the following muscles is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: Orbicularis oris is the muscle of the lips that allows pursing, tightening, and closure of the mouth (essential for breastfeeding and sucking). Weakness causes inability to close lips completely (milk dribbles out). The buccinator keeps food between teeth during chewing; the frontalis and occipitalis are muscles of facial expression in the scalp.
keyConcept: Orbicularis oris surrounds the mouth and is essential for lip closure and sucking; weakness causes dribbling of milk.

subject: anatomy

text: Which facial muscle receives only contralateral cortical innervation?
explanation: The mentalis muscle (chin) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Other lower facial muscles receive partial bilateral innervation, which is why upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead.
keyConcept: Contralateral only innervation of lower face muscles distinguishes UMN from LMN facial palsy.
options: Orbicularis oculi of the upper face
Orbicularis oris of the lower face

subject: anatomy

text: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
keyConcept: Golgi tendon reflex

text: As regards corticobulbar tract, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The corticobulbar tract ends on bilateral cranial nerve nuclei, not only contralateral. Some nuclei (like the lower facial) have predominantly contralateral input, but all have some bilateral contribution.
keyConcept: Corticobulbar has bilateral cranial nerve connections
options: It ends on contralateral cranial nerve nuclei only.
The part of facial nucleus that controls right half of orbicularis oris muscle receives left corticonuclear tract.
The left genioglossus muscle is controlled by right corticonuclear tract.
It forms a part of upper motor neuron.

subject: anatomy

text: Nucleus ambiguuus supplies all the following muscles EXCPT:
explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the first-order neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication. Unique among sensory nuclei, it contains cell bodies of primary afferent neurons.
keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V is 1st neuron for mastication proprioception

text: A 25 year old woman suffers from a traumatic scalp avulsion due to a revolving machinery at her workplace. All the following are considered boundaries for the scalp EXCEPT:
explanation: The scalp is bounded by: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (laterally), and supraorbital arch/ridge (anterior). The EXTERNAL OCCIPITAL PROTUBERANCE is a landmark on the skull but the scalp's posterior boundary is the superior nuchal line, not the protuberance itself. The zygomatic arch is the lateral boundary; zygomatic bone is part of the face, not a boundary of the scalp.
keyConcept: Scalp boundaries: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (lateral), supraorbital arch (anterior). External occipital protuberance is a skull landmark, not scalp boundary.

subject: anatomy

text: One of the relays nuclel of auditory pathway is:
explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus. The trapezoid body also passes through this area.
keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive (binaural hearing) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
explanation: The medial lemniscus carries somatosensory information (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), not auditory information. Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex.
keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: Which structure contains the first order neurons for facial pain and temperature?
explanation: The trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion) contains first-order neurons for facial pain and temperature sensation. Central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve.
keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion is the sensory ganglion for facial pain and temperature via cranial nerve V.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: All characters of spino-tectal tract except:
explanation: The spinotectal tract arises from posterior horn cells (laminae I, V), ascends contralaterally to the superior colliculus for reflex eye/head movements, not the inferior olivary nucleus.
keyConcept: Spinotectal tract
options: arise from nerve cell in posterior horn (I,V)
ascend at all level of spinal on opposite side then tectum in mid brain
drive reflex, movement of eye, head
ascend in inferior olivary nucleus in medulla

subject: anatomy

text: On the medial surface of the infratemporal fossa lies the:
explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall.
keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid muscle lies on medial surface of infratemporal fossa.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: All the following are true about the middle meningeal artery EXCEPT:
explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.
options: It is the largest meningeal artery.
It is a branch from 1st part of maxillary artery.
It enters the cranial cavity through foramen ovale.
It gives frontal and parietal terminal branches.

text: Which of the following nerves supplying the scalp and face is not derived from the trigeminal nerve?
explanation: The greater occipital nerve (C2) is NOT derived from the trigeminal nerve - it's a dorsal ramus of C2.选项A正确. The answer is A. It supplies the scalp posterior to the auricle.
keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) is the only scalp nerve not from trigeminal - supplies posterior scalp.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: anatomy

text: As regards medulla oblongata, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies MEDIAL to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Rootlets emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The statement in option D incorrectly places it lateral to ICP.
keyConcept: Vagus nerve medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Olive lies just lateral to anterior median fissure.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle lies lateral to olive.
XII cranial nerve exits from medulla lateral to pyramid.
X cranial nerve lies medial to inferior cerebellar peduncle.
XI cranial nerve is attached to posterolateral sulcus.

text: Superior colliculus, all true except:
explanation: The superior colliculus is NOT directly connected to the occipital cortex - that connection is via the visual cortex and lateral geniculate body. The superior colliculus is connected to the retina (via retinal ganglion cells), and gives rise to the tectospinal tract and dorsal tegmental decussation.
keyConcept: Superior colliculus: connected to retina, not occipital cortex; gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental decussation.
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental decussation.
Present in tectum of the upper midbrain.

subject: anatomy

text: The crossed corticospinal tract occupies the:
explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract occupies the lateral white column of the spinal cord. It is the continuation of the pyramidal decussation and controls voluntary movement of the contralateral limbs.
keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal tract in lateral white column
options: Lateral white column of spinal cord.

subject: anatomy

text: Fibers of vagus nerve exit ….
explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) exits the brainstem between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle, at the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla. This is the same level where glossopharyngeal and accessary nerves also emerge.
keyConcept: Vagus nerve: exits between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle at posterolateral sulcus.

subject: anatomy

text: Mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve:
explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains pseudo-unipolar neurons (first-order neurons) for proprioception from face, muscles, and temporomandibular joint. It is the only sensory nucleus with cell bodies in the CNS.
keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus contains pseudo-unipolar neurons for facial proprioception (1st order)
options: Formed of 2nd order neuron of proprioception from face.
Extend in the midbrain in the level of inferior colliculus only.
Contain 1st order neurons of pain from face.

text: Which sentence is NOT true about sensitization:
explanation: Sensitization can last much longer than 60 seconds - it can persist for days in long-term sensitization. It does involve serotonergic facilitation, operates in both short and long-term memory, and is associated with noxious stimuli paired to benign ones.
keyConcept: Sensitization: enhanced response to stimuli after noxious input; serotonergic facilitation; can be short or long-term.
options: A prolonged augmented response occurs when a noxious stimulus paired to a benign stimulus.
It is due to serotonin-induced facilitation.
It continues up to 60 seconds after removal of the stimulus.

text: What is responsible for the conscious discrimination of odors?
explanation: Conscious odor discrimination is mediated by the orbitofrontal and frontal neocortex, which receives processed olfactory information via thalamic relays, allowing identification and naming of odors.
keyConcept: Neocortical olfactory discrimination
options: Lateral & VM hypothalamus, septum, Amygdala, thalamus & basal ganglia
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text: The supplementary motor area is primarily responsible for which function?
explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) programs complex motor sequences and bimanual coordination, becoming active before voluntary movement initiation.
keyConcept: SMA mediates motor sequence planning and bimanual coordination prior to primary motor cortex activation.
options: Control of complex movements of both hands

text:
The representational hemisphere is described by which one of the following?
A. It always lies in left hemisphere
B. It has no function
C. It is responsible for visuospatial relations
D. It is concerned with language
E. It contains speech Centre
explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere, usually right, is responsible for visuospatial relationships and perceiving the spatial positions of objects in the environment.
keyConcept: Representational hemisphere: visuospatial relations (usually right).
options: It always lies in left hemisphere
It is responsible for visuospatial relations

text: Which sentence is NOT true about the Amygdala:
explanation: The amygdala is NOT the area for consolidation of memory - that is the hippocampus. The amygdala processes emotional responses and emotional components of memories. Lesion leads to hypoactive emotional response, not hyperphagia. Stimulation causes rage.
keyConcept: Amygdala: emotional processing of memories. Hippocampus: memory consolidation. Different structures.
options: Is involved in processing of the emotional components of memories.
Is involved in processing of the emotional responses to odors.
Its lesion leads to hyperphagia and omniphagia.
Its stimulation leads to rage and aggression.
Is the area for consolidation of memory.

text: Ankle clonus occurs due to:
explanation: Ankle clonus results from hyperactive stretch reflexes where sustained muscle stretch produces rhythmic oscillating contractions due to UMN lesions and increased gamma motor neuron activity.
keyConcept: Clonus is a sustained stretch reflex response from hyperexcitable muscle spindles in UMN lesions.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text:
Which of the following is Not characterizing the pyramidal tract?
A. It has only cortical origin.
B. It terminates on AHCs and cranial nerve nuclei.
C. It is functioning since birth.
D. 90% of it cross to opposite side at medulla.
E. It is only one neuron from cortex to AHCs.
explanation: The pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth (infants have primitive reflexes but lack voluntary control); it matures over the first two years as corticospinal fibers fully develop.
keyConcept: Pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth.
options: It terminates on AHCs and cranial nerve nuclei
90% of it cross to opposite side at medulla
It is only one neuron from cortex to AHCs

subject: physiology

text: Muscle contraction in response to maintained stretch is initiated by sensory inputs from:
explanation: Nuclear bag fibers (type Ia afferents) detect the velocity and degree of muscle stretch and initiate the stretch reflex. Nuclear chain fibers contribute to static sensitivity. Golgi tendon organs detect tension, not stretch per se.
keyConcept: Nuclear bag fibers: dynamic stretch detection; nuclear chain fibers: static stretch detection.
chapter: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa
subject: physiology

text: Which response occurs in a stretch reflex? (variant)
explanation: In a stretch reflex, muscle spindle afferents detect stretch and monosynaptically activate alpha motor neurons causing homonymous muscle contraction, with gamma bias facilitating the response.
keyConcept: Stretch reflex is monosynaptic: spindle afferents directly excite alpha motor neurons causing homonymous contraction.
options: Activation of gamma motor neurons only

subject: physiology

text:
Muscle stretch reflex is facilitated by:
A. Medullary reticular formation
B. Cortical area 4
C. Red nucleus
D. Cortical area 6
E. Lentiform nucleus of basal ganglia
explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) facilitates the muscle stretch reflex through corticospinal influences on gamma motor neurons that regulate muscle spindle sensitivity.
keyConcept: Cortical area 4 facilitates stretch reflex via corticospinal influence on gamma neurons.

subject: physiology

text: Which sentence is NOT true about the reticular formation:
explanation: The excitatory component of reticular formation is located in the PONS, not the medulla. The medullary RF is inhibitory. All other statements about ARAS being excitatory, pontine part facilitating spinal cord, and reticular formation being stimulated by cortical/sensory inputs are true.
keyConcept: Reticular formation: pontine part = excitatory (ARAS); medullary part = inhibitory.
options: Its excitatory component is located in the pons.
Its medullary component is inhibitory to all cortical areas.
Its excitatory components constitutes the ARAS.
Its pontine part is excitatory to spinal cord motor neurons.
It is stimulated by both of Corticofugal and sensory fibers.

subject: physiology

text: Which of the following is NOT involved in decreasing the activity of the pontine reticular formation?
explanation: The red nucleus is a facilitatory center that INCREASES pontine reticular formation activity, not decreases it. Cortical inhibitory areas, medullary RF, basal ganglia, and corticofugal fibers all decrease pontine RF activity.
keyConcept: Red nucleus facilitates pontine RF; cortical areas, basal ganglia, medullary RF inhibit it.

subject: physiology

text: Concerning reticular formation, all are true EXCEPT:
explanation: Red nucleus and paleocerebellum FACILITATE (not inhibit) the pontine reticular formation. The pontine RF is the excitatory ARAS component. The medullary RF is inhibitory to antigravity muscles.
keyConcept: Pontine RF: facilitatory, activated by red nucleus/paleocerebellum. Medullary RF: inhibitory to antigravity muscles.
options: It receives impulses from various somatic and special sense pathways.
Its inhibitory motor part inhibits the spinal cord motor neurons of antigravity muscles.
Its facilitatory motor part excites both the cortex and the spinal cord.
Its intrinsic activities characterized by diffuse electric activity of all its components.
Red nucleus and paleocerebellum inhibit its pontine component.

text: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is inducible?
explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages during inflammatory responses.
keyConcept: iNOS (phagocytic) is the inducible, calcium-independent NOS isozyme

text: Tic douloureux:
explanation: Tic douloureux (trigeminal neuralgia) causes sharp, lancinating facial pain due to trigeminal nerve dysfunction, often triggered by innocuous stimuli like touching the face.
keyConcept: Tic douloureux: sharp lancinating pain in trigeminal distribution.
options: Is due to convergence facilitation theory.
Is due to sensitization of pain receptors by chemicals.
Sharp lancinating pain in the distribution of the facial nerve.
Is an example of secondary hyperalgesia.

text: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the CERVICAL spinal cord, not the whole length. It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination. It does not extend into the lumbosacral cord.
keyConcept: MLF: brainstem to cervical cord; connects vestibular nuclei to control head/neck movements.
options: receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck
extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.

text: Which nucleus is located in the special visceral efferent (SVE) column?
explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is located in the SVE (special visceral efferent) column and innervates muscles derived from pharyngeal arches: stylopharyngeus (IX), pharyngeal muscles (X), sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (XI).
keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus is the SVE column nucleus for pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.

text: Fracture of neck of mandible can lead to injury of all the following EXCEPT:
explanation: The masseteric nerve runs on the lateral surface of the mandibular neck, so it can be injured in fractures; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves are also at risk, but auriculotemporal is not typically affected.
keyConcept: Mandibular neck fracture: masseteric, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves at risk.

text: Which of the following is a tributary of subclavian vein?
explanation: The external jugular vein is a large superficial vein that descends in the neck superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein proximal to its junction with the internal jugular vein. It serves as a major venous drainage pathway from the scalp and face and is clinically important as an easily accessible vein.
keyConcept: External jugular vein drains into subclavian vein.

text: Inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (ICSE) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
explanation: The inferior cervical sympathetic ganglion (often fused with the first thoracic ganglion to form the stellate ganglion) is located at the level of C7 near the neck of the first rib. It gives communicating branches to C7 and C8, vascular plexus around the vertebral artery, cardiac branches to the deep cardiac plexus, and branches to the subclavian artery. It does NOT give pharyngeal branches, which originate from the superior cervical ganglion.
keyConcept: Pharyngeal branches come from superior cervical ganglion, NOT inferior cervical ganglion.
options: A cardiac branch to deep cardiac plexus.

text: Which of the following nerves supplying scalp and face Is not derived from trigeminal nerve?
explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is derived from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. It supplies the skin over the parotid gland and mastoid area. The auriculotemporal, zygomaticotemporal, supraorbital, and supratrochlear are all trigeminal branches.
keyConcept: Great auricular nerve from C2-C3 cervical plexus, not trigeminal (V)
chapter: Anatomy of the Neck
subject: anatomy

text: A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?
explanation: The lesser occipital nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2) that supplies the skin of the scalp posterior to the ear and the upper part of the lateral surface of the auricle. The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the posterior scalp near the midline. The posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII) supplies behind the ear.
keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior and lateral to the ear (posterolateral scalp).

subject: anatomy

text: Which infrahyoid muscle is not supplied by the ansa cervicalis?
explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid (both bellies), and thyrohyoid (via a branch from C1 to hypoglossal). However, the thyrohyoid is officially supplied by a branch from C1 that runs with the hypoglossal nerve and then descends as the nerve to thyrohyoid, bypassing the ansa cervicalis proper. Wait, among the options, thyrohyoid IS supplied by ansa fibers (C1) but NOT by the ansa loop itself. So E is the best answer.
keyConcept: Thyrohyoid is supplied by nerve to thyrohyoid from C1 via hypoglossal, not by the ansa proper.

text: Regarding sternocleidomastoid all are true Except:
explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle arises from the manubrium sterni (anterior surface, not back) and the medial third of the clavicle. The anterior jugular vein crosses superficial (not deep) to the SCM in the superficial fascia. The external jugular vein is superficial to it, the lesser occipital nerve runs along its posterior border, and it is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
keyConcept: Anterior jugular vein crosses superficial, NOT deep, to sternocleidomastoid.
options: It arises from the back of the manubrium.
Anterior jugular vein crosses deep to it.
It is related superficially to the external jugular vein.
Lesser occipital nerve runs along its posterior border.
It is supplied by spinal part of accessory nerve.

text: As regards investing layer of deep cervical fascia, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia lies deep to the platysma, splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, forms the roof of the posterior triangle, and surrounds the submandibular and parotid glands. The sphenomandibular ligament, however, is an accessory ligament of the temporomandibular joint derived from Meckel's cartilage ( cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch), NOT from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament is from Meckel's cartilage, NOT from investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
options: It forms roof of posterior triangle of neck.
It is thickened to form Sphenomandibular ligament.

text: As regards submental triangle, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The submental triangle is bounded on each side by the ANTERIOR bellies of the digastric muscles (not posterior bellies), with the base formed by the hyoid bone and the apex at the symphysis menti of the mandible. It contains the submental lymph nodes and the facial artery. Since the boundary should be anterior bellies, stating posterior bellies is incorrect.
keyConcept: Submental triangle is bounded by anterior bellies of digastric, NOT posterior bellies.
options: Its base is formed by hyoid bone.
It is bounded on each side by posterior belly of digastric.
Its apex is formed by symphysis menti.
It contains the beginning of anterior jugular vein.

text: The posterior triangle of the neck
explanation: The posterior triangle is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, and clavicle (not mandible); it is roofed by the superficial fascia and prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
keyConcept: Posterior triangle boundaries and roof
options: Is bordered by sternocleidomastoid, mandible and trapezius
Has the accessory nerve beneath fascia of its floor
Is roofed by prevertebral layer of fascia
Contains trunks of the brachial plexus

text: The vein running along the roof of the posterior triangle of the neck drains into which vein?
explanation: The external jugular vein drains the posterior triangle of the neck and empties into the subclavian vein (or sometimes the internal jugular vein at the root of the neck).
keyConcept: External jugular vein drains posterior triangle and joins subclavian vein.

text: Which nerve provides cutaneous innervation to the skin overlying the angle of the mandible?
explanation: The great auricular nerve (from C2-C3 cervical plexus) provides cutaneous innervation to the skin overlying the angle of the mandible and parotid region.
keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies sensation over the mandibular angle and parotid area.

text: Regarding accessory nerve: the following statements are true Except:
explanation: The accessory nerve is a motor nerve. Its cranial part takes origin near the nucleus ambiguus but is distinct from it. Its spinal part runs between the investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia in the posterior triangle. The cranial part joins the vagus. However, the accessory nerve (both roots) does NOT emerge at the groove between the pyramid and the olive—that is the exit site of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The accessory nerve emerges lateral to the olive in the postolivary sulcus.

options: It is a purely motor nerve.
Its cranial part takes origin from the nucleus ambiguus.
It emerges at the groove between pyramid and olive.
Its spinal part runs between investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia.
Its cranial part joins the vagus.

text: The structure derived from the intermaxillary segment is the:
explanation: The intermaxillary segment (also called the primary palate) is formed by the fusion of the two medial nasal prominences. options: Lateral part of the upper lip.
Lateral part of the lower lip.

arise from pons in brain stem
