text: The corticospinal tract in the spinal cord is located in which funiculus?
explanation: The corticospinal tract is located primarily in the lateral funiculus (about 85% of fibers), with the remaining fibers traveling in the anterior funiculus as the anterior corticospinal tract.
keyConcept: Corticospinal tract: mainly lateral funiculus, some in anterior funiculus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: As regards pathway of fine touch, choose the CORRECT statement:
explanation: Fine touch pathway: 1st neuron (dorsal root ganglion) ascends in dorsal columns to gracile/cuneate nuclei; 2nd neuron decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in medial lemniscus (not spinal lemniscus) to VPL (not VPM) of thalamus.
keyConcept: Fine touch uses medial lemniscus, not spinal lemniscus
options: Its 1st neuron terminates in posterior horn of spinal cord.
Its 2nd neuron form external arcuate fibers.
Its fibers ascend in brain stem within spinal lemniscus.
VPMN of thalamus forms its 3rd neuron.
Its fibers pass through posterior limb of internal capsule.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: First order neuron in pain, temperature from head face is .............. while second order neuron is ..........
explanation: Pain and temperature from the face: first order neurons are in the trigeminal (spinal) nucleus, second order are in the spinal trigeminal nucleus that projects to the thalamus.
keyConcept: Facial pain pathway
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
explanation: The cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei such as the basal ganglia and thalamus. In the spinal cord, grey matter is central and H-shaped. The brainstem has grey matter surrounded by white matter, and the cerebellar cortex is grey matter externally.
keyConcept: Cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei; spinal cord grey matter is central, white matter peripheral
options: In spinal cord, white matter is H-shaped.
In brain stem, white matter surrounds grey matter.
Cerebral hemispheres contain deep nuclei formed of grey matter.
In cerebellum, white matter forms the outer cortex.
In spinal cord, grey matter surrounds white matter.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of which veins?
explanation: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which drain the deep brain structures including the basal ganglia and thalamus.
keyConcept: Vein of Galen forms from union of internal cerebral veins draining deep brain structures.
options: Right and left internal cerebral veins
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Anterior external arcuate fibres relay in:
explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the arcuate nucleus of the opposite side before projecting to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate relay
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The reticular activating system (RAS) is best described by which statement?
explanation: The RAS receives sensory input from proprioceptors and various sensory modalities to maintain cortical arousal and alertness.
keyConcept: Reticular activating system
options: Its neurons are located only in the medulla oblongata.
Its neurons can be activated by sensory signals from proprioceptors.
Its activity is decreased by stress.
It discharges inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Which tract continues as the neospinothalamic pathway carrying pain and temperature sensations to the thalamus?
explanation: The neospinothalamic tract carries fast, sharp pain and temperature via lateral spinothalamic fibers. It ascends through the brainstem and terminates in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamic nucleus.
keyConcept: Neospinothalamic tract conveys rapid, well-localized pain via direct pathway to thalamus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The inferior petrosal sinus connects the cavernous sinus with the:
explanation: The cavernous part of the internal carotid artery gives off the inferolateral (暴发性) trunk and meningohypophyseal trunk branches, which supply the dura and pituitary gland.
keyConcept: Cavernous ICA gives meningohypophyseal trunk
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: The floor of the body of the lateral ventricle is formed by all the following EXCEPT:
explanation: The floor of the lateral ventricle body is formed by the thalamus, body of caudate nucleus, and body of fornix; the tail of caudate lies in the roof of the inferior horn, not the floor.
keyConcept: Tail of caudate nucleus: in roof of inferior horn, not floor of body.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: anatomy

text: Rigidity is characterized by:
explanation: Rigidity is characterized by increased tone in antigravity muscles. Option A is correct. Rigidity (both lead-pipe and cogwheel) particularly affects anti-gravity muscles due to exaggerated extensor activity. Options B, C, D, E are incorrect: gamma cell hyperactivity alone doesn't cause rigidity; rigidity occurs in UMN lesions (not just associated); static tremors are Parkinsonian; circumduction gait is UMN, not rigidity.
keyConcept: Rigidity preferentially affects antigravity muscles, reflecting the dominance of extensor muscles in human posture.
options: Due to increase gamma cells activities.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Concerning learning:
explanation: Sensitization occurs by presynaptic facilitation of sensory neurons. Habituation involves decreased synaptic transmission (not increased calcium) due to less neurotransmitter release. Operant conditioning uses reinforcement, not neutral stimuli. Classical conditioning pairs unconditioned and conditioned stimuli. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant.
keyConcept: Habituation: decreased response to repeated benign stimulus. Sensitization: enhanced response via presynaptic facilitation.
options: Habituation is due to increase intracellular calcium leading to augmented response.
Operant conditioning occurs by inducing a response to a neutral stimulus.
Classical conditioning occurs by stimulation of reward and punishment centers.
-ve operant conditioning means adding of something to induce learning of a specific task or behavior
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Parkinson,s disease causes:
explanation: Parkinson's disease causes increased resistance throughout range of movement. Option B is correct. Lead-pipe rigidity is constant resistance throughout passive movement range. Options A, C, D are wrong: no paralysis in Parkinsonism; decreased (not increased) facial movements; tremors are at rest (not during movements).
keyConcept: Parkinsonian lead-pipe rigidity shows constant resistance throughout the full range of passive movement.
options: Increased resistance throughout the range of movement.
Tremors, which are obvious during movements.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: lesion of motor area 6 causes:
explanation: Lesion of motor area 6 causes increased muscle tone. Option A is correct. Premotor area 6 has connections with basal ganglia and brainstem motor areas; lesions cause release of extensor tone (rigidity). Option B is wrong (paralysis is area 4 lesion). Option C is wrong (loss of fine movements is area 4). Option D is wrong (positive Babinski with dorsiflexion is corticospinal). Option E is wrong (inhibition of grasp reflex is not expected).
keyConcept: Premotor area 6 lesions release extensor muscle tone due to loss of indirect pathway modulation.
options: Positive Babeniski’s sign with dorsiflexion of the big toe.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: Babinski sign is NOT present in:
explanation: Babinski sign is characteristically absent in extrapyramidal lesions (like Parkinson's) because these affect the basal ganglia, not the corticospinal tracts. It IS present in pyramidal (UMN) lesions, deep sleep, and coma.
keyConcept: Babinski: UMN lesion (+), Extrapyramidal lesion (-), LMN lesion (-), normal infant (-).
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: In memory:
explanation: Episodic memory (remembering events) is stored in hippocampus and neocortex. Explicit memory IS conscious recall (not implicit). Implicit memory includes priming and procedural memory stored in basal ganglia/cerebellum. Semantic memory is general knowledge, not events.
keyConcept: Explicit/declarative: conscious, hippocampus/neocortex. Implicit/non-declarative: unconscious, basal ganglia/cerebellum.
options: Implicit memory is the conscious recall of information.
Explicit memory is stored in basal ganglia and cerebellum.
Explicit memory types include priming and procedural memory.
Episodic memory is stored in the hippocampus and neocortex.
Semantic memory is the recall of events and experiences.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: The reticular formation is responsible for:
explanation: The reticular formation in the brainstem regulates arousal, sleep-wake cycles, and consciousness through ascending reticular activating system projections to the thalamus and cortex.
keyConcept: Reticular formation maintains consciousness and sleep-arousal cycles via diffuse subcortical projections.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: β waves of EEG are:
explanation: Beta waves are faster than alpha (13-30 Hz vs 8-13 Hz) and are recorded during alert, active states, not in relaxed or sleeping states. They disappear (replaced by alpha) when a person relaxes with eyes closed. They are NOT character of relaxed awake state, children, or paradoxical sleep.
keyConcept: Beta waves: alert/active mental state, faster than alpha, low voltage, desynchronized.
options: Faster than α waves, but slower than δ waves.
Disappear when the person becomes alert.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text:
A wife came to the doctor, and complained that her husband talks during his sleep, and that frightens her, the doctor explained that:
A. This is normal in REM sleep
B. She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
C. Teeth grinding is expected to happen
D. She can easily wake him up
E. This probably happens a lot near the morning
explanation: Sleep talking occurs during REM sleep when motor inhibition prevents dream enactment, but the person is difficult to wake from this stage; they typically won't remember the dream.
keyConcept: Sleep talking occurs in REM; difficult to wake, no dream recall.
options: This is normal in REM sleep
She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
Teeth grinding is expected to happen
She can easily wake him up
This probably happens a lot near the morning
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: physiology

text: The clinical picture of classic phenylketonuria results from deficiency of
explanation: Classic PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine deficiency (tyrosine is an essential dietary requirement in PKU).
keyConcept: PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine scarcity
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: biochem

text: Which of the following statements is correct about folate requirement?
explanation: Folate requirement is 300-400 mcg/day, nearly doubles in the third trimester (400-800 mcg), and is present in leafy vegetables, yeast, and liver. All statements are correct.
keyConcept: Folate: 300-400 mcg/day requirement, doubled in pregnancy, found in leafy vegetables
options: Folic acid requirement is about 300-400 μg/day.
The need for folate nearly doubles by the third trimester of pregnancy.
Folic acid is present primarily in leafy vegetables; in addition to yeast and liver.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: biochem

text: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the ARCUATE NUCLEUS (not the cuneate nucleus which projects to cerebellum via dorsal external arcuate fibers). The arcuate nucleus receives corticofugal fibers and projects to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate: from arcuate nucleus → cerebellum (via ICP). Dorsal external arcuate: from accessory cuneate → cerebellum.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: histology

text: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system due to its connections with:
explanation: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system, and the reticular formation modulates hypothalamic function.
keyConcept: Reticular formation → hypothalamus → pituitary → endocrine control. RF also influences autonomic functions via hypothalamus.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: histology

text: Arcuate nucleus is found in:
explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found ventral to the pyramids in the medulla. It is a small nucleus that gives rise to some of the ventral external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus found ventral to pyramids in medulla
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: histology

text: Tanycytes line which of the following:
explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the third ventricle and other ventricular surfaces, particularly in the hypothalamus. They have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and are involved in neuroendocrine regulation.
keyConcept: Tanycytes: specialized ependymal cells lining 3rd ventricle, transport molecules between brain and CSF.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: histology

text: The following is not an adverse effect of BZDS
explanation: Decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal is NOT an adverse effect - it is a withdrawal effect. Option B is incorrect. Insomnia and REM rebound occur on withdrawal, not as direct adverse effects during use. Options A, C, D are correct direct adverse effects: sedation/hangover, cognitive impairment, tolerance/dependence.
keyConcept: Benzodiazepine withdrawal causes REM rebound insomnia; direct adverse effects include sedation, cognitive impairment, and dependence.
options: Insomnia & decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal
Decrease in cognitive function of the brain
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: pharma

text: What is the term for small infarcts in deep non-cortical white matter or the brainstem that result from the occlusion of penetrating branches of cerebral arteries?
explanation: Lacunar infarcts are small deep infarcts in penetrating artery territories causing 'lacunes.' They result from lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries. These small vessel strokes affect basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons. Option A is CORRECT. They differ from cortical infarcts (B) which affect the cortex. The answer is A. Lacunar strokes are associated with hypertension and diabetes.
keyConcept: Lacunar infarcts are small, deep infarcts from lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries - associated with hypertension.
chapter: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy
subject: pathology

text: The spinal dura extends from the level of the foramen magnum to the level of which vertebra?
explanation: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Below this, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament.
keyConcept: Spinal dura extends from foramen magnum to S2
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Astereognosis & receptive aphasia characterize lesions in:
explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and receptive aphasia (inability to understand language) are both features of dominant parietal lobe lesions, particularly involving the angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus.
keyConcept: Dominant parietal lobe lesions cause astereognosis
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: A patient develops behavioral changes and wears inappropriate clothing after an accident affecting frontal bone. Which cortical area is affected?
explanation: The orbitofrontal cortex (ventromedial prefrontal cortex) is associated with personality, social behavior, and impulse control. Damage causes disinhibition, inappropriate social conduct, and lack of insight.
keyConcept: Orbitofrontal lesions cause personality changes and social disinhibition due to impaired impulse control.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: A 28-year-old man sustains a head injury. After recovery, his family reports marked personality change. Which area is affected?
explanation: Damage to the frontal lobe can cause personality changes, poor judgment, and inappropriate social behavior (pseudopendulous swinging describes cerebellar ataxia, not frontal lobe damage).
keyConcept: Frontal lobe damage causes executive dysfunction and behavioral changes rather than primary motor deficits.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following best describes the condition of unilateral inattention (neglect)?
explanation: Unilateral neglect syndrome involves ignoring stimuli from the contralateral side, often manifesting as failure to dress or groom that side, typically caused by right parietal lobe lesions.
keyConcept: Neglect: ignoring contralateral stimuli, often with dressing/grooming deficits on that side.
options: Loss of all sensation on one side of the body
Ignoring stimuli from the opposite side, often with failure to dress or shave that side
Loss of proprioception with preserved touch
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The dural fold which is attached to the skull vault is:
explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Parietal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following Except:
explanation: Facial recognition is processed in the inferior temporal lobe (fusiform gyrus), not the parietal lobe. The parietal lobe is concerned with stereognosis, proprioception, and spatial processing.
keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal, not parietal lobe
options: Comprehension of received auditory & visual information.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Cortical areas in temporal lobe include all the following Except:
explanation: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral eye movements is the occipital eye field (area 18), not the temporal lobe. The temporal lobe contains auditory areas and parts of Wernicke's area and facial recognition area.
keyConcept: Involuntary eye movement control is occipital, not temporal
options: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral movements of eye.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Greater wing of sphenoid shows:
explanation: The greater wing of the sphenoid bone shows the foramen rotundum (transmitting maxillary nerve from middle cranial fossa to pterygopalatine fossa), as well as the superior orbital fissure, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum. The hypoglossal canal, mastoid foramen, sigmoid sinus, and carotid canal are features of the occipital and temporal bones, not the greater wing of sphenoid.
keyConcept: Foramen rotundum is in the greater wing of sphenoid; transmits maxillary nerve (CN V2) to pterygopalatine fossa.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle. The facial motor nucleus is more lateral, and the hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla.
keyConcept: Abducent nucleus: floor of 4th ventricle, lower pons, near midline; supplies lateral rectus.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: All the following venous sinuses lie between outer (endosteal) & inner (meningeal) layers of dura EXCEPT:
explanation: The cavernous sinus is located between the meningeal and endosteal layers of dura in the middle cranial fossa. It is NOT between the layers of the falx cerebri, which contains the sagittal sinuses.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus between meningeal layers in middle fossa
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Infection from dangerous area of face may be transmitted to the following venous sinus:
explanation: Infection from dangerous area of face (upper lip, nose, orbit) may spread via facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus.选项E正确. The answer is E. This is why facial infections can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.
keyConcept: Facial vein connects to cavernous sinus via angular and superior ophthalmic veins - spread route for infection.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Blood brain barrier is formed of tight junctions between:
explanation: The blood-brain barrier uses tight junctions between non-fenestrated (continuous) capillary endothelial cells, unlike fenestrated endothelium elsewhere.
keyConcept: BBB tight junctions
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following is a recess of the fourth ventricle?
explanation: The lateral recess is the only true recess of the fourth ventricle. It extends laterally beneath the superior cerebellar peduncle and opens at the foramen of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
keyConcept: Lateral recess is a recess of fourth ventricle
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which of the following structures forms the roof of the fourth ventricle?
explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle consists of the superior cerebellar peduncles laterally and the tela choroidea with choroid plexus inferiorly. The floor is formed by the pons and upper medulla.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof comprises cerebellar peduncles and tela choroidea with choroid plexus.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in its:
explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in the inferior roof (posterior medullary velum), not the floor or superior roof.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Leptomeninges refer to the:
explanation: The leptomeninges consist of the pia mater and arachnoid mater. The dura mater is the outer meningeal layer and is not part of the leptomeninges.
keyConcept: Leptomeninges = pia + arachnoid mater
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Regarding cerebrospinal fluid (C.S.F.) all statements are true Except:
explanation: CSF reaches the cisterna magna via the foramen of Magendie (fourth ventricle directly to subarachnoid space), NOT through the aqueduct of Sylvius (which connects third and fourth ventricles).
keyConcept: CSF pathway to cisternamagna
options: Is formed by choroid plexuses of ventricles
Reaches cisternamagna through the aqueduct of Sylvius
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: Which dural venous sinus is a paired structure?
explanation: The transverse sinus and sigmoid sinus are paired structures (one on each side). The straight sinus and superior sagittal sinus are unpaired midline structures.
keyConcept: Transverse and sigmoid sinuses are paired lateral structures; sagittal and straight sinuses are midline unpaired.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The blood‑CSF barrier is NOT formed by:
explanation: The blood-CSF barrier uses fenestrated endothelial cells (allowing passage) and is NOT formed by astrocyte foot processes (those form the BBB).
keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier components
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junctions
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The lateral ventricles are connected to the third ventricle via:
explanation: The interventricular foramina of Monro connect each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing CSF flow between these chambers.
keyConcept: Lateral to third ventricle: interventricular foramina of Monro.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: anatomy

text: The apical surface of ependymal Cells has:
explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the brain-CSF barrier, limiting passage between ventricles and brain parenchyma. The blood-brain barrier involves astrocyte foot processes and tight junction endothelial cells.
keyConcept: Ependymal tight junctions = brain-CSF barrier. Astrocyte foot processes + endothelial tight junctions = blood-brain barrier.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: histology

text: The primary role of amygdala in memory is:
explanation: The amygdala processes the emotional significance of memories (fear conditioning, emotional tagging) but does not store semantic memory, initiate synaptic changes, or handle short-term memory operation. The hippocampus handles consolidation and storage.
keyConcept: Amygdala: emotional component of memory (fear, emotional tagging). Hippocampus: consolidation and declarative memory.
options: Processing and remembering the emotional component of memories.
Initiation of synaptic changes needed for memory storage.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: physiology

text: Which sentence is NOT true regarding consolidation of memory?
explanation: Memory consolidation takes hours to days, not minutes. It involves structural and functional synaptic changes in the hippocampus initially, then neocortical storage. Focused attention and rehearsal enhance consolidation efficiency.
keyConcept: Consolidation is a gradual process requiring hours to days for stable long-term memory formation.
options: It is the conversion of short-term memory to a long-term one.
It represents the time needed for the structural and functional synaptic changes to take place.
It increases and fastens by focusing and rehearsal.
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: physiology

text: What is L-Dopa?
explanation: L-Dopa is levodopa, the metabolic precursor of dopamine that crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is converted to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA decarboxylase) in the brain and periphery.选项A正确. The answer is A. L-dopa is combined with carbidopa (a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor) to reduce peripheral side effects and increase CNS delivery.
keyConcept: Levodopa is a dopamine precursor that crosses the BBB - converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase in the brain.
options: A dopamine precursor that can cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB)
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: pharma

text: Brain cells uptake glucose by
explanation: Brain cells uptake glucose via GLUT1 (blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (neurons); GLUT2 is in liver/pancreas, GLUT4 is insulin-dependent in muscle/adipose.
keyConcept: Brain glucose transporters
chapter: Cerebrum, Meninges and Higher Brain Function
subject: biochem

text: The vaccine used for protection against tetanus consists of:
explanation: Tetanus vaccine contains inactivated tetanus toxin (toxoid) that stimulates antibody production without causing disease.
keyConcept: Tetanus vaccine
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: anatomy

text: Cerebellar brain abscess is usually a complication of:
explanation: Cerebellar abscess commonly complicates chronic suppurative otitis media due to direct spread of infection from the middle ear through the tegmen tympani.
keyConcept: Cerebellar abscess etiology
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: pathology

text: colony of Cryptococcus neoformans is………while colony N. meningitides is
explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans colony: creamy, mucoid, tan-colored colonies on Sabouraud dextrose agar. The polysaccharide capsule gives it a mucoid appearance. Neisseria meningitidis colony: smooth, moist, translucent colonies - it does NOT have the mucoid appearance of Cryptococcus. Option A states 'creamy mucoid (Cryptococcus), smooth (N. meningitidis)' - this is correct. The answer is A. N. meningitidis forms greyish, transparent, smooth colonies, while Cryptococcus has the characteristic mucoid appearance due to its capsule.
keyConcept: Cryptococcus colonies are creamy-mucoid; N. meningitidis colonies are smooth - differentiating these two organisms.
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text: Pathogenic Neisseria are characterized by:
explanation: Pathogenic Neisseria (N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis) characteristics: B) Grow on chocolate agar - TRUE (requires chocolate agar enriched with factor V (NAD) and factor X (hemin)); A) Grow on ordinary media - FALSE (requires enriched media); C) Grow at room temperature - FALSE (grow best at 35-37°C, not room temp); D) Oxidase-negative - FALSE (Neisseria are oxidase POSITIVE). The answer is B - chocolate agar provides the nutrients (X and V factors) that Neisseria need for growth.
keyConcept: Neisseria require chocolate agar (enriched with X and V factors) and are oxidase-positive - they don't grow on ordinary media.
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text: A neonate was delivered 3 weeks prematurely.
explanation: Premature neonate (delivered 3 weeks early): Listeria monocytogenes can be transmitted in utero (late pregnancy) leading to congenital infection, or during passage through birth canal. The timing of maternal infection determines transmission route. In utero infection (early in pregnancy) causes more severe anomalies; late pregnancy/delivery causes neonatal sepsis/meningitis. A 3-week premature delivery suggests late-pregnancy transmission. The answer is B - in utero transmission late in pregnancy or during delivery. Listeria can cross the placenta causing fetal infection, presenting as preterm labor or neonatal sepsis.
keyConcept: Listeria monocytogenes transmission to neonates occurs via in utero infection (late pregnancy) or during passage through infected birth canal.
options: In utero transmission early in pregnancy
In utero transmission late in pregnancy
Droplet transmission from anterior nares of health care providers
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text: How can the presence of toxin be detected in botulism?
explanation: Botulinum toxin detection: mouse bioassay (inoculate patient serum/feces into mice - death indicates toxin), PCR for organism, culture.选项D正确. The answer is D. Toxin blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction.
keyConcept: Botulism diagnosis: mouse bioassay detects toxin - blocks ACh release causing flaccid paralysis.
options: In patient blood or food remnants using PCR or ELISA
Isolation of Clostridium botulinum from food
chapter: Infections Affecting Muscle Tone and Nervous System
subject: microbiology

text:
Post exposure Vaccination is successful in rabies because 

A) The virus is weak. 
B) The vaccine is potent.
C) The incubatory period is long. 
D) All of the above
explanation: Post-exposure vaccination works because the incubation period is long (weeks to months), allowing vaccine-induced immunity to develop before the virus reaches the CNS. A) 'Virus is weak' - incorrect; B) 'Vaccine is potent' - not the main reason; C) 'Incubatory period is long' - CORRECT. The long incubation period allows time for vaccine to generate protective antibodies. D) 'All of the above' - incorrect because A and B are wrong. The answer is C. Typical incubation: 1-3 months depending on distance from CNS and viral load.
keyConcept: Rabies vaccine succeeds because the long incubation period (weeks-months) allows vaccine-induced immunity to develop before CNS invasion.

text:
Diagnosis is of rabies in an infected animal can be done by 

A) Detection of specific antibodies in the serum 
B) Detection of Negri bodies in the brain tissue 
C) Both of them 
D) None of them
explanation: Diagnosis of rabies in an infected animal is done by detecting Negri bodies in brain tissue. Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in neurons (especially in hippocampus and Purkinje cells of cerebellum) - they contain viral nucleoproteins. A) Detection of antibodies in serum - not reliable for animal diagnosis; B) Detection of Negri bodies - CORRECT; C) Both - incorrect because serum antibodies alone aren't diagnostic. The answer is B. In humans, PCR of saliva or nuchal biopsy is preferred. Animal diagnosis typically requires brain tissue examination.
keyConcept: Negri bodies (eosinophilic inclusions in neurons) are pathognomonic for rabies in animal brain tissue.
options: Detection of specific antibodies in the serum
Detection of Negri bodies in the brain tissue

text: physical examination of fungal meningitis of CSF is/are.
explanation: Fungal meningitis CSF findings: 1) CSF may be turbid or clear (variable); 2) Protein is ELEVATED (not decreased) - Option B is WRONG; 3) Glucose may be normal or decreased (not typically normal) - but can be normal. The answer is D - none of the above correctly describe fungal meningitis. Fungal meningitis typically shows: mild elevation in protein, normal to low glucose, and lymphocytic pleocytosis. India ink or cryptococcal antigen testing is needed for diagnosis. The CSF appearance in fungal meningitis is variable but often clear initially.
keyConcept: Fungal meningitis typically shows elevated protein and normal-to-low glucose, not the patterns listed in options A, B, or C.

text: Naegleria fowleri infection is diagnosed by:
explanation: Naegleria fowleri (primary amoebic meningoencephalitis) is diagnosed by CSF examination. The CSF shows: neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose, and motile trophozoites visible on wet mount. Skin biopsy (A) is not useful. Stool examination (B) is for intestinal parasites. The answer is C - CSF examination. The characteristic 'ameba' can be seen moving in fresh CSF. This is a fatal infection from water exposure.
keyConcept: Naegleria fowleri is diagnosed by visualizing motile trophozoites in CSF - it's a medical emergency.

Lumbar puncture follows if no contraindications. The answer is A. Every hour of delay increases mortality.

text: Which of the following best describes the gate control theory of pain?
explanation: The gate control theory proposes that large myelinated afferent fibers (touch) can inhibit transmission of pain signals in the dorsal horn through interneurons, effectively 'closing the gate' on pain perception.
keyConcept: Gate control: large afferent fiber activity inhibits dorsal horn pain transmission.
options: Pain is transmitted only by large myelinated fibres.
Activity in large afferent fibres can inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
Pain is solely a cortical phenomenon.
Endorphins are released only from the pituitary.

text: Regarding the hypothalamus:
explanation: Heat gain center is in the POSTERIOR hypothalamus (not anterior). Anterior hypothalamus is for heat loss. Satiety center (ventromedial) does not have intrinsic activity - it responds to signals. Suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythms, not body activities synchronization in that context.
keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: heat loss. Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain. Ventromedial: satiety. Lateral: feeding.
options: Heat gain center is present in the anterior hypothalamus.
Ventromedial nuclei synchronize body activities according to dark-light cycles.
Posterior hypothalamus function as a sleep center.
Anterior hypothalamic nuclei play a role in all of sleep, heat loss, parasympathetic activity and sexual drive.

text: What is the most common cause of cerebral infarction?
explanation: The most common cause of cerebral infarction is arterial occlusion from thrombi or emboli. Thrombosis typically occurs at atherosclerotic plaques in large arteries; emboli usually arise from carotid plaque, cardiac sources (atrial fibrillation, valve vegetations), or aortic arch. Option A is CORRECT. Venous occlusion (B) is less common. Cerebral vasculitis (C) and Moyamoya (D) are uncommon causes. The answer is A. Cardioembolic and large vessel atherosclerotic strokes are most common.
keyConcept: Arterial thrombi/emboli causing large vessel occlusion are the most common cause of cerebral infarction.
options: Arterial occlusion of the cerebral arteries by either thrombi or emboli

text: What causes lacunar infarcts?
explanation: Lacunar infarcts are caused by occlusion of penetrating branches of cerebral arteries (lenticulostriate arteries, etc.). Small vessel disease from lipohyalinosis and fibrinoid necrosis leads to these occlusions. Option A is CORRECT. Large artery occlusion (B) causes larger cortical strokes. Vasculitis (C) and emboli (D) cause different stroke types. The answer is A. Lacunes are associated with chronic hypertension.
keyConcept: Lacunar infarcts result from small penetrating artery occlusion due to lipohyalinosis, commonly from hypertension.
options: Occlusion of penetrating branches of cerebral arteries

text: What is the clinical course of Multiple Sclerosis?
explanation: Multiple sclerosis typically follows a relapsing-remitting course: episodes of neurological dysfunction (relapses) followed by partial or complete recovery (remissions). Over time, deficits accumulate. Option A is CORRECT. Primary progressive MS (B) occurs in ~10-15% but the classic course is relapsing-remitting. Complete recovery (C) doesn't occur - there's typically residual deficit. The answer is A. Most patients eventually transition to secondary progressive MS.
keyConcept: MS follows a relapsing-remitting course with accumulated deficits over time - distinguishing it from other conditions.
options: Relapsing and remitting episodes of neurologic impairment with gradual accumulation of deficits over time.

text: Contents of interpeduncular fossa belong to:

text: Which of the following arteries supplies the midbrain?
explanation: The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and its branches, including the posterior communicating artery. The basilar artery supplies the upper midbrain through its superior cerebellar artery branch.

text: As regards intracranial part of internal carotid artery, choose the INCORRECT statement:
explanation: The intracranial internal carotid artery has four parts: cervical, petrous, cavernous, and cerebral. The petrous part enters through the carotid canal and supplies the middle ear. However, the internal carotid does NOT end opposite the posterior perforated substance; the posterior perforated substance is related to the posterior cerebral artery, not the ICA terminal bifurcation.

text: The nucleus ambiguus does not supply the following muscle(s):
